Name: Alon Amit
Question: If prime numbers thin out tremendously the higher you go, but even numbers remain every other number til infinity, how can the Binary Goldbach Conjecture possibly be true? Aren't there too few prime pairs to go around?
Answer: Prime numbers don’t thin out “tremendously”. They thin out gently and quietly. Suppose that the density of primes was always 1%. Always. Meaning, roughly every 100th number was prime. In that case you would say that the primes don’t thin out at all. Right? Sure, they are pretty sparse, but their sparseness never drops one bit – it’s steady, forever. This isn’t actually the case, of course. The density of primes eventually drops below 1%. But do you know how far you have to go until this happens? Up until around 26881171418161354484126255515800135873600000 , give or take. In contrast, the sequence 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 of powers of 2 drops below 1% right around 100 . This sequence thins out geometrically, which you may call “tremendously” if you like. The primes do nothing even close to that. They thin out… but very, very, very slowly. And in fact, as Nathan showed, this gentle thinning does the exact opposite of what you’re proposing: it makes the Goldbach Conjecture fantastically likely. Once you’ve checked GC for the first, oh, I don’t know, 100,000 numbers, you can virtually stop checking. Larger numbers are ridiculously unlikely to fail the GC conjecture. (…)

Question: Suppose that you have a black box that solves the halting problem: when queried with M and x, the black box tells you whether M(x) halts or not. Assuming this, give an algorithm (using the black box 1 time) that solves Collatz Conjecture?
Answer: You can’t do that. You can write a simple program L which requires no input, and searches for closed loops under the Collatz map. Keep a set of Collatz paths and, at each iteration, advance all paths one step forward, and start a new path at the smallest integer not yet visited. Stop when you identify a closed loop that’s not 1 , 4 , 2 , 1 . Feed L to the halting oracle. If the oracle says L halts, we know that the Collatz conjecture is false: there’s a closed loop other than the trivial one. If the oracle says the program never halts, we know that there isn’t… …but that doesn’t solve Collatz. We still don’t know if there’s an infinite path: a starting value which, upon iterating the Collatz map, keep growing forever, never looping. Determining if there is or isn’t such an infinite path is not something you can solve with a mere halting oracle. The reason is that the assertion that there’s no such infinite path sits at the second level of the arithmetic hierarchy, not the first. For each starting value, you can use an oracle to determine if the path starting at that value does or doesn’t lead to a loop, but you can’t ask an oracle if all of these programs halt: you need a second-level oracle which can determine if a program that calls a halting oracle ever halts. In terms of the arithmetic hierarchy, we are at Σ 2 . In terms of the Turing hierarchy, we are at 0 ′′ rather than merely 0 ′ . It is possible, of course, that there is a proof of the Collatz conjecture, in which case we can solve it with no oracles at all. It’s also possible that someone will present a Σ 1 sentence that’s equivalent to the Collatz conjecture, and at that point we could use a halting oracle to resolve it. But as things stand now, you can’t settle Collatz with an oracle for the halting problem. Added later: the question is phrased like an exercise from a textbook or course. If that’s the case, that source is misguided. The task is not feasible, and the source is of somewhat suspect quality. If I had to guess the root of the misunderstanding, it may be lack of clarity of what “the halting problem” is, exactly. An oracle for the halting problem is supposed to answer correctly the halting question for ordinary programs: Turing machines. It’s not supposed to solve the halting question for programs which themselves have the ability to consult with halting oracles. That’s the whole point of the Turing Jump. The question doesn’t specify what “M” is, exactly. The correct interpretation is that M is a Turing machine, and that’s probably why it’s called “M”, and if so, that’s fine, but the question is wrong. If M is somehow supposed to represent programs with access to a halting oracle, then the question is solvable, but that’s not the correct meaning of the term “black box that solves the halting problem”. Nicolò Bonacorsi, where’s the question taken from? (…)

Question: If f is continuous, do we have that the sum over all rational numbers of f(q) is proportional to the integral from minus infinity to infinity of f(x) dx?
Answer: Not at all. Take the simplest example on [ 0 , 1 ] instead of the whole real line: f ( x ) = 1 . The integral is 1 , but the values f ( q ) for q ∈ Q are all 1 , so if you try to add them up (there are infinitely many of them) you’ll get ∞ . If anything, an integral is approximated by (not “proportional to”) a sequence of values f ( a n ) for a discrete sequence a 1 < a 2 < a 3 < … , each value multiplied by the length of the gap a n + 1 − a n . The rational numbers are not a discrete sequence of sampling points. If you know f ( q ) for every rational q you can compute such Riemann sums by choosing various discrete sequences for q , but not by adding up all the values f ( q ) . That never works. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: What will we do once the seven Millennium Prize problems have been solved?
Answer: If “we” refers to research mathematicians, they will continue to do just what they are doing today: explore any of a thousand other open problems, create theories, build connections, and generally do anything that counts as mathematical research. In fact, the solution to any of the Millennium Problems will very likely open up new directions for research and fantastic new ideas to explore. The Millennium Prize Problem do not represent the totality of things mathematicians are interested in, and in fact I would say they do not cover even 1% of the things mathematicians are interested in. Though many mathematicians are working in areas related to one of the problems, very few are working directly on any of those problems, though everyone wold be happy to come up with an idea for how to make progress on them. If “we” refers to everyone else, I think we will also continue to do exactly what we are doing today, for better or worse. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: Does a general method exist for verifying whether a property is topological, i.e., invariant under homeomorphism?
Answer: No. It’s very easy if the property in question is defined purely in terms of the topology – open sets, closed sets, interior, density and so on. Such properties are certainly topological. But it does happen that something is defined using more elaborate structures, and then confirming invariance under homeomorphisms can be easy, hard, unknown to this day and anything in between. A typical example is simplicial homology. It is often the first example of a homology theory encountered by students, and it is nicely concrete and combinatorial. However, to get going it needs you to triangulate your space, and it’s not at all obvious that different triangulations will lead to the same homology. It was believed at one point that any two triangulations of the same space can be refined to a common triangulation, which would immediately imply the invariance of simplicial homology groups. But this is simply false. The simplicial homology groups are invariant, but not because common refinements must exist. To tie this back to your question: one can define a property of a topological space such as “the second simplicial homology group is Z ⊕ Z ”, defined as “pick a triangulation, and then look at the two-dimensional skeleton, and do this and that…” This property turns out to be topological, but not because you apply some general machinery that checks if things are topological. You need to work specifically on this particular property and prove that homeomorphic spaces, with whatever triangulations, yield the same answer. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: If two topologies are equivalent, does one carry all the properties of the other? This question seems tricky for me.
Answer: “Equivalence” is not a commonly used term for a relation among topologies. You may mean that two topological spaces are homeomorphic, or that two topologies on the same space are equal. In both cases, yes, any topological property holds for one if and only if it holds for the other. I can’t tell why the question seems tricky to you. Topological properties are described purely in terms of the topology of a space, and it follows that if such topologies are in one-to-one correspondence with each other, any such property will hold or not for both. Any other property may or may not be the same. For example, the lines in the plane described by x = 0 and y = 0 , with their induced topologies, are homeomorphic. Once you’ve shown that one of them is connected, you know that the other is, too. Once you’ve shown that one of them isn’t compact, the other one isn’t either. Being connected or being compact are topological properties. However, if you introduce the non-topological notion of “being horizontal” then the line y = 0 is that, while x = 0 is not. Similarly, y = 0 is the graph of a function while x = 0 isn’t. These properties aren’t topological, so there’s no reason to expect that they will carry from one space to another homeomorphic to it. Question: For fixed n, are there infinitely many integer solutions to x^n+y^n+1=z^n?
Answer: Sure (at least when n is odd), but that’s probably not what you meant to ask. Whenever you pose a diophantine equation you must always ask yourself if there are “obvious” solutions, and if there are, you’re likely interested in those solutions that aren’t obvious. Here, for example, if n is odd we may take ( x , y , z ) = ( k , − k , 1 ) or ( x , y , z ) = ( k , − 1 , k ) , for any integer k . This gives us infinitely many solutions, but they are not interesting. When n = 2 we have a ternary quadratic form Q ( x , y , z ) = x 2 + y 2 − z 2 and we seek to solve Q ( x , y , z ) = 1 . This is a classical subject and there are many references online and offline. Yes, there are infinitely many solutions, and they are very well understood. See here, for example. For n = 3 there are also infinitely many non-obvious solutions: ( x , y , z ) = ( 9 k 3 − 1 , 9 k 4 − 3 k , 9 k 4 ) . This infinite family is due to Mahler, and once you see it you may declare it “obvious” because it boils down to a simple polynomial identity, perhaps not materially different from k 3 + ( − 1 ) 3 + 1 = k 3 . I’m finding a bunch of solutions which aren’t of this form, but I don’t know if they come from additional infinite families or if it’s known that there are infinitely many of them. I don’t think there are any solutions at all for n ≥ 4 , and some form of the ABC conjecture probably shows that there cannot be infinitely many. See also the conjecture of Lander, Parkin and Selfridge which precludes solutions for n ≥ 5 . However I wouldn’t expect this to be solved at present. (…)

Question:
What is the largest possible radius of a circle contained in a
4
-dimensional hypercube of side length
1
?
Answer: Ah, yes, B-3 from the 2008 Putnam competition. Here’s how I (think I) approached it (to be clear: offline, not during the competition. I expect it took me something like 2 weeks of thinking on and off to solve it.) We’re in R 4 , and the nicest hypercube to work with is H = { v | − 1 ≤ v 1 , v 2 , v 3 , v 4 ≤ 1 } : the collection of 4 -vectors whose coordinates are all between − 1 and 1 . This hypercube has side length 2 , but never mind: we just need to remember to rescale our answer by a factor of 2 . This choice is just nicer because there are no fractions and the center of the cube is at the origin. A circle in R n , for any n , looks like this: there’s a center O , and some 2 -dimensional plane passing through O , and the circle is the set of vectors on that plane whose distance from O is some fixed radius r . We can find two perpendicular vectors u , v of length r on that plane (just choose an orthonormal basis and rescale it by r ), and then the circle is just the set of points O + u cos θ + v sin θ for 0 ≤ θ < 2 π . Such a circle in R 4 lies inside of H if all of these vectors have coordinates between − 1 and 1 . We may assume that the center O has non-negative coordinates (there’s no difference between this or that “octant” of the cube.) If our circle is best possible, some coordinate of O + u cos θ + v sin θ is ± 1 ; but if it’s − 1 , changing θ to − θ would make it 1 or more, because O contributes something positive (or 0 ). Therefore, zeroing out each coordinate of O keeps such a circle neatly inside H , and we might as well assume O = 0 . The optimal circle is centered at the origin, which make perfect intuitive sense. So now we just have two vectors u and v , and for each index 1 ≤ i ≤ 4 and any angle θ we have | u i cos θ + v i sin θ | ≤ 1 . In particular, this must be true for the angle θ whose cosine is u i / ( u 2 i + v 2 i ) and whose sine is v i / ( u 2 i + v 2 i ) (this is just the angle with tan θ = v i / u i ). From this particular θ we conclude that u 2 i + v 2 i ≤ 1 . Suppose, conversely, that u , v are two orthogonal, equal-length vectors in R 4 satisfying the four inequalities u 2 i + v 2 i ≤ 1 . For any angle θ and any i , consider the 2-d vectors x = ( u i , v i ) and y = ( cos θ , sin θ ) . By Cauchy-Schwartz, | u i cos θ + v i sin θ | 2 = | x ⋅ y | 2 ≤ ⟨ x , x ⟩ ⟨ y , y ⟩ = u 2 i + v 2 i ≤ 1 so, indeed, | u i cos θ + v i sin θ | ≤ 1 and the circle defined by these vectors doesn’t breach the hypercube. Conclusion: the circles contained in H are parametrized precisely by pairs of vectors u , v which are orthogonal of equal length and satisfy u 2 i + v 2 i ≤ 1 for i = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , and such a pair determines a circle of radius r with r 2 = u 2 1 + u 2 2 + u 2 3 + u 2 4 = v 2 1 + v 2 2 + v 2 3 + v 2 4 . But now, adding these equations up we find that 2 r 2 = u 2 1 + v 2 1 + u 2 2 + v 2 2 + u 2 3 + v 2 3 + u 2 4 + v 2 4 ≤ 4 or r 2 ≤ 2 , or r ≤ √ 2 , and we have an upper bound: any circle in H has radius not greater than √ 2 . Furthermore, it’s easy to find a suitable circle of just such a radius: take u = ( 1 , 1 , 0 , 0 ) and v = ( 0 , 0 , 1 , 1 ) . Those are orthogonal vectors, of the same length √ 2 , and they satisfy u 2 i + v 2 i ≤ 1 for i = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . So the largest circle in H has radius √ 2 , and the largest circle in a hypercube of edge-length 1 has radius √ 2 / 2 . ■ (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: If you were to write a topology book, what would be the chapter index? Which theorems would you absolutely include?
Answer: This isn’t the first time I’m citing Stillwell’s opening paragraph of Classical Topology and Combinatorial Group Theory: In recent years, many students have been introduced to topology in high school mathematics. Having met the Möbius band, the seven bridges of Königsberg, Euler's polyhedron formula, and knots, the student is led to expect that these picturesque ideas will come to full flower in university topology courses. What a disappointment "undergraduate topology" proves to be! In most institutions it is either a service course for analysts, on abstract spaces, or else an introduction to homological algebra in which the only geometric activity is the completion of commutative diagrams. Pictures are kept to a minimum, and at the end the student still doesn’t understand the simplest topological facts, such as the reason why knots exist. I’m bringing this up to make the same point made by Andrew Winkler in his answer: “Topology” means different things to different people, even if we’re interpreting “topology book” as “an undergrad textbook suitable for a first course on the subject”. So: if I were to write a topology book, the first question I would ask myself is – who am I writing this for? And why? And what do I mean by “topology”? Here’s the syllabus of Math 432 (Introduction to Topology) at the University of Maryland: For my taste this is actually an excellent introductory course. There’s some “abstract” point-set topology but also a whole lot of what Stillwell is advocating for, and a nice selection of very cool applications. I’m a little surprised by the inclusion of Arzelà-Ascoli; it’s an important theorem but hard to motivate without some applications that would be hard to navigate to (in complex analysis, or ODEs). Cantor sets are a little bit of an outlier here but I would submit that everyone needs to know about them, so why not. In short, this syllabus would make a nice table of contents for a topology textbook. Since a book can do more than a one-semester course I would probably add an introduction to homology and maybe cohomology, I would strengthen the combinatorial topology part with some knot theory, maybe(?) add a bit of Bass-Serre theory, and maybe also the Hopf fibration as a non-trivial example in the homotopy groups of spheres. This isn’t very coherent but it’s a lot of cool stuff. As another example, here’s the (current) syllabus of Math 144 (Introduction to Topology and Geometry) at Stanford: This is also a very nice syllabus but it has very different goals. The topology part is purely point-set, and then we move to the differentiable and smooth categories, probably to satisfy the promise of “Geometry” in the title. You can make an excellent textbook out of these headlines, too. So, short answer: I don’t know. Why am I writing a topology book? (…)

Question: For what primes is 2 a quadratic residue but 3 a quadratic non-residue?
Answer: There’s a cheap way of solving such questions, even if you don’t know or don’t remember the law of quadratic reciprocity. You do need to know one important fact: given a fixed prime q , like the 2 or 3 here, the question of whether or not q is a quadratic reside modulo some p depends only on the residue of p mod 4 q . If you want to know why, study the law of QR; but if you just want to solve this, it’s enough to rely on this as a black box, a fact. Since 24 is divisible by both 4 ⋅ 2 and 4 ⋅ 3 , we know that the answer to your question must be those primes which are some stuff mod 24 , and we just have to find that stuff. Take, for example, the prime 5 . The quadratic residues mod 5 are 1 2 = 1 and 2 2 = 4 (no need to check the rest – see why?), so 2 isn’t a QR (and neither is 3 , but never mind) and 5 is not in the set we’re looking for. But what’s more, every prime congruent to 5 mod 24 is out. We’re done with this whole residue class. What about 7 ? The QRs are 1 2 = 1 , 2 2 = 4 and 3 2 ≡ 2 , so 7 is good, and with it the whole class of primes congruent to 7 mod 24 . Next: 11 ? Here 3 is a QR because 5 2 ≡ 3 , so 11 is out. Next: 13 ? Nope, 3 is a QR again because 4 2 ≡ 3 . Next: 17 ? Aha: 2 is a QR because 6 2 ≡ 2 , but 3 isn’t as you can verify just by squaring 1 , 2 , 3 , … , 8 mod 17 . So 17 is another good one. 19 and 23 are both out ( 19 because neither 2 nor 3 are QRs, and 23 for the opposite reason), and the only residue class left to check is 1 . This is always the slightly more annoying one since 1 itself isn’t prime; we need a prime ≡ 1 ( mod 24 ) . The smallest one is 73 , so now you have two options: either square 36 numbers mod 73 and see if you ever get 3 (you do, with 21 2 ), or you do remember the law of quadratic reciprocity and so you know that ( 3 73 ) = ( 73 3 ) = ( 1 3 ) = 1 , so 3 is a QR mod 73 and the residue 1 is out. All told, you now know that 2 is a QR and 3 is a non-QR mod primes which are 7 or 17 mod 24 . For some reason there’s a whole industry of such questions on Quora, and with this method you can solve all of them with just a little bit of patience. (…)

Here, on the left we have 3 √ − 1 + α , without an α 2 . So my guess was to compute the cube ( a + b α + c α 2 ) 3 and see what needs to be true so that no α 2 remains. We don’t actually need to expand the whole thing: we only care about α 2 and α 5 = 2 α 2 . When you expand that cube (think of it as the product of three identical expressions, where you get to pick on term from each expression and multiply), you get α 2 when you choose two a 's and one c , or one a and two b 's, and you get α 5 when you pick one b and two c 's. Each of these can be done in 3 ways, so the coefficient of α 2 is 3 a 2 c + 3 a b 2 + 6 b c 2 . I want this to vanish, so I want a 2 c + a b 2 + 2 b c 2 to be 0 , and the easiest way of doing that is to make both a 2 c and a b 2 be 1 and b c 2 be − 1 , which you get by a = c = 1 , b = − 1 . Question: Is the advice to young researchers to stay away from Collatz's problem because of the risk of addiction and insanity a real warning or rather an expression of envy of possible success?
Answer: What advice to young researchers to stay away from Collatz’s problem because of the risk of addiction and insanity? Have you seen such advice? By whom? To whom? The only advice I’m aware of is friendly advice to amateurs who think it’s useful for them to attempt to solve the Collatz conjecture with no mathematical training beyond high-school. Such advice may be given by research mathematicians and a few others, such as myself. Here, let me demonstrate: If you don’t have a math degree and you think you should spend your time on the Collatz conjecture, you’re wasting your time. That’s it. It’s just advice. Don’t like it? Don’t take it. Nobody is stopping you. Nobody is limiting your access to papers and books on the subject. Nobody is looking over your shoulder to make sure you’re not scribbling Collatz-related formulas. Nobody is scared, or jealous, or worried. We’re just trying to make you aware that the fact that the problem is easy to understand doesn’t mean it has a simple solution, and in fact it does not have a simple solution. We are by now a million miles beyond the point of oh my god how could we have missed that brilliant yet simple idea that dude thought about because dude has an unspoiled mind and all of us stupid experts were stuck in our stupid expert ways. That amateur fantasy is just that. It’s the silly Disneyesque “anything is possible if you just want it hard enough.” That’s nonsense. But if you don’t want to listen – it’s your life. Knock yourself out. (…)

Question: Why do tools like Desmos convert ratios with few decimal places (e.g., 7.5/18.55) into simplified fractions but struggle to convert ratios involving more decimal places? Is it due to floating-point imprecision? (See comment for more details)
Answer: Because their designers wanted it that way. Floating-point arithmetic, typically implemented in some sort of Floating Point Unit, is a feature of many computer architectures, but that doesn’t mean programmers can’t handle fractions as integer ratios of any magnitude that fits in memory, if they so choose. Any competent programmer can do that in any language. The Desmos programmers are competent enough, yet it exhibits this behavior: Some fractions are retained as integer ratios, others are displayed as decimal approximations with no feature to convert them back to fractions. “Struggle” isn’t the right word: Desmos doesn’t struggle. Its designers simply made the conscious choice to stick to fractions only in a limited range. It’s a very common (and very reasonable) choice for engineering and scientific computation. Here’s Python: Here’s Sage: The Sage designers chose, by default, to keep fractions as fractions. Sage is meant for mathematical applications including relatively “pure” ones where losing precision is unacceptable. Python, by default, sees no need to do that – but of course, there’s a (standard) module if you need it: This just makes the point that there’s no inherent law that says you have to use floating-point arithmetic and lose accuracy. You can do whatever you want. In a comment on the question, the OP asked why don’t more systems choose to implement fractions as explicit integer ratios, with the following rationale: But my understanding is that current computational resources are sufficient to brute force that sort of computation until we start dealing with integers so large they have hundreds or even thousands of digits There’s no such thing as “sufficient to brute force that sort of computation”. Of course no modern system would struggle with 3 / 7 + 98 / 1635 , but if you need to do it a hundred million times in order to compute the stress forces on a bridge, low-level optimization starts to matter a lot – even if the fractions have numerators and denominators less than 10 6 . “Current computational resources” may, or may not, be able to handle integer arithmetic for demanding scientific tasks. Also, denominators don’t tend to stay small for long if you keep doing precise arithmetic: Here we are adding fractions with numerator 1 and 2 -digit denominators, but the result requires much larger integers. This is an easy equation to solve, for m : it is linear. Just re-arrange it, and find ( 3 − x ) m = some blah with  x  and  y We don’t, frankly, care about the blah on the right hand side because remember: x and y now are just parameters, constants. For any given x and y the stuff on the right is just some number, and there’s nothing that number can do to prevent m from existing. But something else can: that ( 3 − x ) coefficient in front of m . If it’s not zero, you can divide by it and obtain m = something, doesn’t matter what, just something. Name: Alon Amit
Question: What would happen if the first proof for Riemann hypothesis/some other major conjecture turned out to be an unreadable coq program generated by some sort of AI?
Answer: When the day comes (and it will come) that computer proof-assistants evolve into proof-discoverers and start producing formal proofs of important results, several interesting things will start happening. First of all, it’s extremely unlikely that the first such discoveries will be complete massive results like the Riemann Hypothesis. More likely, computerized proofs will be produced for lemmas and smaller results that people are interested in. With those, progress will split into 1) Some researchers will accept the lemma as true and continue building the larger structure they are working on, and 2) Others will dive into the formal proof and start to interpret and disentangle it. Coq programs, or (in my mind, more likely) Lean programs, aren’t “unreadable”. They are readable, though reading them could be difficult, and they can be very large. But even if they are, they aren’t a random jumble of assertions – as they are generated there will be intermediate steps, defined structures, and inner connections. See, for instance, the blueprint of the Lean proof of PFR that is currently in progress, and its dependency graph: Granted, this effort is human-guided, but it’s reasonable that such structures will still be there for proofs that are entirely computer-generated. They may be massive and complex, and we may need to develop separate software tools to reverse-engineer and interpret large computer-generated proofs, but there’s no reason to assume that we will be able to do absolutely nothing with a massive, unreadable Coq program. In other words, the efforts to produce human-comprehensible proofs won’t die. They will need to expand from the current methodologies to embracing the study and interpretation of computer-generated proofs. It’ll be fascinating new world, and I’m sure it’ll be different in ways large and small from anything I’m able to imagine right now. But I wouldn’t expect us to be completely stuck just faced with 1.5 petabytes of undecipherable code. (…)

Question: Problem 5 of IMO 2024 is a beautiful problem, approachable, and it does not require technique and theory to solve. What other IMO problems are like this?
Answer: EDIT: The OP clarified that the question is about “IMO problems whose solutions don't require specific formulas, techniques and knowledge beyond middle school.” I think there are such examples that don’t require formulas, though I’m less sure about “techniques” – even problems with an “elementary” solution may require considerable maturity to follow a solution. (let alone to solve.) P5 from 2024 is such a problem, kind of. The statement is elementary, and the solution does not require “formulas” or techniques like induction or maximization of a functional. It’s a tricky problem, and I’m not entirely sure I would label it “beautiful”: the solution is very surprising, in a pleasing way, but the proof is quite tedious to work through and present. If there’s interest I’m happy to explain the solution (but please ask this in a separate question). The AoPS website maintains a nice catalog of IMO problems and their solutions. Starting with 1998, the problems in the table of contents are classified into Combinatorics (C), Number Theory (N), Geometry (G) and (I think) Analysis (A). There’s also an indication of difficulty level, as in G1 is an easy geometry problem and C8 is a difficult combinatorics one. If you’re looking for “elementary” problems, your best best is Combinatorics. Analysis problems would literally never qualify, and neither would geometry unless you consider advanced Euclidean plane geometry “middle school knowledge”. Number theory would very rarely qualify, but maybe. I think going through the C problems would give you a nice list of “other IMO problems like this”. (Original answer below) “Beautiful”, “approachable” and “does not require technique” are very subjective terms. Even “theory” is fuzzy. This is P5 form IMO 2024: So when you say it’s approachable, perhaps you’re saying this because there are no formulas and technical terms. And that’s fine, but it’s misleading: it doesn’t make the problem more accessible, necessarily. And when you say it does not require theory, well, that’s true of all IMO problems, by design - they are meant to be solvable by elementary means, with no group theory or complex analysis or differential geometry. And when you say it doesn’t require technique, I’m a little baffled because I don’t know what that means. This is, I’m quite sure, not an easy question for anyone. I also think it’s very nice, though it doesn’t exactly fit my own personal taste for “beautiful”. The IMO problems are very easily accessible online, so the best advice I can give you is just scan them and see which one catches your attention – it’s really a matter of taste. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: How many everywhere dense subsets can a topological space have?
Answer: What a delightful, oddball question. I never know why some questions latch onto me and refuse to let go. This one did. (By the way, people no longer say “everywhere dense”. The common term is just “dense”. A subset of a topological space is dense if its closure is the whole space.) I don’t think the question is addressed by any of the current posted answers. The question as I see it is this: what are the possible values of n such that some topological space has precisely n dense subsets? We may also wonder about possible infinite cardinalities for n , and I’ll address that too. I spent a lot of time looking for examples for small values of n (far too much time, as I’m prone to do before trying to put some structure into it). I found spaces with n = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 6 , 7 , 8 and 9 dense sets, and I was able to show that 5 and 10 are impossible. Is there something wrong with multiples of 5 ?! This seemed wildly implausible, but believe it or not, it’s not entirely far from the truth. Here are a couple of examples: This space consists of the real numbers 0 , 1 , 2 (in blue) as well as m + 1 / n with m = 0 , 1 , 2 and n = 2 , 3 , 4 , … (in red). The blue points are limit points, and the red ones carry the discrete topology: each one is isolated. To make a dense set, you must take all of the red points but any subset of the blue points you want. There are, therefore, exactly 8 dense sets here. This is a nice topological space: it is Hausdorff, and in fact metrizable. An example with 6 dense sets cannot be either of those things; if fact it cannot even be T 0 ! But it’s pretty easy to describe: This is a topological space with 3 points, and the only open sets are the empty set, the whole space, and the set U of two points marked by the red oval. To make a dense set in this space you must pick one of the points of U or both of them, and you can include or exclude the 3 rd point. There are 6 options overall. If we label the points A , B , Z , the dense sets are A , B , A B , A Z , B Z and A B Z . Notice that no point in this space is isolated. We can generalize some of the things we just observed. In any topological space X , let R (“red”) be the set of isolated points and B the other points, those which aren’t open. Quite simply, p ∈ R if { p } is an open set, and p ∈ B otherwise. Now, a set A ⊆ X is dense precisely when it satisfies the following two criteria: Proof: if A is dense, it cannot miss any red point since the complement of each red point is closed. Therefore 1 holds. Is also cannot be disjoint from any open set, because then it would be contained in the closed complement of such an open set, so 2 must hold as well. Conversely, a set A satisfying 1+2 meets every open set U in X : if U has any red point, A meets it because of 1, and if it doesn’t, A meets it because of 2. A set meeting every open set is dense, because otherwise the complement of its closure would be a non-empty open set disjoint from it. ■ One consequence of this is that if a space X contains infinitely many points in B then it has infinitely many dense sets: every set of the form X ∖ { b } is dense, for any b ∈ B . Any such set grabs all the reds (if any) and the only blue open set it could possibly miss is { b } , but { b } isn’t open. Thus, as long as we’re exploring finite values of the number of possible dense sets, we can focus on spaces with a finite B . For example, suppose that X = B , meaning there are no isolated points at all. In the simplest case B is indiscrete: there are no open sets except for the obligatory empty set and X itself. If B has m elements, how many dense sets are there here? Condition 1 is satisfied vacuously for any candidate dense set, and condition 2 is also satisfied because there are no non-empty open sets to miss… oh, except for one: the whole space. Which subset misses the whole space? Why, the empty set of course. In a non-empty indiscrete space, all subsets are dense except for the empty set, and therefore the number of dense sets is 2 m − 1 . What if we want 2 m dense sets? That’s easy: just add a single red (open) point. Every dense set must contain it, but now B itself need not be open, so choosing just the red point is totally legit, and we get 2 m dense sets, one for every subset of B including the subset B itself. (This is a variation on the first example, above. Instead of infinitely many red points you can use just one, and declare the blue points indiscrete. Once you allow yourself to work with arbitrary topologies and not metric ones, you can use much simpler topological spaces. In fact you can just work with finite spaces.) So we have n = 2 m and n = 2 m − 1 as possible values of the count of dense sets. What else? At this point the task of identifying the possible values of n seemed daunting: we must somehow survey all possible combinations of open subsets of B , and the number of dense sets they allow. I literally walked around for a week thinking that the question has no reasonable answer. I was wrong. Observe that we don’t really care about all open subsets contained in B . We only care about the minimal ones: those containing no smaller non-empty open set. if A meets every minimal open set in B , it surely meets every open set in B , minimal or not. The finiteness of B is key here: in an infinite set, there may not be a minimal open set inside every open set (look at the first example above: a blue point with its red neighbors are an open set, but it doesn’t contain a minimal open set). Those minimal open sets must be disjoint (why?). Furthermore, it’s not hard to count how many dense sets are allowed: suppose the minimal open sets have sizes m 1 , m 2 , … , m k for some k , and there are m blue points not contained in any of those minimal open sets ( m may be 0 ). To choose a dense set you must now pick any non-empty subset of each minimal open set, and any subset (possibly empty) of the remaining m points. Every dense set must have this structure, because its intersection with any minimal open set is non-empty. Therefore the number n of dense sets is n = 2 m ( 2 m 1 − 1 ) ( 2 m 2 − 1 ) ⋯ ( 2 m k − 1 ) (1) Conversely, given a number n of this form, you can make a finite topological space with sufficiently many points to accommodate a family of disjoint open sets of sizes m 1 , … , m k , plus an additional m points, and this is it – its topology is just those open sets and nothing else. The conditions of a topology are clearly satisfied. This example has a topological space with open sets of size 8 , 6 , 5 , 5 , and an extra 8 points. The only open sets are the empty set, the whole space, and the sets marked by ovals. The number of dense sets is n = ( 2 8 − 1 ) ( 2 6 − 1 ) ( 2 5 − 1 ) ( 2 5 − 1 ) ( 2 8 ) , because choosing an dense set requires picking some non-empty subset of each of the ovals, and an arbitrary subset of the remaining 8 points. We’ve shown: if a topological space has a finite number n of dense sets then n must have the form (1), and any number of this form is indeed the number of dense sets of some topological space. A bit of number theory shows that the prime factorization of n can contain any primes you want. However, there are severe restrictions of the exponents of those primes. For instance, if you want n to be divisible by 5 that’s fine, but then it also has to be divisible by 3 (because 2 m − 1 is divisible by 5 iff m is divisible by 4 , and if m is divisible by 4 is must be divisible by 2 , and then 3 divides 2 m − 1 ). If you want n to be divisible by 5 2 that’s also fine, but then you have to have factors of 3 , 11 , 31 and 41 as well. The odd numbers of this type are OEIS sequence A282572 (we really only care about the odd ones because the even ones are just these odd numbers multiplied by an arbitrary power of 2 .) I was delighted to see that it also counts the possible orders of group of units in finite rings - it’s not at all obvious that these numbers and our numbers should be the same. Another thing we can conclude is that if you’re interested in the number of dense sets in Hausdorff spaces (or even T 1 spaces, and I think even T 0 ) then the answer is much simpler: a Hausdorff space with finitely many dense sets has 2 m dense sets for some m . No other value is possible. What about infinite cardinalities? An indiscrete space X of infinite cardinality λ has 2 λ dense sets (every non-empty subset is dense). Therefore every cardinal κ which is 2 λ for some λ is a possible cardinality of the family of dense sets. Which infinite cardinals are not 2 λ ? Well, first and foremost there’s our good friend ℵ 0 . Then there are various kinds of weirdos, like violators of GCH and inaccessible cardinals. I won’t say anything about those. And what about ℵ 0 ? Is there a topological space with exactly ℵ 0 dense subsets? So, as I write this on Sun evening, I’m quite sure there isn’t, and I almost have a proof, which is a nice way of saying that I had a proof, and I started typing it here, and while doing so I realized that I don’t, actually, have a proof. So, I prefer to post this answer and not let it hang in my Drafts folder, because I think we’ve made some nice progress on the finite situation and even an observation or two on the infinite one. If you see a solution to the ℵ 0 case, do share, and if I manage to prove it I’ll update this answer. UPDATE: OK, I got it. There is indeed no topological space with exactly ℵ 0 dense subsets. Proof: Let X be such a space and as before let B ⊆ X be the set of non-isolated points. A set D is dense iff it contains X ∖ B and meets every open set contained in B . There cannot be more than 2 | B | dense sets, so B is infinite. Every dense set D is co-finite, meaning | X ∖ D | < ∞ , because if D has an infinite complement we obtain 2 ℵ 0 dense sets containing D . Consequently, every infinite subset of B must contain a non-empty open set (or else its complement would be dense). Since B is infinite we can partition it into infinitely many disjoint infinite sets, each of which contains a non-empty open set, so we obtain infinitely many disjoint non-empty open sets U i . Pick an element x i in each U i . The set { x i } is infinite, so it contains a non-empty open set U . The intersection of U with some U j is exactly { x j } , forcing x j to be an isolated point, contradicting the definition of B . ■ (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: Will there ever be infinitely many known prime numbers?
Answer: Let me ask you a simpler question: are there infinitely many known numbers? You may say: of course! Here: 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on. We know them. And I’ll ask: Do we? We know them? All of them? Do we have them written up somewhere? Stored? Recorded? And you may say: Well no, of course not, there are infinitely many of them, but why would we need to write them up or record them? They are obvious. Here they are again: 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on. Don’t you know how to count? And I will say: Oh, I see, sure, great. So yes, to your original question, we do know infinitely many prime numbers, in fact we know all of them! Here: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and so on. You: Huh? What’s “and so on”? Me: The rule is simple: the next number is the first one not divisible by anything already on the list. You: Are you kidding me? We need to know the prime numbers! That’s not knowing! The rule is useless, it just repeats the definition of prime number! Me: Oh I see, sorry, this isn’t knowing. But help me understand, why is “1, 2, 3, 4 and so on” knowing, but “2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and so on” not knowing? You: Because it’s obvious what comes after any number in the first sequence, but we don’t know what comes after every number in the second sequence! You know what comes after 196884 in the sequence of natural numbers, but what comes after 196901 in the sequence of primes? Me: Why, 196907 of course. I just checked a few numbers and this is the next prime. You: You didn’t know that, you had to compute and it took you two hours. That’s not knowing. That’s laboriously computing one by one. Me: And going 1, 2, 3, 4 isn’t? You: No it isn’t. It’s trivial. Me: By “trivial” you mean that there’s a simple algorithm for producing the next number, represented in decimal. After 6354359999999 you know you need to change all the 9 's to 0 's and increase the 5 to a 6 . That’s not a tremendous amount of work but it’s still work, and if you keep going you’ll get to numbers with a quadrillion digits and trillions of 9 's in the end and it’s going to be quite a bit of work. And the thing is, finding the next prime is just work. The same kind of work. Looking at the digits, doing some manipulations, producing the next number. It’s a bit more complex, sure, but it doesn’t make sense to call easier work “knowing” and somewhat harder work “not knowing”. You: Ok, look, for the natural numbers I can give you a formula: After n comes n + 1 . Can you give me a formula for the next prime number? Me: Sure I can. After n comes min { k ∣ k > n ∧ ( m < n ⟹ k mod m ≠ 0 ) } . You: That’s not a formula! That’s an algorithm / a definition with symbols / what is that even / you can’t solve this / it’s not a closed form formula / it’s not an expression / it’s not elementary / some other rejection (I can’t quite guess what your push-back will be, but I’ve seen all of the above and others.) Me: So we know an infinite sequence of numbers when we have a simple/elementary/closed form formula for the next number, but we don’t know an infinite sequence of numbers when we have a slightly more complicated formula? You: That’s not “slightly”. Me: Fine. So you have a formal definition of “elementary” which is the dividing line between knowing and not knowing? Is n ! + 1 “knowing”? Is ⌊ ∫ n 0 exp ( cos 2 ( t + t 5 ) ) d t ⌋ knowing? You: Yeah, n ! + 1 is fine. But the integral isn’t, you can’t solve it. Me: I actually can. Why is n ! ok? It’s an algorithm: it tells you to start with 1 and multiply all the numbers up to n . Computing 10000 ! is a lot of work, and computing that integral is also a lot of work, but both are doable, algorithmic tasks. Why does one merit the name “knowing” and the other does not? You: When you put it this way… In fact, we have some beautiful concepts of what it means to know an infinite sequence of natural numbers. Sequence of type 1 are called recursive or computable. Sequences of type 2 are called recursively enumerable or listable or semi-decidable. Sequences of type 3 are uncomputable. There are many, many sequences of all of these types. It’s not unreasonable to brand sequences of type 3 “unknowable” or “unknown”. There’s a very meaningful dividing line between things we can compute and things we absolutely can’t. The sequence of primes resides in category 1. We have an algorithm that correctly determines if a number is prime. In fact, as algorithms for checking natural numbers go, this algorithm belongs in one of the easiest classes: P, or polynomial-time algorithms. It’s very, very hard to argue that the sequence of primes is particularly “difficult”, and it’s entirely unreasonable to argue that it’s not “known”. We already know the primes, in the same sense that we “know” the natural numbers. If your philosophical position is that we don’t “know” the natural numbers, that’s fine, but then we can’t “know” any infinite sequence of natural numbers, including the primes. You can still ask some interesting questions about infinite sequences of primes. It’s possible, though highly unlikely. We don’t know. More likely none of these numbers is prime. It’s possible, and very likely, but also don’t know. No, there isn’t. Exercise. Maybe. We don’t know. Yes. It’s a fun exercise to show that there is a number A > 1 such that ⌊ A 3 n ⌋ is prime for all n . Use Bertrand’s postulate. Yes, there is. This is another sense in which the sequence of primes is knowable: it is Diophantine. We now know that every recursively enumerable sequence of natural numbers is diophantine. This wasn’t easy to prove. There are many other questions you can ask, some easy, some hard, many unknown to this day. But I’m afraid I can’t put meaning behind the question “will there ever be infinitely many known prime numbers”. In the most reasonable way we can expect to “know” any infinite set, we already know the set of primes. We know it very, very well. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: Why do mathematicians do research on Collatz's conjunctions? What are they going to achieve or gain?
Answer: (It’s the Collatz conjecture.) Here’s a simple syllogism which somehow isn’t sufficiently well-known: People do things for fun, for the sheer joy of it. You could argue that there’s this personal “gain” from such activities (enjoyment), but it’s not the same kind of “gain” you seem to be looking for. You don’t “gain” anything necessarily by going on a hike, reading a novel or playing something on your guitar, but you do this anyway. Fun. (You wouldn’t ask “Why do people have sex? What are they going to achieve or gain?”, would you? Same thing.) Exploring the Collatz conjecture can reasonably be done by a person just because they are intrigued, and they want to walk down a path and see where it leads them. Perfectly normal. Nevertheless, in the context of mathematical research, there are deeper reasons. The Collatz conjecture deals with iterations of a simple map, and exploring such iterations is a beautiful domain of mathematics called dynamical systems. People dedicate entire lives to studying dynamical systems, because they find them fascinating and sometimes useful for making discoveries in other parts of math. (You may now ask, but why do people do research on dynamical systems? What are they going to achieve or gain? This is the same as asking why do people do math research at all, and the answer is because they can’t imagine anything better to do with their lives, and luckily society appreciates that for many good reasons.) So, people may explore the Collatz iteration as a toy example to better understand something more general that they are thinking about. We study toy examples all the time. We can’t solve the very general problem of classifying the orbits of arbitrary maps on arbitrary spaces, so we’re looking for simpler problems we could possibly solve, and Collatz is one of the seemingly simplest ones. As an example, let’s read carefully what is perhaps the most recent major paper on the Collatz conjecture, Terry Tao’s Almost all orbits. In the paper you find a whole lot of subtle analysis of the Collatz map, but you also find things like Nevertheless, in this paper we show that it is possible to locate an alternate probability measure (or more precisely, a family of probability measures) on the natural numbers with enough invariance properties that an iterative argument does become fruitful. and In this analogy, Theorem 1.6 then corresponds to an “almost sure almost global well-posedness” result, where one needs to control the solution for times so large that the evolution gets arbitrary close to the bounded state N = O ( 1 ) . To bootstrap from almost sure local well-posedness to almost sure almost global well-posedness, we were inspired by the work of Bourgain [4], who demonstrated an almost sure global well-posedness result for a certain nonlinear Schrödinger equation by combining local well-posedness theory with a construction of an invariant probability measure for the dynamics. Roughly speaking, the point was that the invariance of the measure would almost surely keep the solution in a “bounded” region of the state space for arbitrarily long times, allowing one to iterate the local well-posedness theory indefinitely. What these two brief quotes tell you is that Tao’s study of Collatz isn’t an isolated, random pastime. He is connecting it with broader ideas of invariant measures for dynamical systems and PDEs. Much of math research seeks to find connections between diverse areas, elucidating or harnessing them in different directions. So, bottom line: there are some serious motivations for studying the Collatz conjecture as a useful sandbox for ideas about dynamical systems, invariance and local-global principles, but it is also fine to study the Collatz conjecture just because it is there, and it’s interesting, and it’s fun. That’s all. (…)

Question:
Let a "Derivative Polynomial" be a polynomial with first term

, and each following term being the derivative of the previous (e.g

Answer: The polynomial has the structure x n + n x n − 1 + … + n ! x + n ! By the rational root theorem, any rational root of this polynomial must be an integer dividing n ! . If n = 1 , the problem is trivial: the polynomial is x + 1 and there is, indeed, a rational root x = − 1 . From now on assume that n ≥ 2 . We will need the following result (our lemma): If p is a prime number, the highest power of p dividing k ! is < k . For example, 100 ! is divisible by 2 97 but not by 2 98 , so the highest power of 2 dividing 100 ! is 97 < 100 . We’ve talked many times about this highest power, denoted v p ( k ! ) and called the p -valuation of k ! , and if you’re not sure why this is true – make it an exercise. Or ask separately. Since n ≥ 2 there’s a prime p dividing n , and let’s set t = v p ( n ! ) , the highest power of p dividing n ! . Observe that t < n , by the lemma. We will need that in a minute, but first observe that all of the coefficients of the polynomial, except the leading coefficient (which is 1 ), are divisible by p , and therefore if x is an integer and a root of the polynomial, x had better be divisible by p as well. Every term of the polynomial is n ! k ! x k . When k = 0 this is just n ! , the last term. When k = 1 this is n ! x , the linear term. When k = n − 1 this is n x n − 1 , and when k = n it’s x n . It’s good to check the extreme, or “corner”, cases, and they work fine here. We will now look at the p -valuations of those terms, with x being the wannabe root. The very last term, n ! , has a p -valuation of t , because this is how we defined t . The fraction n ! k ! has p -valuation of t minus the p -valuation of k ! , and that p -valuation of k ! is at most k − 1 by the lemma. Therefore the p -valuation of n ! k ! is at least t − k + 1 . And then, since x is divisible by p , x k is divisible by (at least) p k , so the p -valuation of the whole term is at least t + 1 . Just to check, this is still true even for the leading term: x n has p -valuation at least n , and t < n by our lemma. Answer: The meaning of a b is always a b − 1 : it’s a times the inverse of b . “Inverse” means reciprocal, or multiplicative inverse. The thing that yields 1 when multiplied by b . When we ordinarily write fractions, this means that we need to avoid a denominator of 0 , because 0 doesn’t have a multiplicative inverse. So when you see the expression k k − 2 it’s understood that k cannot be 2 . It’s the same when you’re working modulo m , for some m . You just need to know what is invertible mod m . For example, since 3 × 5 ≡ 1 ( mod 7 ) , any fraction with 3 in the denominator makes sense mod 7 : instead of dividing by 3 , just multiply by 5 . For example, 2 3 ≡ 2 × 5 ≡ 3 ( mod 7 ) . On the other hand, 4 7 makes no sense mod 7 , because 7 ≡ 0 ( mod 7 ) so it’s not invertible. In general, the numbers that are invertible mod m , and therefore are legal denominators when working mod m , are precisely those numbers that are relatively prime to m . The reason is that when b and m are relatively prime, there are always numbers u , v such that u b + v m = 1 (this is called Bezout’s identity, and is an immediate consequence of the Euclidean algorithm), and this means that u b ≡ 1 ( mod m ) so u is the inverse of b mod m . So, what is 6 7 mod 17 ? Clearly 7 is relatively prime to 17 , and you can use the Euclidean algorithm or just trial and error to find that 5 × 7 ≡ 1 ( mod 17 ) , so 6 7 is just 30 or 13 mod 17 . 6 7 ≡ 13 ( mod 17 ) . You can double check that as you normally would: multiply both sides of this congruence by 7 to find 6 ≡ 13 × 7 ( mod 17 ) and that’s indeed true, because 91 − 6 is divisible by 17 . To be fair, this style of expressing things isn’t super common. Many people would prefer to write 6 × 7 − 1 ≡ 13 ( mod 17 ) because it’s more readily understood what 7 − 1 mod 17 means. (…)

Question: Is there a relationship between Godel's first incompleteness theorem and the cardinality of: (a) the set of all well formed sentences, (b) the set of all correct proofs?
Answer: No, there’s no relationship. I tried to guess why you’d expect such a relationship, and I think I failed. The “set of all well-formed sentences” is indeed a well-defined set once you specify a language (=set of non-logical symbols). For example, 1 = 1 + 1 is a well-formed sentence in the language of arithmetic (which includes the symbols 0 , 1 , + , × ) but it’s not a well-formed sentence in the language of set theory (which only has one non-logical symbol, ∈ ). So, assuming we’re working in the context of some specified language, and even more broadly within some context of formal logic where “well-formed sentence” is a meaningful concept, there is indeed a set of well-formed sentences, and this set is always countably infinite, meaning it has cardinality ℵ 0 . This is simply due to the fact that “well-formed sentence” is a finite sequence of symbols from some finite alphabet, aka a string. The set of strings is countable, regardless of whether the strings are well-formed or not. And since we can produce arbitrarily long well-formed sentences (for example by doing things like ¬ ( ¬ ( ¬ ( 1 = 1 + 1 ) ) ) , the set of well-formed sentences is infinite. Hence, ℵ 0 . As to the set of correct proofs, here we are presumably working in the context of some formal proof system, in which a proof is a sequence of sentences each of which is either an axiom of the theory or a formal consequence of some previous sentences in the proof, and “formal consequence” is defined by some specific set of allowed derivations. And once again, this set is ultimately a collection of strings, so it’s countable, and it’s once again infinite since you can make arbitrarily long proofs. So, ℵ 0 again. None of that has anything to do with Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems. Perhaps you’re under the impression that Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems somehow restrict the universe of allowed proofs, and this reduces the cardinality of the set of proofs. So, doubly no: GIT does not change the set of allowed proofs, and even if it did, that set would still be countably infinite. Any reasonable proof formalism allows for arbitrarily long proofs (for example, proofs of arbitrarily long sentences), so the set of proofs is definitely infinite, and it certainly cannot be more than countably infinite. Question: It has been proven that the Continuum Hypothesis (CH) cannot be proven true or false using the axioms of ZFC. But it must actually be true or false because either there is a set of Reals with cardinality between N and R or there isn't. Am I wrong?
Answer: You may be right, or wrong, or something else. Let me explain. How you may be right: there may be an actual, unique structure deserving of the name “the real numbers”, and in that structure there either is or isn’t a subset of intermediate cardinality. If there is, then CH is false, and if there isn’t, then it’s true. This state of affairs does not contradict the observation that ZFC is powerless to settle CH. ZFC is under no obligation to prove every true statement and disprove every false one; in fact no consistent, recursive theory powerful enough to prove certain statements about the natural numbers can do that. ZFC is not a categorical theory. It talks about a universe of sets, but it doesn’t dictate a unique such universe. It has many models (as does every sufficiently rich, consistent, first-order theory). Each universe of sets has its own version of R , and in some of those versions CH holds, and in others it does not. This is precisely what Gödel and Cohen proved: Gödel constructed a model of ZFC in which CH is true, and Cohen constructed a model in which it is false. Ergo, ZFC cannot decide CH. Nevertheless, you may hold the position that some of these models are “non-standard” or “irrelevant”, and they are there just because the formalism of first-order theories necessitates that rich-enough theories must have a variety of models. That philosophical position may be easy or hard to defend, but it is not contradicted outright by the independence of CH from ZFC. How you may be wrong: the alternative philosophical position is that the different versions of R in the different models of ZFC are all equally legitimate, or at least, some of them are equally legitimate (and others perhaps less so). This “multiverse” view of set theory is also prima facie tenable, and is held by a good number of set theorists. In this view, the assertion “either there is an intermediate set of reals or there isn’t” is incorrect, because there is no single, definite object referenced by the symbol R . What we know and prove about R are consequences of our axioms, and they are properties shared by all versions of R , but things that aren’t consequences of our axioms are simply true for some R s and not others, just like things that aren’t consequences of the axioms of groups (like being abelian, or finite) are true of some groups and not others. How you may be something else: It is not clear that there is a fact-of-the-matter as to these two alternatives. We don’t have a mathematical framework to determine if there is or isn’t a unique R , and we don’t even have a precise philosophical framework to decide this, which is why some people (Smullyan, for example) espoused the “either there is or there isn’t” view, and others (like Joel David Hamkins) don’t. Feferman argued that this “indeterminate” state is, indeed, the case: to him, CH is simply not a definite mathematical question. Note that I’m avoiding using the term “Platonist” to describe the former perspective and “non-Platonist” for the latter, because full-fledged platonism is more sweeping than the claim that there is a definite R . You may claim there is a definite R without claiming that there’s a definite truth value to some other things, and you may also claim that there’s a definite R without arguing that it “exists” in some metaphysical sense. Simply, you may argue that there’s something we really mean when we say R because it better aligns with our intuition, and additional axioms may settle CH while seeming perfectly reasonable to us. Admittedly, after 50 years of research it seems less and less likely that this will happen. There’s a model of R in ZF (without choice) in which every set of real numbers is measurable. I don’t think anyone wants to take that model as “the actual real numbers”; it is clearly seen as exotic, and if anything it motivates us to adopt the axiom of choice as actually holding in the universe we care about. Again, this just requires us to wish to explore certain models more than others because they seem more natural and less exotic. We don’t necessarily argue that they “are the only one in existence”. In summary, the only thing about your question which may be deemed wrong is the word “but”. There’s no “but” between the fact that ZFC fails to decide CH and the belief that there is a set of real numbers in which CH is or isn’t true. Those two assertions are perfectly in agreement. (…)

Answer: That’s a very nice question. Thanks to m = n = 1 , 2 has the same color as 3 . That’s a good start, but how do we show that they have the same color as 4 ? Trying other small values of m , n doesn’t seem to lead us back to 4 . So…? Oh but you see, 3 has the same color as 6 (why?), which has the same color as 19 (why?), which has the same color as 206 (see why?), and then 17 , 146 , 13 , 86 , 11 and finally 4 . So yeah, 4 must carry the same color as 2 and 3 , but the chaotic path we needed to follow to see this is a bit disheartening. What to do? When you look at that path, you can’t miss the fact that the numbers zig-zag between small and large. This isn’t at all surprising: you have some small m , n and they let you connect m + n (small) to m 2 + n 2 + 1 (much larger), and what happens then is that this number m 2 + n 2 + 1 happens to have another representation as M 2 + N 2 + 1 , which leads you back to M + N , roughly the same size as m + n . For example, 13 → 86 because 13 = 6 + 7 and 6 2 + 7 2 + 1 = 86 , but also 9 2 + 2 2 + 1 = 86 and that gives us 86 → 9 + 2 = 11 . In two hops we’ve connected 11 and 13 , which seems much more useful than connecting 13 to 86 . (When I say “connecting” I just mean that these two numbers must be colored in the same color, as per the specification of the question. The question here is really about proving that the implied graph is connected.) The key here wasn’t the number 86 , it was the number 85 : it’s the sum of two squares in two different ways, just like Ramanujan’s 1729 but with squares instead of cubes. So my idea was to manufacture lots of numbers that are sums of squares in two different ways, and from that infer lots of nearby connections like 11 ↔ 13 , and from that conclude that all the integers > 1 are eventually connected. That turned out to be easier said than done. There was one thing the confused me briefly: if all we’re doing is hopping from m + n to M + N whenever m 2 + n 2 = M 2 + N 2 , why the + 1 ? As far as we’re concerned it doesn’t seem to matter at all… but I quickly realized that if the question had m 2 + n 2 instead of m 2 + n 2 + 1 , the conclusion would certainly be false: even numbers and odd numbers would never get connected. The + 1 is what let us connect 2 to 3 , and that explains why it’s there. Right. So how do we find many instance of m 2 + n 2 = M 2 + N 2 ? I thought I knew the answer to that, and it turned out that I was not as learned as I thought I was. My first approach was to rewrite this as m 2 − M 2 = N 2 − n 2 , so ( m − M ) ( m + M ) = ( N − n ) ( N + n ) , and that’s just some number which affords two factorizations in which the factors have the same parity. Any two numbers of the same parity can be written as X − x and X + x . So yes, sure, there are many composite numbers and most of them can be expressed in a few different ways like that, but it was hard to put enough structure on this to obtain a nice family of connections. (That was a mistake; I just didn’t look at it the right way. But I needed a jolt from a different direction to see this). The jolt came when I arranged a few square-pairs and noticed that they follow a pattern. The first observation, for some odd reason, was this: ( x + 3 ) 2 + ( 3 x − 1 ) 2 = ( x − 3 ) 2 + ( 3 x + 1 ) 2 Once you see this, it’s hard to unsee it: this is pretty darn obvious. The square terms on both sides are the same, the constant terms on both sides are the same, and the linear terms on both sides are missing. Of course that’s true. It’s a simple polynomial identity, but I have to admit I never noticed the existence of such simple polynomial identities. Now I know. I like this question for teaching me that. This observation means, for our question, that all numbers of the form ( x + 3 ) + ( 3 x − 1 ) = 4 x + 2 are connected (in two hops) to ( x − 3 ) + ( 3 x + 1 ) = 4 x − 2 , as soon as x ≥ 4 (because otherwise x − 3 isn’t a positive integer, and the question only allows m , n to be positive integers.) I then generalized this in an obvious way: ( a x + b ) 2 + ( b x − a ) 2 = ( a x − b ) 2 + ( b x + a ) 2 (1) for any positive integers a , b you like. Now take, for example, a = 1 , b = 2 to see ( x + 2 ) 2 + ( 2 x − 1 ) 2 = ( x − 2 ) 2 + ( 2 x + 1 ) 2 which lets us connect 3 x − 1 to 3 x + 1 whenever x ≥ 3 is an integer. Nice! We now have two connecting rules with different multipliers, which seems to make our colors very restricted. I figured that if I collected enough of these I’d be done. That’s right, and I’ll show how, but I have this nagging feeling that there’s a much more elegant way to do this that I’m completely missing. Whatever. I’m never as smart as I think I am. Now, I said that the composite numbers view could work and I just missed it. In fact, if you rearrange the identity (1) as a difference of squares and then replace X 2 − x 2 with ( X + x ) ( X − x ) , you’ll see that it is simply 2 a x ⋅ 2 b = 2 b x ⋅ 2 a , so duh. Of course that’s true, and the only thing I should have done is look at simple factorizations such as 4 a b = 4 b a and throw a parameter x inside, to get a whole family of sum-of-squares identities. Here’s another example: from 2 x ⋅ 12 = 4 x ⋅ 6 we can infer ( x + 6 ) 2 − ( x − 6 ) 2 = ( 2 x + 3 ) 2 − ( 2 x − 3 ) 2 , another identity which seems obvious in hindsight, and it lets us assert that the numbers 3 x + 3 and 3 x − 3 are connected. That’s genuinely different from 3 x + 1 and 3 x − 1 . Their weakness is that they connect something linear to something quadratic, which is a lot less helpful in general. But it’s still convenient to have it at our disposal, as we’ll see in a minute. Question: If a(n) and b(n) are two possibly finite or infinite sequences of real numbers, and the density of a(n) is higher than that of b(n), but b(n) is infinite, does that imply that a(n) is also infinite?
Answer: There isn’t a single definition of “density” for sequences of real numbers. There’s density in the topological sense (which is just a yes/no affair), there’s natural density and logarithmic density and Dirichlet density for sets (or sequences) of natural numbers, and a variety of other similar concepts. But let’s put it this way: if you have any notion of density and it assigns to some finite sequence a higher density than some infinite sequence, “density” is probably the wrong name for it. (…)

Question: Why don't we use an ultimate large cardinal axiom that says all large cardinals whose existence are consistent with ZFC exist?
Answer: Because there’s no such thing as “all large cardinals”. There’s no generic definition of a large cardinal axiom. Also, most (possibly all) large cardinal axioms that have been developed are linearly ordered by consistency strength, so assuming any one of them implies the consistency of everything underneath. There isn’t much point in assuming several of them; just pick the strongest. And of course, if such a linear order is unknown (or downright violated, which hasn’t happened yet) then you simply can’t assume such two incompatible axioms. (…)

The assertion I just made is denoted g ( 3 ) = 9 , which is the standard notation for Waring’s problem. This has been known since 1912. It is known that only finitely many numbers actually require 9 and even 8 cubes; in other words we know that every sufficiently large natural number is the sum of at most 7 cubes, which is succinctly captured by the inequality G ( 3 ) ≤ 7 . Question:

100
positive integers not exceeding
