such that all pairwise sums of them are different?
Answer: Yes! Like Jonathan Devor, I also tried various heuristic algorithms to construct large sets with distinct pairwise sums, but I couldn’t get to 100 elements. So I switched gears to look for a theoretical approach, under the (dubious) assumption that the question is supposed to be answerable positively. After various false starts (Fibonacci etc.) I landed on something I’m sure I’ve seen somewhere: take an arithmetic progression and add a perturbation. In other words, pick a basic skip m , and look at 0 , m , 2 m , 3 m etc. As it stands this is, of course, a terrible sequence with plenty of identical pairwise sums, but at least we know exactly what those collisions are. Then, we add a perturbation in the form of some kind of hash function: for each k we have some f ( k ) with 0 ≤ f ( k ) < m / 2 , and now instead of k m we look at k m + f ( k ) , with k = 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 etc until some limit we want to make large. Why do I want the range of f to be no larger than m / 2 ? Because when this is the case, a collision of the form a m + f ( a ) + b m + f ( b ) = c m + f ( c ) + d m + f ( d ) can only happen if a m + b m = c m + d m . The sum of two f values cannot exceed m , so the perturbations keep us in the same m -bucket. How should we pick f ? The simplest functions are polynomials, and the simplest polynomials are quadratics (linear isn’t going to cut it). We can’t just take f ( k ) = k 2 because that quickly exceeds m , but maybe we can take f ( k ) = k 2 mod p where p is about half of m and mod denotes the standard reduction mod p , yielding a value between 0 and p − 1 . It’s easiest to explore reductions mod primes, and in fact why don’t we just set m = 2 p . So our current attempt goes like this: pick a prime p , and denote by ¯¯¯ k the reduction of k mod p (for instance, if p = 11 then ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ 100 = 1 ¯ ). Our set consists of a m + ¯¯¯¯¯ a 2 for a = 0 , 1 , 2 , … , and we need to see how far we can push a before we start getting collisions. A collision is this: a m + ¯¯¯¯¯ a 2 + b m + ¯¯¯¯¯ b 2 = c m + ¯¯¯¯¯ c 2 + d m + ¯¯¯¯¯ d 2 Since m = 2 p , and all the ¯¯¯¯¯ k 2 ¯ things are < p , this equation forces a m + b m = c m + d m , namely a + b = c + d (this simplification is exactly why it’s convenient to start with something linear). Furthermore, the equation ¯¯¯¯¯ a 2 + ¯¯¯¯¯ b 2 = ¯¯¯¯¯ c 2 + ¯¯¯¯¯ d 2 is the same thing as a 2 + b 2 ≡ c 2 + d 2 ( mod m ) . But from a + b = c + d we conclude that ( a + b ) 2 ≡ ( c + d ) 2 ( mod m ) , and combining these two we get a b ≡ c d ( mod m ) . So now, the pairs ( a , b ) and ( c , d ) share both a sum and a product mod p . As long as 0 ≤ a , b , c , d < p , this can’t happen: in any field, pairs of numbers are uniquely determined by their sum and product, since we can solve the corresponding quadratic uniquely. We conclude that for any prime p , with m = 2 p , the set S = { k m + ¯¯¯¯¯ k 2 ∣ k = 0 , 1 , 2 , … , p − 1 } has pairwise distinct sums, where ¯¯¯ a simply denotes the least residue of a mod p . Let’s see an example: take p = 5 , m = 10 . The set is { 0 , 11 , 24 , 34 , 41 } , which is rather easy to parse: the units digits are 0 , 1 , 4 , the squares mod 5 , and the 10 's digits are just 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . The pairwise sums are distinct: we have, for example, 0 + 3 = 1 + 2 , but here we get 0 + 34 ≠ 11 + 24 . The unit “hash” digits break the collisions. Now, say someone asks you for a large set S with distinct pairwise sums and elements not exceeding N . The largest element in our construction is ( p − 1 ) 2 m + ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ ( p − 1 ) 2 < ( p − 1 ) 4 p + p . With N = 25 000 this lets us push p to p = 109 (whew!), and the set S with that p gives us 109 numbers not exceeding 25 000 with the required property. in fact, the largest number is just 23 545 , significantly less than 25 000 (but the next prime, p = 113 , is too large). Oh, the question says “positive integers”. So either give up on the 0 or, better, push everything up by 1 . We have enough headroom to enable that. For the record, here’s the sequence obtained with this method: I’m sure you can, at a glance, observe that no two numbers in this list have the same sum as any other two numbers. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: An infinite number of people take turns slicing and taking a random amount of cake (each subsequent person selects a random portion from what remains.) What’s the probability that the first person got the largest slice?
Answer: Nice! Michael Lamar has asked why the answer is the Golomb-Dickman constant, as it appears to be from random simulations. I think I know why. It is a little surprising, isn’t it, since Golomb-Dickman comes from random permutations, and in the cake model there don’t seem to be any permutations around. The cake model is continuous. To make it precise, we can start with the cake being the interval [ 0 , 1 ] , and the first person chooses a slice x 1 ∼ U ( 0 , 1 ) , a uniformly distributed magnitude between 0 and 1 . The cake is now reduced to the interval [ 0 , 1 − x 1 ] , so the next person chooses a random slice x 2 ∼ U ( 0 , 1 − x 1 ) , and the third person x 3 ∼ U ( 0 , 1 − x 1 − x 2 ) , and so on. Observe that we do really need an infinite number of people, as the event that the cake is actually completely depleted is negligible. But it doesn’t matter much, since the largest slice X = max ( x i ) is decided long before we get to fighting over microscopic cake crumbs. For instance, with probability 1 2 the very first slice is > 1 2 and it’s game over, as it has to be the largest slice. But now let’s replace this continuous model with a discrete one. Part of the reason is that discrete models are (sometimes) easier to reason about, but the main reason is that a discrete model lets us connect the distribution of slice sizes to random permutation statistics. So we pick a positive integer N , which you can think of as being like a million, and the cake now consists of N molecules. The first person grabs m 1 molecules with m 1 uniformly distributed between 1 and N , leaving a cake with N − m 1 molecules. The next person then chooses m 2 uniformly between 1 and N − m 1 , leaving N − m 1 − m 2 molecules, and so on. We get a random vector ( m 1 , m 2 , … , m k ) with m 1 + m 2 + … + m k = N . Note that here the process does necessarily terminate: at worst, each person picks one molecule and at stage k = N we are done. As we’ve observed, the vector ( m 1 , … , m k ) has this cool distribution: the first component m 1 is uniformly distributed between 1 and N , always, but the second component m 2 has a distribution which depends on the value of m 1 , as it’s distributed uniformly between 1 and N − m 1 . Then m 3 is uniform between 1 and N − m 1 − m 2 , and so on. If you’ve ever looked at random permutations, this distribution may remind you of something: this is how the cycle lengths of random permutations are distributed! Recall that any permutation σ ∈ S N can be written as a product of disjoint cycles, and we can order them naturally as follows: the first cycle is the one with 1 in it; the next cycle starts with the smallest value which isn’t in the first cycle; and so on. For instance, a typical permutation σ in S 10 may look like ( 1 6 3 2 9 ) ( 4 8 ) ( 5 ) ( 7 10 ) (This notation means that σ ( 1 ) = 6 , σ ( 6 ) = 3 , σ ( 3 ) = 2 and so on.) It is customary to omit fixed points like ( 5 ) from cycle notation, but I wish to keep it so as not to forget that there’s a cycle of length 1 here. This particular permutation has cycle lengths ( 5 , 2 , 1 , 2 ) . Observe that I’m writing down the cycle lengths in the same order as the cycles themselves, which isn’t by decreasing lengths! A fun fact which many people find counterintuitive (I remember I did) is that the length of the first cycle, the one with 1 in it, is uniform between 1 and N . The probability that 1 is a fixed point is 1 N , the probability that it’s part of a 2 -cycle ( 1 a ) is also 1 N , and so on. If you haven’t seen this, take it as an exercise. But look - this means that the cycle-length vector ( m 1 , m 2 , … , m k ) of a random permutation σ ∈ S N is distributed exactly like our molecular cake model. The length of m 1 is uniform between 1 and N , the length of m 2 is uniform between 1 and N − m 1 , and so on. We can now ask two questions: The first question isn’t very simple; the answer is well-known, but we don’t quite need it here. All we need is to recognize that M has an expectation, which I will call a N (because it clearly depends on N ). The notation a N is chosen to match the notation in the Wikipedia article on the Golomb-Dickman constant: That constant is defined as λ = lim N → ∞ a N / N . We can answer the second question by symmetry. Recall that ( m 1 , m 2 , … , m k ) are the cycle lengths of a random permutation, ordered in the natural way; but random permutations don’t offer any special consideration to the element 1 . The probability that the cycle containing 1 is as long as the longest cycle is the same as the probability that the cycle containing j is as long as the longest cycle, for any j = 1 , 2 , … , N . We now apply the usual trick of indicator random variables: let Z j be the random variable with value 1 if j is in the longest cycle and 0 if it’s not. The sum of the variables Z j is just the length of the longest cycle, so the probability p = Pr ( Z j = 1 ) is simply a N / N , where a N is the expected longest length. I’m cheating here a little bit, because if there are multiple cycles of maximum length, “being in the longest cycle” happens to more elements than the size of that cycle. But this effect diminishes as N grows, since the probability of having two cycles of maximum length tends to 0 (I didn’t quite write down a formal proof, but it looks very reasonable). Therefore we can assert that lim N → ∞ ( Pr ( m 1 = M ) − a N / N ) = 0 or, in other words lim N → ∞ Pr ( m 1 = M ) = λ The probability that the first cake eater has the largest piece tends to λ , the Golomb-Dickman constant, as the number of molecules N tends to infinity. This was all done with discrete cakes. To finish, we just need to argue that the same conclusion holds in the continuous case. Indeed, our discrete variables m i , once normalized to y i = m i / N , tend in distribution to x i , the sizes of the continuous random slices. I’m happy to invoke the old “details are left to the reader” here: it’s really not hard. I found it very pleasing to observe that cycle lengths of random permutations are distributed just like random cake slices, and therefore that the Golomb-Dickman pops up as the probability of player 1 having the largest piece. (…)

Question: What types of objects obey the quadratic formula, besides real and complex variables?
Answer: I assume you mean the familiar formula for the roots of a quadratic equation a x 2 + b x + c = 0 , x = − b ± √ b 2 − 4 a c 2 a This works in any field of characteristic ≠ 2 , which is just a way of saying – in any context where you have addition, multiplication, inverses and the usual commutative, associative and distributive laws, and 1 + 1 ≠ 0 (that’s the “characteristic” part). You can get away with less – for example, in a non-commutative ring when 2 a is invertible and the coefficients are in the center. This covers quite a bit of ground beyond real and complex numbers. There are many other fields, such as finite fields, number fields and fields of functions and the formula works fine in all of them. The square root may or may not be in your field, just like it may or may not be in the real numbers. You can then say that the equation has no solutions in that field, or you can move up to an extension field where the square root does exist. (…)

Question: What is the exact area of a 2” diameter circle?
Answer: The crash course on the exactness of real numbers will be followed by a crash course on the inexactness of the inch. The area of a circle of diameter 2 units is π square units. π is a real number, which is totally and precisely exact. The OP appears to have reservations: Most people have no trouble branding the natural numbers 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 … “exact”. The integers (including negative ones) are typically fine too. The rational numbers is where we begin to lose some folks: No one (I think) has a problem with 6 23 , but many people become somewhat concerned when 1 3 is represented as 0.33333 … , and the confusion skyrockets when this simple equality is multiplied by 3 . For the sake of brevity, I’m going to assume that the reader has no such concerns with rational numbers, and is happy to acknowledge that any rational number m n with m , n integers and n > 0 is nice, concise and precise. We will make no use or mention of infinite decimal expansions. We will need some specific rational numbers, pretty simple ones. Here they are: 4 ( 1 − 1 3 ) = 8 3 4 ( 1 − 1 3 + 1 5 − 1 7 ) = 304 105 4 ( 1 − 1 3 + 1 5 − 1 7 + 1 9 − 1 11 ) = 10312 3465 ...and so on . The expressions on the left make it very easy to understand which numbers we’re looking at. The fractions on the right are just a reminder that those are simple, specific, exact, ordinary numbers. If you like formulas, those numbers are given by 4 2 n + 1 ∑ k = 0 ( − 1 ) k 2 k + 1 Now, all rational numbers fall into two groups: If a number is in group A then all larger numbers are also in A, and if a number is in group B than all smaller numbers are also in B. No number is in both groups, and every rational number is in one of them. Group B has no single number which is greater than all other numbers in group B. Such a “splitting” of the rational numbers into two groups is called a Dedekind cut. Let’s acknowledge that the cut it simple and precise. Every rational number is either here or there. Nobody is going anywhere. Nobody is fuzzy, shaky, uncertain or imprecise. The rational numbers 22 7 and 355 113 are in group A. The numbers 3 and 157 50 are in B. Any rational number can unambiguously be so placed. The number π is these two groups of rational numbers. Yes, really. Real numbers are Dedekind cuts, and π happens to be this Dedekind cut. So, likewise, π is fully, totally, absolutely, irrevocably and completely precise and unmoving. This was crash course on how π is exact. Now, the inch. The inch is nowadays defined as 0.0254 m. The meter (m) is defined as the distance traveled by light in vacuum during 1 299 792 458 seconds, while the second is that period of time during which the radiation emitted by the transition between the two hyperfine ground states of Caesium-133 cycles exactly 9 192 631 770 times. We have no idea if any of those magnitudes are the same each time we look at them, if “the same” attempts to take into account variations by 10 − 10000 seconds or meters or whatever unit. Physical space ceases to make sense long before such precisions are attempted. There is no meaning to “an inch” vs “an inch plus one over googol meters”. Likewise, there’s no “circle” in the physical universe, no precise diameter, no precise area. At the microscopic level everything is fuzzy, chunky and shimmering. A circle of diameter 2″ is not a specific geometric or physical object, and it has no exact area. If you’re willing to ignore all of those details and just abstractly ask about an ideal, mathematical circle of diameter 2 in units you call “inches”, and that 2 is the mathematical 2 , the real number, the Dedekind cut, precise and unmoving, then the area is π square inches in the same sense. As far as physics or engineering are concerned, there’s no “exact” anything. As far as the ideal mathematical circle is concerned, the area is always π R 2 , exactly. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: Are there theorems of number theory that can't be proven using elementary methods?
Answer: Most number theoretic results that earned the title “theorem” cannot by proved with elementary methods, and many of them cannot be proved with methods far more sophisticated than “elementary”. Instead, they require massive amounts of modern theory, language, techniques, and very deep hierarchies of prior theorems. The law of quadratic reciprocity can reasonably be said to have elementary proofs. None of them are very easy or obvious, but they can certainly be taught to students with no advanced knowledge. The Prime Number Theorem is most naturally proved with techniques from complex function theory, which I don’t think I would call “elementary”. Famously, there’s also a proof found independently by Selberg and Erdős which is considered elementary because it avoids complex variables, but if you try to study it you may feel that the adjective is quite misleading. It is not an easy proof. See the illuminating comments here, for example. And then, more recent results (as in, most anything less than 100 years old) are typically extremely far from elementary, even if their statement is entirely elementary. For example, thanks to Zhang, Maynard and others we now know that there are infinitely many pairs of primes that differ by 246 or less. The proof isn’t elementary, and that’s putting it mildly. Or, consider Faltings’s theorem which says (to simplify somewhat) that polynomial equations with two variables, rational coefficients and degree exceeding 4 (and one mild technical condition) can only have finitely many rational solutions. This is an extremely difficult theorem which landed Faltings the Fields medal in 1986. Few professional mathematicians are equipped to fully understand the proof. (…)

Question: Is it correct to define abs(x) as sqrt(x^2) and therefore as an elementary function? Isn't sqrt multi-valued?
Answer: For a real argument x , the equality | x | = √ x 2 is perfectly valid, with the usual interpretation of the square root symbol as denoting a (single valued) function √ ⋅ : R ≥ 0 → R ≥ 0 There are, indeed, various other functions denoted by the same symbol, such as the principal square root of a complex number (single-valued) and the multi-valued function assigning to a complex number its two square roots. But it’s generally accepted and understood that if the argument is a non-negative real number then square root means what it means in school. Whether or not this observation renders | x | an “elementary” function depends on context. There’s no single, universally accepted definition of “elementary”, and different authors may use the term in different ways. One reason for this discrepancy is that most elementary functions are not only continuous but actually smooth and, in fact, locally analytic wherever they are defined. This is also the case for the square root function except at x = 0 , where it fails to be differentiable. As a result, the composition √ x 2 also fails to be differentiable at x = 0 . In many contexts it’s useful to require elementary functions to be smooth everywhere they are defined, and in such contexts we would only use the square root function away from 0 . In other contexts this may not be a concern. So, again, there’s no universal agreement on the definition of elementary, and the observation that | x | = √ x 2 doesn’t force us to accept or reject | x | as elementary. I believe most people would not regard it as elementary, but if someone does, that’s fine – they would likely make that explicit, however. Of course, if the context is complex variables, one would use the variable name z instead of x , and in that context | z | is not at all equal to √ z 2 . (…)

Question: How do you help an adult learner become a mathematician and win a Fields Medal one day?
Answer: An adult learner may learn as much mathematics as they are able to dedicate time to, and they can get as far as their previous knowledge, time, talent, taste and teachers permit. It may be a little, or it may be more than a little. “Becoming a mathematician” is vague; if the goal is to land a research position at a university, this is quite difficult nowadays for anyone in many locales, and for someone starting off as an adult it may be harder, depending on just how adult is “adult”. “Win a Fields medal one day” is, I’m afraid, entirely nonsensical. As to “how do you help” – I have no idea what your and their resources and assets are, so there really is no way to answer the question. The best way for anyone to study mathematics is to attend a college or university and earn a degree, and then proceed to graduate studies. You can do that at any age, once you qualify by earning the necessary prerequisites. If you are able to help someone do that by tutoring, mentoring, guiding, testing, encouraging or running errands, fantastic – go right ahead. Just drop the Fields business from the project plan. (…)

Question:

2010

(

2017

Answer: A residue a is an m th power mod a prime p which is congruent to 1 mod m precisely when a ( p − 1 ) / m ≡ 1 ( mod p ) . If you’re not familiar with this fact, you can prove it for yourself: use the fact that the multiplicative group mod p is cyclic. Therefore, 2010 ≡ ( − 7 ) is a 4 th power mod p = 2017 (a prime) if ( − 7 ) 504 ≡ 1 ( mod 2017 ) . This is a computation you could do by hand with considerable patience; it’s not so bad since 504 factors nicely as 2 3 ⋅ 3 2 ⋅ 7 , so we need to perform six operations of raising something to a small power mod 2017 . It’s arduous, but doable. It’s hard to say if that’s what the question wants you to do. In the context of a course in computational number theory where you’re expected to use a computer, it’s a trivial calculation. In the context of an exam paper, it’s unreasonable to expect a student to carry out this computation, so presumably something else is intended. Perhaps some instance of quartic reciprocity was taught, though I’m hard pressed to see which version would be helpful here for a manual computation. ( − 7 ) happens to be a quadratic residue mod 2017 ; the question would be trivial if it hadn’t been. The question would also have been trivial if 2017 wasn’t 1 mod 4 . But as it stands, the only way I see is to compute ( − 7 ) 504 ≡ − 1 ( mod 2017 ) which proves that − 7 , and 2010 , are not quartic residues mod 2017 . (…)

Question: What is the difference between IMO and IMOCSEA? Can I use resoures of IMO to study IMOCSEA?
Answer: IMO is the International Math Olympiad. It is the most prestigious worldwide math competition for high-school students, held annually since 1959 with over 100 countries participating. The IMOCSEA is, as far as I can tell, a convex combination of a joke, a clueless endeavor and an outright scam. It is organized by an organization calling itself the Global League of Winners, a “duly registered” nonprofit. The letters OC in the name stand for “Olympiad Competition”. To participate in the IMO you need to be selected by your country to represent it, which requires excelling in an increasingly challenging sequence of exams and contests at the national level. To participate in the IMOCSEA you need nothing at all. All problems require proving things. The problems of the IMOCSEA require knowing how to add, multiply, subtract and – I think – divide. They require calculating things. Question: How do you prove or disprove that all highly composite numbers after 60 are divisible by 60?
Answer: The prime factors of highly composite numbers are always the first k primes, for some k . A number N whose prime factorization contains a prime p but misses a prime q < p cannot be highly composite, since there’s a smaller number with just as many divisors: the number you’d obtain by replacing p with q in the prime factorization of N , with the same exponent. Therefore once 2 , 3 and 5 show up in the prime factorization of highly composite numbers, they never disappear, meaning every highly composite number beyond 60 must be divisible by 30 . The sequence of exponents in the prime decomposition of a highly composite number is non-increasing, for the same reason (otherwise, move the higher exponent to the earlier prime to obtain a smaller number with the same number of divisors). Therefore if 2 appears just once in the prime decomposition, every prime must appear just once, meaning the number is squarefree. But this, too, is easy to rule out: if N = 2 ⋅ 3 ⋅ 5 ⋯ p k is a supposed highly composite number with p k ≥ 5 , you can eliminate the last prime p k and replace the 2 by 2 3 to obtain a smaller number with the same number of divisors. So, all highly composite numbers past 60 are divisible by 60 . (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: Intuitively, is the second incompleteness theorem due to a proof of a theory's consistency being more comprehensive (extensive) than the theory itself? (Association: Like a set cannot be a member of itself?)
Answer: No. A consistency proof is not in any way “more comprehensive” than any theory, let alone that theory itself. It helps not at all to look for vague intuitions such as this. The fact that we disallow sets to be members of themselves is, frankly, a choice of convenience, and not a terribly important one. The Axiom of Regularity, which is the axiom in charge of outlawing this, is probably the least important of the ZFC axioms, and you can get a whole lot of mileage without it. In fact, people developed pretty interesting theories of sets which assume its downright negation. The second incompleteness theorem, on the other hand, is a statement of fact about what theories with certain characteristics can and cannot do. It’s not even close to being the same kind of thing as, or an analogue of, the Axiom of Regularity. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: I've worked on several conjectures and mathematically proved them for large numbers. Is it publishable?
Answer: To be publishable, a result needs to be correct, new, and significant. Correctness is non-negotiable. Novelty is also non-negotiable, except that a new proof of a known result could be of interest, and some journals would publish interesting new presentations and summaries of known material. Significance is more vaguely defined, and different publishers would have different thresholds. Nevertheless, some measure of significance is essential: proving some random assertion isn’t sufficient, even if the result is correct and technically new. Proving something “for large numbers” could be a dramatic achievement or an uninteresting realization. There’s nothing inherent that makes it publishable or not. It may be good to point out that there’s a big difference between proving an assertion for infinitely many numbers and proving it for all numbers above a certain threshold. I’ve seen people confuse the two, and they are very much not the same thing. If you need an honest assessment of your work, just post it, and be ready for a critique. (…)

Answer: I previously wrote an answer here about a small pedagogical lesson, which I’m now going to turn into a somewhat larger pedagogical lesson. Some folks who commented on the original answer made progress but fell back into variants of the same trap, and I feel I should reflect that back so we can all learn from these efforts. Plus, there’s a really cool observation here about symmetries of roots of polynomials in the spirit of Galois theory. (I’m leaving the original answer at the bottom, for the record.) So let’s solve the darn thing, but carefully. Step 1: Evaluating the Symmetric Polynomials Questions about several variables obeying various symmetric-looking equations are very often addressed by calculating the values of the symmetric polynomials in those variables; in the case of 3 variables, those are simply s 1 = a + b + c , s 2 = a b + a c + b c and s 3 = a b c . So let’s do that, it’s not terribly difficult. Here, for reference, is our starting point: ⎧ ⎨ ⎩ a + a b = c b + b c = a c + c a = b (*) Adding these equations together, we find a + b + c + a b + b c + a c = a + b + c from which we immediately conclude that s 2 = a b + a c + b c = 0 (2) Having seen massive success from adding the equations, let’s multiply them: ( a + a b ) ( b + b c ) ( c + c a ) = a b c and extract common terms from the things on the left: a b c ( 1 + b ) ( 1 + c ) ( 1 + a ) = a b c This (and the original equations (*)) is obviously satisfied if any one of a , b , c is zero, but <boring> and anyway we got explicitly told that a , b , c are nonzero. Therefore we can cancel a b c to find that ( a + 1 ) ( b + 1 ) ( c + 1 ) = 1 or a b c + a b + a c + b c + a + b + c + 1 = 1 but we already know by (2) that the a b + a c + b c part vanishes, so finally s 1 = a + b + c = − a b c = − s 3 (1+3) To make further progress, we “symmetrize” the original equations by multiplying each one by the variable on the right-hand side, with the goal of having a b c show up in all equations (it’s ok, again, because none of a , b , c is zero): ⎧ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎩ a c + a b c = c 2 b a + a b c = a 2 c b + a b c = b 2 (A) If we now add together these three equations we get a b + a c + b c + 3 a b c = a 2 + b 2 + c 2 (B) and, remembering our previous finding, this is just 3 a b c = a 2 + b 2 + c 2 = ( a + b + c ) 2 Here, the seemingly-wrong equation a 2 + b 2 + c 2 = ( a + b + c ) 2 is justified, once again, by the fact the the second symmetric polynomial a b + a c + b c vanishes, which is the very useful equation (2). If we replace a + b + c by − a b c as we may by (1+3), we get 3 a b c = ( a b c ) 2 and since a b c ≠ 0 , a b c = 3 (3) and by (1+3), a + b + c = − 3 (1) We are done with step 1 of our plan: we’ve determined s 1 , s 2 and s 3 : ⎧ ⎨ ⎩ s 1 = a + b + c = − 3 s 2 = a b + a c + b c = 0 s 3 = a b c = 3 (123) Step 2: PITFALLS! Wait. What was the question again? Oh yes, to find out what a b c can be. Great, we did that: equation (3) says, clear as day, that a b c = 3 . So we’re done, right? Right? We’re not. Here’s why. The question asks to find all possible values of a b c . We showed that the given equations (*), if they are indeed satisfied by three nonzero numbers a , b , c , imply that a b c = 3 . We didn’t show that (*) is actually satisfied by three nonzero numbers – not even complex ones, let alone real. If they’re not, then the value 3 is not possible for a b c . Nothing is. This is Pitfall #1. Some insightful commenters suggested that the pitfall isn’t really so bad. Any three numbers a , b , c are roots of the polynomial p ( X ) = ( X − a ) ( X − b ) ( X − c ) = X 3 − s 1 X 2 + s 2 X − s 3 (If you’ve never seen that, just expand the product form of the polynomial.) Since we’ve taken the trouble to figure out s 1 , s 2 and s 3 , we know exactly what p ( X ) is: p ( X ) = X 3 + 3 X 2 − 3 This polynomial has three roots, and it’s rather easy to show that they are distinct, nonzero and real. So, there: here are our needed a , b , c . They do exist, and of course they satisfy a b c = 3 (as we already know that they must), and we’re done. Right? Right? We’re not. Here’s why: The logical flow is still wrong. We’ve started with (*), did blah blah blah, and arrived at the conclusion that a , b , c must be roots of p ( X ) = 0 . What we never did was show that if we solve p ( X ) = 0 , call the roots a , b , c , and plug them into (*), it’ll work. We’ve never retraced the moves in Step 1 to check that, starting at the end (roots of p ( X ) = 0 ), we can get back at the beginning (satisfying (*)). This is Pitfall #2. It’s a very common error in algebra: manipulating equations often involves steps that are not equivalences, and cannot be traced back. This is how students encounter “extraneous” solutions when doing things like squaring both sides of an equation. So, can we do that here? Can we start with equation (123) and work backwards to get to equation (*)? Go ahead, try it. An interesting step to explore is the move from system (A) to equation (B). We’ve added three equations together and reached a nice conclusion. Can you work that backwards? Can you conclude (A) from (B)? Obviously, you can’t – not in a single, easy step. But perhaps with some more clever work? I can tell you the answer without even trying: YOU CAN’T. Not only are we missing a justification, the assertion we just implicitly made, that the roots of p ( X ) = 0 satisfy (*), is literally false. How do I know? Well, why don’t we just try? The roots of p ( X ) = 0 are not entirely trivial to find by hand, and we will get to that, but for now it’s enough to find approximate, numerical solutions. A quick trip to Desmos and we have them: roots ≈ { 0.879 , − 1.347 , − 2.532 } And here they are, our a , b , c , in full glory. Surely they satisfy (*)? Let’s check: a + a b ≈ − 0.3 which… isn’t even close to c ≈ − 2.532 . This is Pitfall #3, and it’s the coolest one. If we numerically check our own work we determine that it’s simply incorrect. In the context of a problem solving test or something, this is a really tough realization. You may have noticed the little prank I pulled: I’ve listed the roots in decreasing order, which most people probably wouldn’t do. You’d list them in increasing order, right? And then you’d do the same check, and it would work just fine, right? And you’d be justified in declaring victory, right? Right? Well, hell no. Nothing in our analysis suggests a particular way of ordering the roots. If anything, the fact that half the time the numerical verification checks up only makes things worse: we truly don’t understand what’s going on here, do we? Step 3: A Cyclic Cubic I now contend that we could have seen that trouble from the get go. Look again at (*). It’s easy to see that a = b = c is impossible when a , b , c ≠ 0 , so let’s assume that a ≠ b . If someone hands you a legit solution ( a , b , c ) , an ordered triplet of numbers which satisfies (*), what would happen if you flipped a and b ? Would that still work? No, of course not. It would mean that both a + a b = c and b + b a = c which is nonsense. So, from the very beginning we should have known this: nonzero solutions to (*), if they exist (real, complex, doesn’t matter), can by cyclically permuted, meaning you can go a → b , b → c , c → a but not otherwise permuted. You can’t just swap two of them. And once we’ve discovered that these solutions, if they exist, must be roots of p ( X ) = X 3 + 3 X 2 − 3 = 0 , we knew something quite fantastic about this polynomial: its roots have this very unusual symmetry structure. They can be permuted cyclically but not freely. The Galois group is C 3 rather than the much, much more common S 3 . (We should also verify that p ( X ) is irreducible over Q , which is very easy here with, say, the rational root theorem). I once wrote a whole answer about finding such polynomials, and it’s very interesting that this question led us to one (the same one, actually, with a simple shift). You see, the person who devised this question had to work with roots of such a rare polynomial. Roots of fully-symmetric polynomials, whose Galois group is S 3 , cannot satisfy asymmetric equations without also satisfying their symmetrized forms. I honestly never noticed that quite in this form. For a “typical” polynomial with roots a , b , c , if some equation like a + a b = c is true, it must also be true that b + b a = c , because the rich Galois group ensures that any rational relation still holds after any permutation. Again, this is obvious with the ideas of Galois theory (frankly, Lagrange would see through that immediately too), but it’s really nice to be faced with this in such a blatant form. From a pedagogical perspective, this question is awesome in that it forces us to see just how badly things can break if we treat the roots of some polynomial as the answer to a problem. Roots are sets. Variables in problems are ordered sets, or lists. Most polynomials do, actually, allow us to assign their roots to the variables in any way we want, because their roots are fully symmetric. This one doesn’t. A huge pedagogical win. Step 4: Solving and Verifying Furthermore, this property of our polynomial p ( X ) actually holds the key to finally, correctly, solving the original question in full. You see, cyclic polynomials have another nice aspect to them: their roots all belong to the field extension generated by any one of them, which means they can all be expressed as polynomials with rational coefficients of a single root. (I won’t go into the whole theory here, as this answer is already long. Some of the details are in the previous answer on cyclic cubic extensions. Just be aware that this is usually very far from true. The roots of X 3 − 2 , for example, certainly aren’t rational polynomials in 3 √ 2 3 .) I admit that I’m not experienced in carrying out such a calculation by hand. I know what needs to be done, and I could do it with lots of labor, but there are probably shortcuts I’m unaware of. However, it’s very easy to do with Sage (you can see me do it here in a few lines), and once done, it’s very easy to verify the answer by hand. It goes like this: let a be any root of p ( X ) = 0 , so a satisfies a 3 = − 3 a 2 + 3 , and from here we can derive the following simply by multiplying by a and replacing each a 3 with − 3 a 2 + 3 : ⎧ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎩ a 4 = 9 a 2 + 3 a − 9 a 5 = − 24 a 2 − 9 a + 27 a 6 = 63 a 2 + 27 a − 72 { (You can think of these as evaluations of powers of X in the quotient ring Q [ X ] / ⟨ p ( X ) ⟩ . It’s a little tedious, but nothing clever.) Now, set b = − ( a 2 + 2 a ) . This is the magical formula I got from Sage. We can now compute, again completely mechanically: b 2 = a 4 + 4 a 3 + 4 a 2 = a 2 + 3 a + 3 and b 3 = − 3 a 2 − 9 a − 6 and verify that indeed b 3 + 3 b 2 − 3 = 0 , so b is yet another root of p ( X ) = 0 . And since the procedure was completely formal, it follows that c = − ( b 2 + 2 b ) is also a root, and those are the distinct roots (by a simple comparison of elements in a quotient ring). So now we’ve expressed b and c as simple expressions in a , and we have the natural order of the roots emerge – not because of how they are ordered on the real line (which, honestly, is totally random), but because of the way roots of cyclic polynomials must behave. And finally, it is now a completely routine computation to verify that a + a b = c . These are all polynomial expressions in a , or elements in Q [ X ] / ⟨ p ( X ) ⟩ , and it just works. There’s no need to even check the other two equations, as the symmetry of Q [ a ] ensures it. [Note: All of that could have been done by explicitly solving p ( X ) = 0 , most reasonably with trigonometric functions. The substitution X = Z − 1 turns p ( X ) into Z 3 − 3 Z − 1 which is exactly the polynomial discussed in that same answer, so we have explicit trig expressions for the roots of p . I’m sure with some trig effort you can also prove a + a b = c etc.] With that, we have actually proved that the three roots of p ( X ) = 0 , ordered naturally as a (any one of them), b = − ( a 2 + 2 a ) and c = − ( b 2 + 2 b ) , do indeed satisfy (*), and therefore a b c = 3 is indeed a possible outcome. But I argue that before we’ve done that, or something morally equivalent, we could not have made a good faith assertion that 3 is indeed a possible value of a b c given that a , b , c are nonzero reals satisfying (*). And I suspect that the designers of this problem, if it was meant for some contest or something, didn’t notice that or they simply assumed that the students wouldn’t worry about this subtlety either, and they let it slide. (Original answer below.) I think there’s a small but useful pedagogical lesson here. As I’m writing this, the question has two answers, by Doug Dillon and by Ragu Rajagopalan. Both answers are very good: they start with the given information, perform a series of clever manipulations, and conclude with a b c = 3 . That’s it, right? The answer is that a b c must be 3 . But the question asks to find all possible values of a b c . Those other answers show that it can’t be anything other than 3 , but they don’t show that it can actually be 3 . If this system of equations has any solution in nonzero real numbers, then yes, we know that such a solution must satisfy a b c = 3 , great. But what if there’s no solution in nonzero real numbers at all? If that’s the case then the correct answer is nothing. The magnitude a b c can’t be anything since there’s no solution. (If you wish to nitpick, it can be argued that the answer in this case is everything. If a , b , c are three real numbers satisfying a system of equations that cannot be satisfied, then a b c = 23 , a b c = − 5 and Donald Trump is a decent human being. But never mind.) The pedagogical lesson here is that when we are solving equations we are actually working in the wrong direction. We start with the equations, manipulate, and arrive at x = 17 . But we’re not done: we now need to work backwards from x = 17 and show that it does indeed satisfy the given equation. If all the steps in our derivation are equivalences then it’s fine and there’s no need to check anything. But many students have learned the hard way that many algebraic manipulations of equations are not equivalences: for example, squaring both sides of an equation may yield incorrect, extraneous solutions. One must always check. The sequence of steps in the solutions by Doug and Ragu are not equivalences, because it’s certainly not true that if a b c = 3 them the system is satisfied. Try, for example, a = b = c = 3 √ 3 . Doesn’t work. Therefore the condition a b c = 3 is necessary, but not sufficient, for the system to hold. I have a sneaking suspicion that the designers of this question didn’t consider that subtlety themselves, because as far as I can tell, showing that this system is satisfiable over the nonzero reals is not easy, and arguably much harder than the proof of a b c = 3 ! If you see a slick argument, please share. I can see numerically that solutions exist, possibly just one solution up to cyclic permutations, but I don’t know how I would prove it in a problem-solving context. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question:
There are
122
integer points in a convex polygon.
How do I show that there must exists
12
points collinear?
Answer: Imagine if, instead of 122 lattice points, the question had indicated 123 . Or 125 . Or, gasp, 144 . The result would still be true – obviously, if something like this is true with some number of lattice points, then it surely holds with a larger number. But if the problem authors wanted to be really, really, evil, they could have used a larger number and I guarantee you, fewer people would solve it. How can that be? How can a question become harder when the data is more lenient? The reason is that the numbers 12 and 122 have a fairly obvious connection: 122 = 11 2 + 1 . Therefore, the problem is handing is a huge hint: the general case is about a convex polygon with n 2 + 1 lattice points for some n , and you need to prove the existence of n + 1 colinear points. This is true, and it gives us a lot more to work with. We can check small cases of n . We can try to guess why n 2 + 1 , which turns out to be a major clue. With seemingly random parameters the question is completely opaque, and with 144 instead of 122 it is downright misleading – it would suggest needing n 2 lattice points for n colinear ones, which is misleading. You don’t need that many, but the obvious wrong formula suggests itself. Moral: problem designers are sometimes, but not always, on your side. Try to guess why they came up with the parameters they came up with. This may be a helping hand. With that side speech out of the way, let’s go back to the actual question. We have a convex polygon in the plane with n 2 + 1 lattice points (points with integer coordinates) inside of it. It’s not made very clear whether we should or shouldn’t count points on the very edges of the polygon, but it doesn’t really matter as long as we keep the interpretation consistent for both the given and the thing to prove. Now, what’s up with that n 2 + 1 ? What can you do with n 2 + 1 objects that you can’t do with n 2 ? Your problem solving experience should have an answer handy: you can throw them into n 2 boxes and guarantee a collision. The good old Schubfachprinzip. How do you map lattice points into n 2 boxes? If you’ve seen questions in combinatorial geometry, such as “given 5 lattice points show that some lattice point lies on the line segment connecting two of them”, you may see an almost obvious, almost inevitable mapping: map the point with integer coordinates ( a , b ) to ( a mod n , b mod n ) . Just reduce the coordinates mod n . There are n 2 possible combinations ( r , s ) for those residues, and in our case there must be lattice points inside the polygon, let’s call them ( a 1 , b 1 ) and ( a 2 , b 2 ) , with the same pair of residues: a 1 ≡ a 2 ( mod n ) and b 1 ≡ b 2 ( mod n ) . From here it’s plain sailing: say a 2 = a 1 + k 1 n and b 2 = b 1 + k 2 n . The points ( a 1 + k 1 j , a 2 + k 2 j ) for j = 0 , 1 , … , n are all on the line segment from ( a 1 , b 1 ) to ( a 2 , b 2 ) , so they are all inside our convex polygon, and they are clearly colinear, and there’s clearly n + 1 of them, and that’s all. ■ I’m seriously saying that I wouldn’t be able to solve this as quickly, or at all, if the question had 125 instead of 122 . (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: Are mathematics students at HYPSM able to prove anything asked on abstract algebra exams without looking into textbooks and/or memorizing known proofs? Is too hard for any student to do proofs out of their own heads under time pressure?
Answer: Such questions get asked quite regularly, and they reveal some common misunderstandings. Math students generally won’t be able to answer anything asked on a test for a course they haven’t taken yet. If it’s a course they did take then yes, many serious students of math could do well on a test for a course they just took and sometimes, but not always, for a course they took last semester or last year. “Memorizing proofs” is a strange myth. It’s really not a thing. Proofs you understand you don’t need to memorize – in fact you can’t memorize. “Memorizing” is just not the right term to describe proofs you’ve internalized. I know many proofs, and I won’t describe any of them as something I’ve “memorized”. On the other hand, if you somehow commit full proofs to memory, you won’t do well on the exam. You won’t be able to apply your understanding to any new problem you haven’t seen before. Even if an exam question asks to present the proof of a known theorem, it takes two sentences to see if a student is writing up a reasoned argument they understand or regurgitating some textbook proof, verbatim. Now, sometimes there’s a key trick or approach that may not be obvious and you may need to remember. That’s fine. It’s not “memorizing a proof”, it’s recalling an idea. There’s another related myth, and that is that exam problems are about specific things you’ve learned. They are not. A final exam looks to see if students are able to apply their understanding to questions they’ve never seen before. That’s the whole point. Consequently, the exam questions (which sometimes show up) that ask to prove a specific theorem studied in class are the easiest questions on the exam. They are considered a giveaway. All of the above is true A) regardless of the course, be it abstract algebra or complex variables or measure theory, and B) regardless of whether the school is “HYPSM” (an acronym I had to look up) or the University of Milan or Warwick or Ohio State. Good students retain their knowledge and are able to apply their understanding throughout their undergrad years and beyond. Students who struggle with the material may not be able to do so, and it doesn’t matter if they are at Harvard or a small community college. To the second question, “Is it too hard for any students to do proofs out of their own heads under time pressure” – like everything else, it’s hard for some students and not very challenging for others. In fact, n ! is exactly the number of bijections (one-to-one, onto functions) of a set of n elements to itself. It doesn’t matter which set of n elements; they have the same number of permutations. Question: Do there exist finitely generated groups that have an infinite minimal generating set?
Answer: Nice question. The answer is no. First, to eliminate any confusion: a minimal generating set doesn’t mean a generating set with the smallest possible cardinality. It means a generating set for which any proper subset is no longer a generating set. In other words, it’s a generating set that has no redundancy: removing any element makes the set no longer generate the whole group. For example, in the additive group Z of integers, { 1 } is a generating set that’s obviously minimal, but { 2 , 3 } is also a minimal generating set, as is { 6 , 10 , 15 } . In fact (exercise), there are minimal generating sets with k elements, for any k ∈ N > 0 . However, Z does not possess an infinite minimal generating set, not does any other finitely-generated group. To see this, let G be a finitely-generated group, S a finite generating set of G , and X an infinite generating set. For every s ∈ S we can pick a subset X s ⊂ X such that s ∈ ⟨ X s ⟩ : this is possible because ⟨ X ⟩ = G . The key point is that X s can be taken to be finite: the element s can be expressed as a product of the elements of X and their inverses, and any such expression is, by definition, finite. So s already belongs to ⟨ X s ⟩ for some finite set X s . Now, the union ⋃ s ∈ S X s ⊂ X is finite, and it generates S , so it generates G . Therefore X , the infinite generating set, isn’t minimal: it has a finite generating subset. ■ (…)

Answer: (You meant to write that A ′ is the set of accumulation points of A . This is standard notation, and A ′ is called the derived set of A .) In any topological space, a set A is closed if, and only if, A ′ ⊆ A . This is just a rephrasing of the definition: a set is closed iff it contains each of its accumulation points. Therefore, ( A ′ ) ′ ⊆ A ′ precisely when A ′ is closed. The question, therefore, is whether derived sets are always closed. The answer is No, but it’s Yes for “reasonable spaces”. It’s a characteristic feature of point-set topology that the sheer definition of a topology accommodates plenty of unusual situations, and in many contexts people prefer to assume a few separation axioms in order to avoid such situations. For a simple counterexample, take any space X with the trivial (indiscrete) topology, where the only open sets are ∅ ∅ and X . As long as X has more than a single point, you’ll observe that A = { a } , a singleton, has a derived set A ′ = X ∖ { a } , because for any b ≠ a , any open set containing b contains a (since the only available such open set is X ). So any point other than a itself is an accumulation point, and A ′ is not closed (because { a } is not open). However, in a T 1 space, for every pair of distinct points a , b you have a neighborhood of a that doesn’t contain b and a neighborhood of b that doesn’t contain a . Under those circumstances you can show that a derived set A ′ is always closed. The axiom T 1 is pretty mild: Every Hausdorff space, and therefore every metric space, is T 1 . (…)

Question: Similar rational fractions, like say 1/7 produce a decimal loop, say 0. (142857). Is there a fast way to determine the length of a loop for any fraction a/b without calculating it?
Answer: Yes. The short version: the “length of the loop”, called the period, is the order of 10 mod m where m the denominator b after eliminating any common factors with a and any factors of 2 and 5 . This may not make a lot of sense to you, so here’s the long version: Step 1. reduce the fraction. If the numerator a and the denominator b have any common factors, divide both of them by these common factors. For example, if you’re looking at the fraction 12 63 , reduce it to 4 21 . Step 2. From now on we can forget about a and focus just on the denominator b . If b is divisible by 2 or 5 , divide it by 2 or 5 and keep doing this until you’re left with a number, call it m , which is divisible by neither 2 nor 5 . For example, if the denominator was 2920 , divide it by 10 to get 292 , then by 2 to get 146 , then by 2 again to get 73 = m . Step 3. This is the fun part. Starting with the number 1 , repeat the following procedure: A) Multiply the number you have by 10 . B) Reduce the number mod m , meaning, compute the remainder when dividing by m . This remainder is your new number. C) If the result is 1 , stop. If not, go back to A). The number of times you did step A), meaning the number of times you multiplied by 10 , is the length of the (decimal) period of the fraction a b . For example, if the original fraction was 77 20440 , you’d need to notice that the fraction isn’t reduced because numerator and denominator are both divisible by 7 . Per step 1, reduce it to find 11 2920 . Then, per step 2, eliminate factors of 2 and 5 from 2920 to obtain m = 73 . Now let’s go through step 3. We start with 1 , and then: If you kept count, you multiplied by 10 exactly 8 times, so that’s the length of the period: 77 20440 = 11 2920 = 0.003 ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ 76712328 The 76712328 part keeps repeating, and it has length 8 . If the denominator is a prime number p , the period will always be a divisor of p − 1 . In general, if the denominator is m (after reducing the fraction and eliminating 2 's and 5 's), the period is never more than m , and in fact it’s a divisor of an easy-to-compute number called φ ( m ) , the Euler totient function of m . The procedure I described may not, strictly speaking, be faster than actually computing the decimal expansion of a b using long division. The speed of carrying out either procedure depends on the time cost of the individual steps in the process, which may vary between people and computational models. Still, for doing things by hand this procedure is usually much faster, and it has the added bonus that it teaches you to ignore the numerator. Once you know the period of 11 73 , you know the period of 1 73 and 72 73 and whatever. Blindly doing long division for each of these fractions would be a wasteful way of finding the period. I gave you a mysterious recipe without explaining why it works. I don’t like doing such things, but explaining why this works from basic principles of arithmetic would make this answer very long. This gets easier once you’ve learned a bit more of elementary number theory. (…)

Question: How do I find the cyclic subgroup of order 24 of Q (Surd [m,12],ξ12) where m is a square free integer?
Answer: It’s not entirely clear what is being asked here, but I found the question interesting nonetheless – at least, my interpretation of the question. Here’s my understanding. We have an integer m ≥ 2 , and we form the number field K = Q ( α , ζ ) where ζ = ζ 12 is a primitive 12 th root of unity, and α = 12 √ m . The field K is, in fact, the splitting field (over Q ) of the polynomial X 12 − m . Take this as an exercise if you don’t immediately see why. Now, finding a cyclic subgroup of order 24 in (the multiplicative group of) K is equivalent to locating, in K , an element of order 24 , which is the same thing as a 24 th root of unity. So, this raises a few questions: We can take ζ to be √ 3 + i 2 , simply because this is exp ( 2 π i / 12 ) . This already tells you some interesting things: the field Q ( ζ ) , even before we threw in α , contains i (because i = ζ 3 ), and therefore it also contains √ 3 (consider 2 ζ − i ), and √ − 3 . You can also show that ζ 4 − ζ 2 + 1 = 0 either by direct computation, or by factoring X 12 − 1 to uncover the 12 th cyclotomic polynomial Φ 12 ( X ) = X 4 − X 2 + 1 . The elements of order 24 are the primitive 24 th roots of unity, of which ω = exp ( 2 π i / 24 ) is one. With a bit of trigonometry you can find that ω = √ 2 + √ 6 4 + i √ 3 − 1 2 √ 2 The precise formula is not super important; what’s important is this: if our field K contains √ 2 then it contains ω , and if not, it doesn’t. You can also see this without any trigonometry at all: purely algebraically, using the relation ζ 4 = ζ 2 − 1 , you can check that ( ζ 3 − ζ 2 − ζ ) 2 = 2 ζ And from this, you conclude that √ 2 2 ( ζ 3 − ζ 2 − ζ ) is an element whose square is ζ , so it is our ω (or − ω ). And reciprocally, if the field has ω then you can isolate √ 2 from this equation, concluding that √ 2 must be in the field. Conclusion so far: the field K contains ω , an element of order 24 , if and only if it contains √ 2 . There are two simple cases where this does indeed happen: This answers question 2 when m = 2 or m = 6 . To answer question 1, with proof (which is really question 3), we must show that for other values of m it is not the case that √ 2 ∈ K , and therefore also ω ∉ K . As a warm up, let’s show that √ 2 ∉ Q ( ζ ) . This actually follows from our observation that, had that not been true, we would have ω ∈ Q ( ζ ) , and that would mean that the cyclotomic fields of order 12 and 24 coincide, and that’s not so. But let’s suppose we don’t know any of that. Here’s a more direct argument. Since ζ has degree 4 over Q , the Galois group G = Gal ( Q ( ζ ) / Q ) has order 4 . In fact, it is the Klein 4 -group, but let’s not even worry about that: whatever that group is, it can’t have more than 3 subgroups of index 2 . But we already know that Q ( ζ ) contains 3 quadratic subfields: Q ( √ 3 ) , Q ( √ − 3 ) and Q ( i ) . By the fundamental theorem of Galois theory, there cannot be any other quadratic subfields, since any extension of Q which is contained in Q ( ζ ) and has degree 2 is the fixed field of a subgroup of index 2 of G , and there are no more such subgroups. We conclude that √ 2 ∉ Q ( ζ ) . We can follow a similar procedure to show that √ 2 ∉ K , with the caveat that the computation of Gal ( K / Q ) is more elaborate. Briefly, the field K is the compositum of the two fields Q ( ζ ) , which is a Galois extension of Q , and Q ( α ) , which is not. Nevertheless, we can view K as the Galois extension of Q ( ζ ) by the polynomial X 12 − m which is irreducible except when m = 3 (the irreducibility of X n − a is a classical result – it’s in Lang’s Algebra, VIII sec. 9, or see here). The exceptional case is X 12 − 3 = ( X 6 + √ 3 ) ( X 6 − √ 3 ) = ( X 6 − ζ 3 + 2 ζ ) ( X 6 + ζ 3 − 2 ζ ) From this we can identify the Galois group G = Gal ( K / Q ) as a group of order 48 , and it’s the same group no matter what m is except that it’s a different group, of order 24 , when m = 3 . Computing this group by hand is doable, but I used Sage to compute it and count its index- 2 subgroups. There are 7 of them, and they correspond to i , √ 3 , √ − 3 , √ m , √ − m , √ 3 m and √ − 3 m . None of these fields includes √ 2 unless m = 6 , which completes our analysis: The field K = Q ( α , ζ ) contains a subgroup of order 24 if, and only if, m = 2 or m = 6 , in which case we can present the element (or “find” the group) explicitly using the formulas displayed above. ■ (…)

This isn’t just to warm up: it’ll actually be helpful. On the real number line R , the interior of a “circle” of radius r with center Q is just the open interval ( Q − r , Q + r ) , which we will denote B ( Q , r ) . The “lattice points” are the integers Z , and B ( Q , r ) doesn’t contain a lattice point precisely when the distance from Q to the nearest integer is at least r . So, for which r is it true that for any d > 0 you can find to open intervals B ( Q 1 , r ) and B ( Q 2 , r ) which do not contain lattice points and such that d ( Q 1 , Q 2 ) = | Q 1 − Q 2 | = d ? Instead of saying “there’s no lattice point in B ( Q , r ) ", we can say “ Q lies outside of B ( N , r ) for every integer N ∈ Z ". It’s a bit easier to form this mental model: draw the circle of radius r around every lattice point N . The allowed centers Q are now just those centers which lie outside of, or on, those circles. The question is whether we can find, for any given d > 0 , two points Q 1 , Q 2 at a distance d that are both in the “safe zone” outside of those intervals B ( N , r ) . On the other hand, as soon as r > 1 4 , you can no longer do that. We can achieve very small distances: but larger distances that are just short of 2 r cannot be achieved. Question: Is the conjecture correct that every even number greater than 2 can be represented as the sum of the digit sums of two prime numbers?
Answer: Yes, this is true. The reason has little to do with even numbers being the sum of two such digit-sums: it follows from a more natural fact. The fact is this: for any desired digit-sum k that’s not divisible by 3 , there exists some prime number p whose digit-sum is k . For example: 2 is the digit sum of 11 , 4 is the digit sum of 13 , 5 of 23 , 7 of 43 and so on. Multiples of 3 must be excluded, for obvious reasons (except that 3 itself is fine.) This is a consequence of Theorem 1.1 in the paper Primes with an Average Sum of Digits by Drmota, Mauduit and Rivat. The notation used here is that s q ( p ) is the sum of the base- q digits of the prime p , μ q = ( q − 1 ) / 2 and σ 2 q = ( q 2 − 1 ) / 12 . The requirement ( k , q − 1 ) = 1 is just the right generalization of our requirement that k is not divisible by 3 . Digit-sums that are not relatively prime to q − 1 , the base minus 1 , are not generally possible to obtain. Among other things, this theorem says that for large enough x there do indeed exist primes p ≤ x whose digit-sum in base 10 , is k for our pre-selected desired k . Now, given any number n (doesn’t matter if it’s even or odd, actually), either n − 2 or n − 4 is not divisible by 3 . Set k = n − 2 or k = n − 4 accordingly, find a prime p with digit sum s ( p ) = k , and add 2 (given by the prime 11 ) or 4 (given by the prime 13 ) to produce n . (…)

Question: If the Riemann Hypothesis were proven true, how would one go about using the result to calculate the exact formula for the nth prime (not an algorithm!) given no knowledge of any other prime?
Answer: The question rests on several deeply entrenched misunderstandings. First, if the Riemann Hypothesis enabled us to calculate something, we would calculate that something now, regardless of whether a proof is or isn’t available. We would say “here’s a formula for the n th prime, but be aware that it may be not quite correct if RH is false”. In fact, people say such things all the time. We have many formulas that are only known to be true if the RH holds, but that doesn’t stop anyone from producing, publishing, sharing, studying and improving these formulas. Second, there is no standard interpretation of the phrase “exact formula (not an algorithm!)”. What’s an exact formula that’s not an algorithm? All formulas are simply succinctly described algorithms. You can choose a small set of allowed operations and demand that they, and only they, are to be used in a formula-not-an-algorithm, but there’s no such restricted set that people have settled on. Finally, even if you gave me your definition of formula-not-an-algorithm, quite regardless of what you would choose to permit or ban, there’s zero reason to believe that the RH, with or without proof, would let us produce a formula for the n th prime. There’s a pervasive belief that the RH yields “a formula for primes”, whatever that means, and I honestly don’t know why that happened. The Riemann Hypothesis does not do that. (…)

Pick any two points P , Q inside U = B ( 0 , 1 ) ∖ { 0 } such that the line segment ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ P Q is contained in U . We want to use the mean value theorem to compare f ( P ) and f ( Q ) , but maybe you haven’t seen a multivariable MVT. An easy way to put us back in single-variable land is to consider the function g ( t ) = f ( P + t ( Q − P ) ) . This is a differentiable function of a single variable with g ( 0 ) = f ( P ) and g ( 1 ) = f ( Q ) ; it’s just what you get when you walk at a steady pace from P to Q , watching f as you go. The ordinary MVT says that g ( 1 ) − g ( 0 ) = g ′ ( c ) for some c between 0 and 1 . Now you need the (multivariable) chain rule to compute g ′ ( c ) , and it comes to g ′ ( c ) = ∇ f ( P + c ( Q − P ) ) ⋅ ( Q − P ) On the right hand side we have the dot product of the gradient of f at the intermediate point and the vector Q − P . You can also write this out explicitly using the components of P and Q and the partial derivatives. The point is, if the partial derivatives are bounded, this dot product is also bounded, uniformly. If the partial derivatives never exceed 100 (in absolute value), and since the complements of Q − P cannot exceed 2 , the whole dot product cannot exceed like 400 or something. Therefore the value f ( P ) keeps the values of f ( Q ) bounded, as long as there’s a straight line segment from P to Q inside our region U . But this small restriction isn’t a problem: you can get from P to any point R by first walking along a straight line segment P Q and then another straight line segment Q R . The value f ( R ) lies within 800 of the value f ( P ) . So, a function on B ( 0 , 1 ) , with or without removing a point, must be bounded if its partial derivatives are bounded. There are many other sets you can apply the same argument to; it’s not specific to B ( 0 , 1 ) . (…)

Answer: This is the kind of problem that suits a rather narrow interval of mathematical maturity. Too early it is useless, and too late it’s a bit too easy. Many such students are already familiar with the general result (for numbers above 3 , or more precisely above e , the larger between a b and b a is the one with the larger exponent and smaller base). Question: Is there any way to iterate fractions in collatz conjecture eg finding the collatz iteration of 7/3?
Answer: Of course. You can define a function C ( q ) in any number of ways which takes a rational number q and returns a rational number, such that if q happens to be an integer then C ( q ) is precisely the Collatz iteration ( q / 2 if q is even, 3 q + 1 it it’s odd). Whenever you ask yourself “can I extend some function to have a broader domain of applicability”, you should immediately answer yourself “yes”, and then ask yourself a follow-up question: what would I want this extended function to do? What properties should it have so I can learn something from it? See, I can define C ( q ) to be q / 2 if q is an even integer, 3 q + 1 if q is an odd integer, and 17 / 23 if q is not an integer. Now I can happily iterate C ( q ) on any rational input q . So? The behavior on the non-integers is very boring, and it doesn’t teach us anything useful about the Collatz conjecture. Perhaps you want C ( q ) to be a little bit more than C ( ⌊ q ⌋ ) , like C ( 23 1 17 ) should be just a bit more than 70 ? Of course this can be arranged as well, easily. And again, so? What have we learned about Collatz? (Hint: nothing). In your question, you’ve used the expression “finding the Collatz iteration of 7 / 3 ", as if there’s something we need to find. There isn’t. Collatz doesn’t say anything about rational numbers, so there isn’t anything for us to find. We can define the “Collatz” iteration of 7 / 3 to be whatever we want, but unless we find some clever way of making it do something really interesting, there’s nothing to solve here. I’m not aware of anything really interesting from Q to Q , but there are quite intriguing extensions of C to things like Z 2 , the 2 -adic integers; see here, for example. Name: Alon Amit
Question: Some Quora users claim that all finite state games, like tic-tac-toe, chess or Go, if played optimally by both players, would end in draw. Is that so? In particular, what's known about chess and Go?
Answer: Of course that’s not true. Many games (such as common variants of Go) don’t have draw as a possible outcome, and among the games that do it’s entirely possible that under optimal play it’s the first player that always wins, or that the second player always does. This is Zermelo’s Theorem, and it’s not a difficult thing to prove. You can spend a few minutes inventing short, simple games that exhibit any of those behaviors. Chess and Go are covered by the theorem, so either the first player has a winning strategy, or the second, or (in chess) they can force a draw. It is not known which. (…)

If you’ve never observed or encountered this fact, that’s ok: you’re probably aware that the multiplicative group of any finite field is cyclic. Pick a generator of the group, observe that some power of that generator is 1 , and conclude that the whole field is an extension of the base field generated by this single element, and this extension is therefore radical. As for part (b), in most sources I’m familiar with, a polynomial is said to be solvable by radicals iff its splitting field is contained in some radical extension. Here, the splitting field is a radical extension, so the answer is also yes. Yes, but. I’m not sure this is what the question is getting at. Answer: I could defend each of the answers “yes”, “no” and “we don’t know”. Let’s start with the “no”. Let’s take a very special case of your question, like 2 x 5 − 10 x + 5 = 0 . This equation defines 5 complex numbers which are its roots; but what are they? Can we express them in some kind of “formula”? We know that we can’t express them with radicals, the way we do with equations of degree n = 2 , 3 , 4 . Galois theory precisely shows that (the Galois group of this particular polynomial is the non-solvable group S 5 ). So that’s a first-degree “no” answer to the question. But what about other expressions? Trig functions, logs, etc.? In the paper What is a closed-form number, Tim Chow uses the very same polynomial equation as an example. He then proves that, under the well-known Schanuel conjecture, the roots of this equation (or any other polynomial equation with non-solvable Galois group) are not EL-numbers, which means they cannot be expressed with any of the familiar elementary functions (logs, exponents, trig functions, roots and any combination thereof.) So that’s a second-degree “no” answer: the roots of such equations aren’t EL numbers, which means that they cannot be expressed with formulas consisting of logs, exponents, sines, cosines, arctangents and other familiar functions. Even specific polynomial equations don’t have roots that are expressible in this way, let alone a general formula. But, to be fair, Chow’s result rests on a big, unproven conjecture. It’s possible (though extremely unlikely) that the conjecture is false and that somehow, miraculously, there’s some EL expression for the roots of polynomial equations. So, in that sense, and sticking with EL numbers as the correct universe of “formulas”, the precise answer is “we don’t know”. Finally, the answer may reasonably be “yes” if you allow more flexibility in the concept of “formula”. For example, polynomial equations of degree n = 5 can be solved with the Bring radical, and higher-degree polynomials can be handled with other fancy functions. From a different perspective, polynomial equations with rational coefficients can be solved efficiently with methods such as Newton-Raphson. Those are iterative in nature, and I often see people object to them because they don’t offer a “closed” expression. But you may want to ask yourself, why would you accept a formula such as tan ( log ( 5 ) ) as a solution? What does this expression do for you that Newton-Raphson does not? Sure, we’re familiar with those functions and may feel we “get” them, but computing the value of such an expression is exactly the same kind of iterative procedure as Newton-Raphson: you can iterate and produce an approximation at any desired accuracy. From this perspective, the roots of polynomial equations with rational coefficients are computable numbers, and it’s reasonable to equate computability with “having a formula”, even if the formula isn’t as succinct and friendly as the quadratic formula. Question: If multiplication is basically repeated addition, why must Peano arithmetic have separate axioms for multiplication?
Answer: The Peano Axioms don’t need to have separate axioms for multiplication, and in fact they don’t even need to have separate axioms for addition either. It’s possible to formalize Peano Arithmetic with just two non-logical symbols: 0 and S , a constant symbol and a unary function symbol. Those are understood to mean the natural number 0 and the successor function S ( n ) = n + 1 . Both addition and multiplication are just shortcuts on top of these operators, defined through induction. You can see this carried out, for example, in the Wikipedia article on Peano Arithmetic. (EDIT: I usually refer to first-order Peano axioms when I write about Peano arithmetic, and I didn’t do that here, I’m sorry. This narrative as it stands conveniently fits the framework of second-order logic, which may be fine in context but I shouldn’t implicitly assume that. In first-order formalization you need to explicitly add axioms for both addition and multiplication – essentially for the same reason: you can’t define addition from the successor function and you can’t define multiplication from addition. Thanks, Senia, for pointing that out.) (…)

Answer: Almost! But no. You can do 1999 , but not 2000 . Let’s try to figure out how many numbers we can pick among the integers from 1 to n so as not to have any number and its double. To illustrate this, here is the situation with n = 24 , where we drew a connection between any number and its double: The rule is that if we pick any number, we can’t pick any other number connected to it. In the language of graph theory, we’re looking for a maximal independent set in this graph. There are two big pieces of good news here: In fact, you should be able to see that the following procedure is optimal: in each chain, pick the first element, skip, pick the third element, skip, pick the fifth element and so on. Here’s what you would do here: For chains of odd length this is literally the only possible choice in getting the maximum number of elements. For chains of even length, like 3 , 6 , 12 , 24 , we could have also flipped things around and chosen 6 , 24 instead of 3 , 12 , but that wouldn’t get us anything larger – just an alternative way of getting the same amount of numbers. To keep things simple and consistent, we can always start with the smallest number in the chain, which (as you can see) is always the unique odd number starting the chain. So what numbers are we picking here? Another way to characterize these numbers is as follows: those are the numbers with even 2 -valuation. The 2 -valuation of a natural number is the largest power k such that 2 k divides the number. Odd numbers have 2 -valuation 0 , odd numbers × 2 have 2 -valuation 1 , odd numbers × 4 have 2 -valuation 2 , and so on. (In other words, the 2 -valuation is the number of trailing zeroes in the binary representation of a number.) We need exactly the numbers with even 2 -valuation. Every number with an even 2 -valuation has a double with an odd 2 -valuation, so we never pick a number and its double. At the same time, we are picking the maximum possible number of elements from any chain b , 2 b , 4 b , 8 b , … with b odd, so this choice is indeed optimal. For brevity, let’s call numbers with even 2 -valuation “useful”. If you need to keep as many numbers as possible from 1 to n without picking any number and its double, pick the useful numbers. So now we know what numbers we need to pick for any given n , but how many are there? How many useful numbers are there from 1 to n ? In the example n = 24 we found 16 useful numbers, or exactly 2 / 3 . In the question we are asked about 2000 out of 3000 , also 2 / 3 . We are led to expect something like 2 / 3 of the numbers from 1 to n to be useful. But why? Here’s how I went about finding a way to count useful numbers. Let’s denote the number of useful numbers from 1 to n by f ( n ) . For example, we have f ( 1 ) = 1 , f ( 8 ) = 5 , f ( 24 ) = 16 and we will find that f ( 3000 ) = 1999 . Given the definition of useful numbers, you should expect some simple recursive relations between f ( n ) and f ( 2 n ) and f ( 2 n + 1 ) . Indeed, consider f ( 2 n ) . There are two kinds of useful numbers from 1 to 2 n : all odd numbers (there are n of those), and the useful even numbers, each of which is twice a non-useful number between 1 and n . This means that f ( 2 n ) = n + ( n − f ( n ) ) or f ( 2 n ) = 2 n − f ( n ) Also, f ( 2 n + 1 ) is simply f ( 2 n ) + 1 , since the useful numbers through 2 n + 1 are simply the useful numbers through 2 n plus the number 2 n + 1 itself, which is always odd and therefore always useful. But this means that f ( 2 n + 1 ) = f ( 2 n ) + 1 = ( 2 n − f ( n ) ) + 1 , or f ( 2 n + 1 ) = 2 n + 1 − f ( n ) Putting these together, we find that for any number N (even or odd), f ( N ) = N − f ( ⌊ N / 2 ⌋ ) Let’s see this in action for N = 24 . f ( 24 ) = 24 − f ( 12 ) = 24 − 12 + f ( 6 ) = 24 − 12 + 6 − f ( 3 ) = 24 − 12 + 6 − 3 + f ( 1 ) = 24 − 12 + 6 − 3 + 1 = 16 In general, we find that f ( N ) = N − ⌊ N 2 ⌋ + ⌊ N 4 ⌋ − ⌊ N 8 ⌋ + … (This a finite sum, since eventually the denominator 2 k will exceed N ). With that, I was able to do f ( 3000 ) literally in my head while walking the dogs: f ( 3000 ) = 3000 − 1500 + 750 − 375 + 187 − 93 + 46 − 23 + 11 − 5 + 2 − 1 = 1999 (This isn’t as hard as it may look; the intermediate steps are all centered around 2000 , jumping up and down in fairly easy ways.) We also see now why f ( n ) ≈ 2 3 n : the infinite series 1 − 1 2 + 1 4 − 1 8 converges to exactly 2 3 . Answer: I prefer to phrase this a little differently: if p ( X ) = 0 has no solution in Q , must there be some m such that p ( X ) ≡ 0 ( mod m ) has no solutions in integers? Or even better, contrapositively: if p ( X ) ≡ 0 ( mod m ) is solvable for every m (“locally”), must p ( X ) = 0 be solvable in Q (“globally”)? This is an instance of the “local-global” principle which does hold in certain contexts, but these contexts are usually of relatively low degree. In high degree, things get complicated, so we expect the answer to be No, that’s not true. There’s a little subtlety here: a somewhat weaker statement would only assert solvability mod p for p prime. It is then easier to find counterexamples: p ( X ) = ( X 2 + 1 ) ( X 2 − 2 ) ( X 2 + 2 ) has no rational solutions, yet at least one of − 1 , 2 , − 2 is a quadratic residue mod any given prime, so p ( X ) ≡ 0 ( mod p ) is always solvable. So this particular polynomial doesn’t satisfy the stronger requirement that p ( X ) ≡ 0 ( mod m ) be solvable for all moduli m , not just the prime ones. But this isn’t too hard to fix: the quadratic factor x 2 + 7 does have roots mod 8 and in fact mod any higher power of 2 . Therefore, the improved polynomial p ( X ) = ( X 2 + 1 ) ( X 2 − 2 ) ( X 2 + 2 ) ( X 2 + 7 ) still has no rational roots, but it’s solvable mod m for any m . In other words, there’s no integer which doesn’t divide any value p ( n ) . Proving the assertions I made is an application of quadratic reciprocity, Hensel’s lemma and the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Answer: Every non-empty set of positive integers has a smallest element. This is one form of the principle of induction. If there are any initial values of the Collatz iteration which don’t reach 1 , there must be a smallest one n 0 . But if any initial value reaches a lower value then starting the iteration at n 0 will get you to some n 1 < n 0 , and this n 1 as a starting value eventually reaches 1 (because n 0 is the smallest one that supposedly doesn’t), and that’s a contradiction. Therefore, if it’s true that every initial value > 1 hits a lower value, then every initial value reaches 1 . (…)
