Answer: If n is even, 8 n ≡ ( − 1 ) n ≡ 1 ( mod 3 ) , and then 8 n + 47 ≡ 0 ( mod 3 ) and it cannot be prime. If n ≡ 1 ( mod 4 ) then 8 n ≡ 3 n ≡ 3 ( mod 5 ) (Fermat’s Little Theorem) and then 8 n + 47 ≡ 0 ( mod 5 ) and it cannot be prime. If n ≡ 3 ( mod 4 ) then 8 n ≡ 5 ( mod 13 ) (observe that 8 2 ≡ − 1 ( mod 13 ) ) and then 8 n + 47 ≡ 0 ( mod 13 ) and it cannot be prime. So no, 8 n + 47 is never prime. It’s always divisible by 3 , 5 or 13 (and it is much larger than any of those factors, so it can’t be any of them.) ■ How did I find these congruences? I assumed the answer to the question is No, since if it had been Yes it’s either because 8 n + 47 is prime for some very small n (which it’s not), or else it’s prime for some n that’s impossible to find by hand, and I assumed this question is meant to be solvable by hand. We don’t have any useful methods for showing that a prime number must exist in any expression more complicated than a n + b . So it must be a No. And if it’s a No it must be because of some clever factorization, or (more likely) due to some simple congruences that cover all possible values of n . The prime moduli which are most useful are those primes p for which the order of 8 mod p is small, which you can find by factoring 8 n ± 1 for small n . For example, the prime p = 7 would be ideal, because 8 − 1 = 7 and so 8 n is always 1 mod 7 , but alas, 1 + 47 isn’t divisible by 7 . It would have been an easy question with 8 n + 41 , for example, for that reason. The next best thing are factors of 8 + 1 , which is just the prime 3 , and indeed 8 has order 2 mod 3 and this gives us the first useful congruence. Next I looked at 8 2 − 1 (nothing new, of course; there was no need to actually check) and 8 2 + 1 = 65 . The primes 5 and 13 , therefore, offer an order of 4 (meaning 8 4 ≡ 1 mod both 5 and 13 ), and indeed one of them worked for n = 4 k + 1 and the other for n = 4 k + 3 . Harder questions of this kind rely on some non-obvious factorizations, such as Sophie Germain’s identity or more general Aurifeuillean factorizations. I was mentally ready for such, but they weren’t necessary. (…)

Question: What is the remainder of: (sqrt(2) + sqrt(3)) ^ (2000) mod 1111, and how close to an integer is the remainder?
Answer: Ok, so I tried to do this entirely in my head. it’s not as hard as it seems. The second part of the question, “how close to an integer is the remainder”, is a strong hint that we’re looking at a Pisot-Vijayaraghavan situation, as I explained here - but don’t worry, you don’t actually need any of that theory to solve this problem. Briefly, some algebraic numbers have powers which are extremely close to being integers, and this is just what happens here for reasons that are pretty easy to understand even if you’ve never seen PV numbers before. The number √ 2 + √ 3 itself is not a PV number, but its square 5 + 2 √ 6 is. I guessed this is so because we’re being asked about the 2000 th power rather than the more natural 1000 . (Also, I could see at a glance that √ 2 + √ 3 isn’t PV, but again, if you don’t know why, that’s ok.) Even if you don’t observe or anticipate any shenanigans you should prefer to work with 5 + 2 √ 6 because it is a quadratic irrationality (an algebraic number of degree 2 ), while √ 2 + √ 3 is more complicated (it has degree 4 ). Computing powers such as ( 5 + 2 √ 6 ) n is greatly facilitated by adding the conjugate powers. Let’s denote α = 5 + 2 √ 6 , β = 5 − 2 √ 6 and define a n = α n + β n (1) You can see, in more than one way, that the numbers a n are integers. One way to understand this is via linear recurrences a-la Fibonacci. The numbers α and β are the two roots of the same quadratic polynomial, and it’s easy to find this polynomial: a short calculation shows that α + β = 10 while α β = 1 , so they are both roots of X 2 − 10 X + 1 . This means that powers of α , and powers of β , and linear combinations of such powers, all satisfy the recurrence relation a n + 1 = 10 a n − a n − 1 (2) Let’s check this: a 0 is clearly 2 , while a 1 = 10 as we’ve already observed. What about a 2 ? Computing α 2 + β 2 is easy once you notice that the √ 6 parts are going to cancel out, so we’re left with 25 + 24 twice, meaning a 2 = 98 , and yay, 98 = 10 ⋅ 10 − 2 . Now, we are asked about α n and not about α n + β n , but thankfully (and obviously) | β | < 1 , in fact 0 < β < 1 (see why? No computation is needed), and therefore β n becomes exponentially negligible as n grows. We’re interested in n = 1000 , which renders β n tiny indeed. Great: So we have a simple linearly recurrent sequence of integers a n , given by a 0 = 2 , a 1 = 10 and then (2), and thanks to (1) we know that α n is very, very close to a n . Now, we’re not actually asked to calculate a 1000 . We merely want to know its remainder mod 1111 , from which we can compute the remainder left by α 1000 mod the same modulus. You can quickly see that 1111 = 11 ⋅ 101 , so we need to understand a n mod 11 and mod 101 . With some trepidation I started looking at a n mod 11 , but it’s really nice: after the initial 2 , 10 we need 10 ⋅ 10 − 2 , which mod 11 is the same as ( − 1 ) ⋅ ( − 1 ) − 2 = − 1 = 10 again. Nice, so we start with 2 , 10 , 10 . What’s next? Now we have 10 ⋅ 10 − 10 = − 9 = 2 , and then 10 ⋅ 2 − 10 = 10 , and hooray we’re in a cycle: mod 11 our sequence is simply 2 , − 1 , − 1 , 2 , − 1 , − 1 and so on. More precisely, a 3 k ≡ 2 ( mod 11 ) while a 3 k + 1 ≡ a 3 k + 2 ≡ − 1 ( mod 11 ) and we have a full understanding of the situation mod 11 . While jogging, I tried to repeat that process mod 101 , hoping that the designers of this problem chose 101 benevolently. They did, but not in the way I expected. Here is how far I’ve gotten: 2 , 10 , 100 − 2 = − 3 , − 40 , − 400 + 3 = 7 (at this point I was sure I’m making a mistake, since it would be so nice if this was − 400 − 3 = 1 . But it’s not. I had to redo those computations five times to be sure). After − 40 , 7 we find 70 + 40 = 9 , and then 90 − 7 = 83 = − 18 , and then − 180 − 9 = − 189 = 13 , and here I gave up. The cycle doesn’t seem to be short. I was ready to give up and resort to the computer, but it nagged me that someone seems to have chosen 1111 specifically, and the exponent 1000 specifically. Could there be something here? The period mod 101 seems long, but could it be… simple? I confess that I first assumed that the period mod 101 is 100 , since that would make the question so nice. It’s not such a wild guess: powers mod p often do have period p − 1 , except that here we aren’t raising integers mod p but rather algebraic numbers. Nevertheless I felt that this would be reasonable, and since it makes the question easy, it must be true… Under that assumption, we know that a 1000 is − 1 mod 11 and 2 mod 101 . Which residue mod 1111 achieves both? 2 doesn’t, 103 doesn’t, 204 doesn’t, 305 doesn’t, 406 does! Since 407 is divisible by 11 , 406 is both − 1 mod 11 and 2 mod 101 . We now know that a 1000 ≡ 406 ( mod 1111 ) . Clearly, α 1000 is a tiny bit less than a 1000 , so its remainder mod 1111 is 406 − ϵ where ϵ = β 1000 . This, then, is the answer: the remainder is 406 − β 1000 and it’s β 1000 away from being the integer 406 . Even better: since α + β = 10 and α β = 1 we know that β ≈ 0.1 , so β 1000 ≈ 10 − 1000 . Very tiny. What’s left is to prove the claim that the period of a n mod 101 is indeed 100 . Here’s the argument I came up with: we are trying to compute α n + β n mod p . Now α and β aren’t integers and we can’t appeal to Fermat and Euler and such, but: if it just so happens that √ 6 ∈ F p , meaning if 6 is a quadratic residue mod p , then α and β are both represented by ordinary residues of integers mod p , and we can resurrect Fermat’s Little Theorem and argue that α p − 1 ≡ β p − 1 ≡ 1 ( mod p ) . I first checked to see if 6 is a quadratic residue mod 11 . I already knew that the period mod 11 is 3 , which does not divide 10 , so 6 had better not be a quadratic residue mod 11 , and indeed it isn’t. However, using the law of quadratic reciprocity I was able to mentally check that 6 is a quadratic residue mod 101 (since both 2 and 3 are not, their product is), and from this I glibly concluded that 100 must be a period of α n and β n mod 101 . And indeed, it is (verified this now with a computer to be safe). Score. I’ve always known that part of my attraction to mathematics is that it provides a safe, reliable, resilient, unchanging, uncaring-in-a-good-way mental environment for me. Rarely have I felt this so strongly as I have over the last 6 months. And that’s my (…) for today. (…)

Question: How do I Find the least possible cardinality of a set A of natural numbers, the smallest and greatest of which are 1 and 100, and having the property that every element of A except for 1 equals the sum of two elements of A?
Answer: This is called an optimal addition chain. Addition chains are described at great depth in Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, vol. 2, Ch. 4.6.3. We’ve also discussed them on Quora, for instance here, and the answers to this question offer several efficient algorithms for computing optimal addition chains (see the excellent answers by Anita S Vasu, Sridhar Ramesh, Raziman T.V. and Jonathan Paulson, specifically). In this question we’re asked to provide an optimal addition chain for 100 (BTW, you can find here an optimal tree with addition chains up to 148 ). It’s easy to find chains with 9 elements (those are typically called chains of length 8 , since they require 8 addition steps): I don’t see a slick argument showing that no shorter chain is possible. A lower bound of 8 elements ( 7 steps) is easy to derive. Theorem B in Knuth (loc. cit.) shows that l ( 2 A + 2 B + 2 C ) = A + 2 when A > B > C and l ( n ) is the number of steps in an optimal addition chain for n . Since 100 = 2 6 + 2 5 + 2 2 , the theorem applies and shows that indeed l ( 100 ) = 8 . Knuth provides the proof, and though it’s not long it’s a little tedious. There may be a quicker argument for this particular instance. (…)

Answer: After manually searching for small solutions we don’t find anything, which is good news: equations that have no solutions are often easier to handle than equations that have a few. For example, an equation may have no solutions due to some modular constraint; if an equation has even a single solution, you can’t rule out other solutions by merely looking mod something, since there’s obviously at least one solution mod anything. A popular trick in such equations is to add some constant to both sides and make it factor. You can see this trick in Keith Conrad’s Examples of Mordell’s Equation, for instance in Theorem 2.1: Conrad replaces y 2 = x 3 + 7 with y 2 + 1 = x 3 + 8 , which is a good move since x 3 + 8 is divisible by x + 2 . This is usually coupled with a parity argument, so we can say something intelligent about the factors. We can try a very similar trick here, following almost the exact same steps. First of all, x can’t be even since if it were, x 5 would be divisible by 4 and so x 5 + 31 would be 3 mod 4 and that’s incompatible with the y 2 (squares are never 3 mod 4 ). So x is odd. File that. Now do the same rewrite as in Conrad’s example: instead of y 2 = x 5 + 31 we write y 2 + 1 = x 5 + 32 The point being that 32 = 2 5 , so x 5 + 2 5 is divisible by x + 2 . With polynomial division we find: y 2 + 1 = ( x + 2 ) ( x 4 − 2 x 3 + 4 x 2 − 8 x + 16 ) = ( x + 2 ) q ( x ) Next (following Conrad) we need a positivity argument. Observe that the sign of x 5 + 32 is the same as the sign of x + 2 (both are positive when x > − 2 and negative when x < − 2 ) , implying that q ( x ) is positive. Furthermore, x is odd (the file!), and q ( x ) ≡ 3 ( mod 4 ) whenever x is odd because x 5 ≡ x for odd x . A positive integer ≡ 3 ( mod 4 ) cannot have all of its prime factors be 1 ( mod 4 ) , since the product of 1 's mod 4 is still 1 . (That’s why we needed positivity: for negative integers this isn’t so, since the factor of − 1 flips 1 and 3 mod 4 .) Therefore, q ( x ) has a prime factor p which is ≡ 3 ( mod 4 ) . But now we have y 2 + 1 ≡ 0 ( mod p ) which is impossible, since ( − 1 ) is not a quadratic residue mod such primes. So, the equation has no integer solutions. ■ As a general comment: high-genus curves like y 2 = f ( x ) with deg ( f ) > 4 are almost always very hard to handle as a Diophantine equation. If this problem was given to you in a number theory course or problem solving context, there must be a reasonably elementary argument – the non-elementary arguments are really non-elementary. I assumed the question was posed in such a context, so I expected a relatively simple modular consideration. (…)

Question: What is the topology of Zariski and what is its relevance in the study of algebraic varieties?
Answer: It’s called the Zariski topology, not “the topology of Zariski”. At the most basic level, the Zariski topology is a topology on affine space A n ( k ) = k n , the set of n -tuples of elements from a field k which you can take to be C or R or any other favorite field. The Zariski topology declares the closed sets to be those sets which are the solutions of sets of polynomial equations. For example, in the usual Euclidean plane R 2 , these are some Zariski-closed sets: Each of the red, blue and green sets are Zariski closed. The red set is the solution set of ( x + 1 ) 2 + y 4 = 1 , the blue is x y = 4 , and the green is 5 y 2 = ( x − 4 ) ( x 2 − 6 x + 5 ) . Of course, the union of these three sets is also Zariski closed, as it must be since finite unions of closed sets in any topology are also closed. In fact, the union is simply the solution set of f 1 f 2 f 3 = 0 where f 1 , f 2 , f 3 are the polynomials defining each of the sets separately. Single points in the plane are also Zariski closed (since the system of polynomial equations x = a , y = b defines the single point ( a , b ) ), and the whole plane is also closed. In a way, this is it: the Zariski closed sets in the (real) plane are points, algebraic curves and the whole plane. Compare this with plane sets which are closed in the usual topology: I kept the previous curves in the diagram to remind us that Zariski-closed sets are also ordinary-closed sets. There are way, way more ordinary-closed sets in the plane than Zariski-closed ones: the Zariski topology is very, very coarse, or “weak”. So this is it, at the most basic level. One consequence of this definition is that Zariski-open sets are very “large”: they are “everything except the vanishing points of certain polynomials”. So when you read that this or that happens in a Zariski-open set, you should translate this into “most everywhere”. For instance, the set of invertible n × n matrices over R or C is Zariski-open, since it is the complement of the set of matrices for which the determinant (a polynomial) vanishes. Most matrices are invertible. Algebraic geometry is, roughly, the study of algebraic varieties, which are (irreducible) solution sets of polynomial equations. I trust that this makes the “relevance” obvious: the Zariski-closed sets are the same as our object of study. It’s simply that introducing the language of topology allows us to bring a huge amount of theoretical machinery from a different domain (topology) to bear on our domain (algebraic geometry), with the caveat that large portions of “standard” topology assume that the topology is “nice” (e.g. Hausdorff). The Zariski topology isn’t nice. (…)

Question: If it can be proved from the axioms of Set Theory that a certain large cardinal exists, does that imply that all lesser cardinals also exist?
Answer: Kinda. Some issues with the question. First: the axioms of set theory can’t prove that any large cardinal exists. That’s the whole point of large cardinal axioms. If ZFC proves that some cardinal exists, it’s not a large cardinal. So I’ll change the question to go: “If we add a certain large cardinal axiom LC to ZFC, does the consistency of ZFC+LC imply the consistency of ZFC+lc?” Here lc is an axiom for a “Lesser” cardinal. And that’s the second issue with the question: the term “lesser” doesn’t carry any standard meaning. There’s an amazing and not-well-understood observation about large cardinal axioms: they all seem to be linearly ordered by consistency strength. That is, for any two large cardinal axioms we know, either they are equivalent, or the consistency of one implies the consistency of the other. At least, we’re not aware of any violation of that observation. So yes, we can speak of one LC axiom being weaker than another, in the sense that the consistency of ZFC+the latter implies the consistency of ZFC+the former. You can interpret “lesser” in this way, with the caveat that this interpretation makes the answer to your question tautological. There’s another sense in which you can consider one large cardinal axiom to be “lesser” than another, and that is by the size of the smallest witness. This sense is not identical to the previous sense, a point made by the Wikipedia article that I admit I was not previously aware of. At any rate, this too isn’t a standard interpretation of the term “lesser” among large cardinal axioms. (…)

Question: Are there examples of infinite dimensional vector spaces that are not Hilbert but are isomorphic to their dual?
Answer: Hold up. No infinite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to its dual. A Hilbert space is more than a vector space: it’s an inner product space, and when we talk about the dual in this context we mean the continuous dual. But for a general vector space there’s no inner product and no continuous dual, there’s just a dual: the vector space of all linear functionals on the original space. This is sometimes called the “algebraic dual” for emphasis, but the point is that this is the only dual that’s available to you when you merely have a vector space without an inner product, or a norm, or a topology. And this algebraic dual is isomorphic to the original space precisely when the original space is finite dimensional. It’s never the case for infinite-dimensional spaces. You can find some nice proofs here. Now, perhaps we can refine the question: what if we have a topological vector space (TVS)? Now we can talk about the continuous dual, and the space may or may not be a Hilbert space. With that, are there topological vector spaces that aren’t Hilbert and are isomorphic to their continuous dual? The answer to that question is yes. One example I can think of is: take a reflexive TVS W , meaning a TVS which is isomorphic to its double dual W ∗ ∗ . There are many such spaces; for example many Banach spaces are reflexive, regardless of whether or not they are also Hilbert spaces. Now consider V = W ⊕ W ∗ . This isn’t a Hilbert space (there’s no inner product, and I’m sure in most cases it doesn’t even support an inner product which would induce its topology). However, V ∗ = W ∗ ⊕ W ∗ ∗ ≅ W ∗ ⊕ W ≅ V I’m sure there are many other examples. (…)

Question: I made a discovery in mathematics (prime numbers), can I get it peer reviewed although I only have a BSc and am unaffiliated?
Answer: There are a few steps between “I made a discovery” and peer review. The hurdles have nothing to do with the fact that you only have a B.Sc. and are unaffiliated. Undergrad students and high schoolers publish papers without a B.Sc., and people publish papers with no affiliation or no relevant affiliation. The hurdles are: Your lack of graduate training and involvement in the research community aren’t the reasons you can’t submit your paper to some journal – you can – but they are the reason you are very, very, very likely to misjudge the answers to those questions. Get someone who knows number theory to look at it, or post it online and ask for comments. Better yet, if you’d like to do research in number theory, get a graduate degree with a focus on number theory. Trying to do it otherwise is an excellent path to frustration, disappointment and a waste of everyone’s time. (…)

Answer: No, there are infinitely many primes p for which this doesn’t happen. There are many ways to understand this, in many contexts. The easiest way to see that this isn’t true is just to try. The first odd prime is p = 3 , and here of course we have a solution, n = 1 . But at the very next prime, p = 5 , we get a counterexample: n 2 + n + 1 is never divisible by 5 , as you can check by merely testing n = 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . Done: the answer is No. You can drop here. But you may wonder: which primes do, or don’t, accommodate such an n ? And how do I know that there are infinitely many that don’t? One way to answer this is to recall how we solve the equation X 2 + X + 1 = 0 as usual, in the real (or complex) numbers. You see, “ p divides n 2 + n + 1 for some n " is exactly the same thing as “ X 2 + X + 1 has a root mod p , which is n ". Right? p divides n 2 + n + 1 means that n 2 + n + 1 ≡ 0 ( mod p ) , so n is a “mod p solution” of X 2 + X + 1 = 0 . So how do we solve a quadratic? Well, X = 1 2 ( − 1 + √ − 3 ) The key insight is that this formula works just fine mod p , with the appropriate interpretation. If p = 2 then this 1 / 2 up front doesn’t make sense. So now we know why the question says “odd prime”. For odd p we have a 1 / 2 ( 2 is invertible mod p for any odd prime p ), and we have − 1 , and we can add and multiply. The only head-scratching component of this formula is the √ − 3 thingie. But that’s not too difficult either. You see, √ − 3 just means “anything which, when squared, yields − 3 ", and modulo p , − 3 just means the residue p − 3 modulo p . For example, 6 2 = 36 ≡ 10 ≡ − 3 ( mod 13 ) So with p = 13 we can make sense of √ − 3 as √ − 3 ≡ 6 , and then 1 2 ( − 1 + √ − 3 ) = 1 2 ( − 1 + 6 ) ≡ 7 ⋅ 5 ≡ 35 ≡ 9 ( mod 13 ) which tells us that n = 9 should work for p = 13 . And indeed, 9 2 + 9 + 1 = 91 is divisible by 13 . (Of course, as usual, there are two square roots of − 3 mod 13 , and the other one is − 6 = 7 . This gives another solution, n = 3 ). But for some primes there’s nothing that squares to − 3 mod p , and we say that − 3 is a quadratic non-residue mod p . In fact there’s a well-known procedure to determine which primes have − 3 as a quadratic residue and which don’t, and it rests on the famous Law of Quadratic Reciprocity, one of Gauss’s proudest achievements. Even if you don’t know quadratic reciprocity, you can figure out exactly which primes do or don’t have − 3 as a quadratic residue by knowing just one universal law: whether or not k is a quadratic residue mod p can only depend on the residue class of p mod 4 | k | . In our case, we just need to figure out which residue classes mod 12 work, and the only residue classes that matter are 1 , 5 , 7 and 11 . (Why?) Conclusion: an odd prime p divides n 2 + n + 1 for some n precisely when p ≡ 1 , 7 ( mod 12 ) , or if p = 3 . There are infinitely many primes congruent to 5 or 11 mod 12 , and they don’t have such an n . You can take this further, in many directions. What if the polynomial isn’t merely a quadratic? Does the answer always involve residue classes? There’s a truly vast universe to be explored, but I guess I’ll need to leave it at that for now. (…)

Question: How precisely do infinitesimals and monads resolve the issues with standard set theory axioms that lead to paradoxes like Russell's Paradox?
Answer: They don’t. “Standard set theory axioms” don’t lead to paradoxes like Russell’s Paradox. Russell’s paradox results from allowing unrestricted comprehension, which attempts to assert that there’s a set satisfying any arbitrary predicate. The first collection of axioms for set theory which can reasonably be labeled “standard” is ZF, and it was developed precisely to avoid this paradox. You may have meant “natural” or “naive” axioms, and indeed early attempts at formalizing the idea of sets, such as the one proposed by Frege, were flawed for being susceptible to the paradox. But these issues were resolved by disallowing unrestricted comprehension (ZF), or by drawing a distinction between sets and classes (NBG), or by Russell’s type system which didn’t gain much traction. None of these things have anything to do with monads or infinitesimals. (…)

Question: Let ε > 0 and q_n a sequence of all rational numbers in [0,1]. Consider the open intervals Q_n= (q_n-ε/2^n , q_n+ε/2^n). Why do Q_n not cover the irrationals in [0,1]?

Your intuition tells you that it’s true; great - follow it! What goes wrong? When you ask the question like that, in the negative, all I can say is “well because it doesn’t”, in the same way as I would answer “why does 3 not divide 23 ?”. I mean, I could say “because when you divide 23 by 3 you have 2 left over”, but that’s like saying “because some irrational numbers are left uncovered by your intervals”. Whenever you focus on any particular irrational number u ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , you’ll notice that there’s no way for you to prove that it is indeed covered by one of those intervals. Sure, there’s some rational number that’s no more than a millionth away from u ; but this rational number may be q 99999 , and the open interval Q n around it would be too tiny to even come close to u . And then you can find another rational that’s even closer, but that rational may come even later in your list, so it supports an even smaller interval. And, as it turns out, that’s exactly what happens here. Since the total length of your intervals is ϵ , they cannot cover more than ϵ of [ 0 , 1 ] , and once ϵ < 1 that means you’ll have infinitely many irrational numbers left uncovered. Answer: I think that by “with its complex numbers in it” you mean that you’re looking for a visual representation of the complex function f : C → C , f ( z ) = ln ( z ) . We do have various standard ways of representing complex functions of a complex variable. One of the common ones is to treat the input variable z as a point in the plane, in the usual way: we represent z = x + i y as the point ( x , y ) with cartesian coordinates x and y . On the other hand, the output w = f ( z ) of the function is represented differently: we use brightness to capture the absolute value | w | , and color to represent the argument Arg ( w ) . Therefore, we color each point z in the plane in a way that represents the absolute value and argument of w = f ( z ) . When we do this for w = ln ( z ) we see something like that: To be precise, this is what’s called the principal branch of the logarithm. A few things are nicely visible here: the fact that ln ( 1 ) = 0 is represented by the black dot at z = 1 . The branch cut at the negative real numbers is seen by the mismatching colors (green and blue) right above and below the left part of the x axis: the argument of w = ln ( z ) is close to + π in the northwest, and to − π in the southwest. This is inevitable, and profoundly important in the theory of complex functions. At z = 0 , the logarithm is not defined. You should imagine a “missing point” right at the origin of this diagram. The absolute value | ln ( z ) | is very high near z = 0 , and this is a limitation of this representation method: we can only make the pixels have full “brightness” (value), but we can’t make them shine like a thousand suns. You’ll just have to imagine that ln ( z ) has those extreme value in the vicinity of z = 0 . (…)

Furthermore, in all of those statements, m is the smallest possible exponent which makes it work. There is no power of 2 smaller than 6 which is 1 more than a multiple of 7 . Let’s take the prime 7 , for example. The order of 2 mod 7 is 6 , which means exactly that 2 6 is the smallest positive power of 2 which is 1 mod 6 . But we can say much more: Claim: The order of 2 mod 7 j is 6 ⋅ 7 j − 1 . This says two things: first of all, that 2 6 ⋅ 7 j − 1 ≡ 1 ( mod 7 j ) , and also that this is the smallest power of 2 with that property. To prove the claim, we argue by induction that 2 6 ⋅ 7 j − 1 = 7 j k j + 1 for some integer k j relatively prime to 7 . When j = 1 this is simply the claim 2 6 = 7 ⋅ 9 + 1 we started with. Assuming this is already known to be true for some j , compute 2 6 ⋅ 7 j = ( 2 6 ⋅ 7 j − 1 ) 7 = ( 7 j k j + 1 ) 7 = 7 ∑ i = 0 ( 7 i ) ( 7 j k j ) i = 1 + 7 j + 1 k j + 7 j + 2 M j = 1 + 7 j + 1 ( k j + 7 M j ) = 1 + 7 j + 1 k j + 1 To understand the magnitude M j , observe that 7 j i is divisible by at least 7 j + 2 as soon as i ≥ 2 , so we simply pull out a factor of 7 j + 2 and collect everything that remains into this M j . The new coefficient k j + 1 = k j + 7 M j is still relatively prime to 7 regardless of what M j is. This already shows that the order of 2 mod 7 j + 1 is at most 6 ⋅ 7 j , but it can’t be less: whatever that order is must divide 6 ⋅ 7 j and also be a multiple of 6 ⋅ 7 j − 1 , since you can’t be 1 mod 7 j + 1 without first of all being 1 mod 7 j . So the only possible smaller exponent is 6 ⋅ 7 j − 1 itself, but it’s not since 7 j k j + 1 is not 1 mod 7 j + 1 , thanks to k j being relatively prime to 7 . ■ This is a standard lemma in number theory, often going by the name “lifting the exponent”. In our case, it tells us the order of 2 mod any power of 3 , 5 and 7 , and that’s all we need. A word of caution may be helpful here: we started with 2 m = p k + 1 with k relatively prime to p . It’s important to observe that this “relatively prime to p " is not necessarily true when you’re just getting started. For example, the order of 3 mod 11 is 5 , but 3 5 = 11 ⋅ 22 + 1 and 22 is not relatively prime to 11 . in other words, as soon as you raise 3 to some power which is 1 mod 11 , you automatically also have it be 1 mod 11 2 . In terms of our claim, this means that when you move up from the order of 3 mod 11 to the order of 3 mod 11 2 , the order, which is 5 , stays 5 rather than become 55 . From this point onwards, however, the exponent lemma proceeds normally. Our base here is 2 , not 3 , but this happens with base 2 as well: there are two known primes ( 1093 and 3511 ), called Wieferich primes, for which the order of 2 mod p is also the order of 2 mod p 2 . It doesn’t affect us here, obviously, but it’s useful to know. (While writing this answer I did some computer experimentation and discovered something which is surely known but I wasn’t aware of: the order of 68 mod 113 , which is 112 , is also the order mod 113 2 and mod 113 3 . I never knew this was possible, but here it is. I don’t know if this ever happens again.) Anyway, why is this claim helpful to us? The thing is, it says that 2 n − 1 cannot be divisible by very high powers of 3 , 5 or 7 , because making it divisible by such high powers forces n to be very, very large. That’s the key to the problem. Can 2 n − 1 = 1 ? Sure, if n = 1 , but that’s it. Can 2 n − 1 = 3 a with a > 0 ? If so, then n is at least 2 ⋅ 3 a − 1 , and we have 2 2 ⋅ 3 a − 1 ≤ 3 a + 1 , which works fine for a = 1 but obviously never beyond that. So n = 2 works here, but that’s it. Can 2 n − 1 = 5 b with b > 0 ? If so, then n is at least 4 ⋅ 5 b − 1 , and we have 2 4 ⋅ 5 b − 1 ≤ 5 b + 1 , which doesn’t work for any b . Similarly, you can rule out 7 c except 2 3 − 1 = 7 , 3 a 5 b except 2 4 − 1 = 15 , 3 a 7 c except 2 6 − 1 = 63 , and so on. So, finally, 2 n − 1 has no prime factor > 7 when n = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 6 and for no other value of n . ■ (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: The first two pages of Apostol’s mathematical analysis textbook he lists the field and order axioms. In Tao’s and other sources these are proved. I am referring to associativity etc. How can one treat as an axiom and other as a theorem?
Answer: When you’re driving your car, you know that pressing down on the gas pedal makes the car accelerate, and that turning the wheel by this much would make it turn like that, and so on. You probably don’t know how these things work in detail; you just know that they do, and that’s good enough for you as a driver. You take those things as axioms. A car mechanic can tell you why pressing down on the gas pedal makes the car accelerate. They can explain about throttle linkages, and how they control the air flow into the engine, and how air flow affects combustion. They can prove that pressing the gas pedal would make the car accelerate, but they also take certain things as axioms, which a physicist could prove from more basic principles of thermodynamics. Funny enough, if you’re driving an electric vehicle, you use pretty much the same axiom about the accelerator pedal – it behaves quite similarly to the gas pedal in an ICE car, and since you don’t care about the internal construction of things, you merrily use the pedal in pretty much the same way. That is why people who learned to drive ICE cars can switch to EVs pretty easily, even though the inner workings are wildly different. It’s the same thing. Apostol offers a quickstart guide to real analysis: there’s this thing called the real number field, and it is an ordered field satisfying these rules which you may call “axioms”. We won’t try to prove them from more basic principles, and off you go – you may start driving. Doesn’t matter if it’s an ICE car or an EV: the axioms are the axioms. Go. Tao takes a very different approach, working through the actual constructions and proofs from more basic principles. He starts the construction of the real numbers in chapter 5, on page 94! He chooses to construct the reals as Cauchy sequences, which is like choosing an ICE engine to justify the axiom of the acceleration pedal. My personal preference is Dedekind cuts, which is like an EV. Some people choose decimal expansions, which is trying to build a car from human bones. Either way, you end up with the same axioms Apostol starts with. If you read Tao’s Preface to the First Edition, as well as Chapter 1 – Introduction, and then the first paragraphs of Chapter 2, you’ll see that he spends almost all of this introductory material on precisely this question: his choice of going back not just to the construction of the real numbers but even to the natural numbers, starting with the Peano axioms. We will consider the following question: how does one actually define the natural numbers? (This is a very different question from how to use the natural numbers, which is something you of course know how to do very well. It’s like the difference between knowing how to use, say, a computer, versus knowing how to build that computer.) In the honours real analysis course Tao taught in 2003, his students were quickly behind their friends at the non-honours class. One student told me how difficult it was to explain to his friends in the non-honours real analysis sequence (a) why he was still learning how to show why all rational numbers are either positive, negative, or zero (Exercise 4.2.4), while the non-honours sequence was already distinguishing absolutely convergent and conditionally convergent series, and (b) why, despite this, he thought his homework was significantly harder than that of his friends. This is why the second chapter of Tao’s book looks like this: In this text, we will review the material you have learnt in high school and in elementary calculus classes, but as rigorously as possible. To do so we will have to begin at the very basics - indeed, we will go back to the concept of numbers and what their properties are. Of course, you have dealt with numbers for over ten years and you know how to manipulate the rules of algebra to simplify any expression involving numbers, but we will now turn to a more fundamental issue, which is: why do the rules of algebra work at all? For instance, why is it true that a ( b + c ) is equal to a b + a c for any three numbers a , b , c ? This is not an arbitrary choice of rule; it can be proven from more primitive, and more fundamental, properties of the number system. This will teach you a new skill - how to prove complicated properties from simpler ones. You will find that even though a statement may be “obvious”, it may not be easy to prove; the material here will give you plenty of practice in doing so, and in the process will lead you to think about why an obvious statement really is obvious. One skill in particular that you will pick up here is the use of mathematical induction, which is a basic tool in proving things in many areas of mathematics. This is Tao’s choice, and it was the choice of my teachers, when I was a student, and it will be my choice if I ever get a chance to teach this stuff. It’s not the only correct choice. There are many reasons to study, say, differentiation and integration, and many people can happily use these things without being able to prove the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. But some people care about the foundations, and some actually need those foundations in order to gain a real understanding. (In fact, Tao’s starting point is not in itself the most foundational one imaginable. In an appropriate sense, one can derive the Peano Axioms themselves in, for example, Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory. But it is very common, and very reasonable, to start with something familiar like the natural numbers rather than something as abstract and demanding as sets.) So, that’s how. You can treat something as an axiom, or you can prove it from more basic principles. It’s a choice of presentation of the material, not a statement on the philosophical nature of things. It’s very common to see this material presented in different ways by different writers. (…)

Question: Why is the complex limit as z tends to 0 of tan(z)/ (z^2* (z^2+1)) = infinity? Why not -infinity? How does the computation differ from the real case (where x can tend to 0 either from the positive side or from the negative side)?
Answer: Let’s study the real case first. The real numbers R don’t have any infinite element among their ranks. Every real number is finite – in fact, every real number is nestled between two integers. This is the Archimedean property of the real ordered field. Now, when we study sequences or functions, we are often interested in understanding their limiting behavior: where do they go, what do they tend to when some parameter approaches some limit? We find that several things could happen: there may be a particular, finite, real limit; there may be no limit at all; and sometimes it seems like the limit itself is “infinite”: the sequence, or function, grows without bound, eventually exceeding any prescribed value. We now have two distinct options. A) We can distinguish between “flying off to + ∞ " and “flying off to − ∞ ", as follows: if for every M there’s a point beyond which our sequence, or function, exceeds M , we call this “tending to + ∞ ", and if for every M there’s a point beyond which our sequence, or function, falls below M , we call this “tending to − ∞ ". B) Perhaps we care less about the difference between right and left, but we do care about magnitude. In this case we could say that a sequence, or function, “tends to infinity” whenever its absolute value eventually exceeds any prescribed threshold M . It’s fine even if the sequence hops between positive billion and negative trillion and back – we simply ignore the sign. Visually, option A) looks like this, with a + ∞ off to the right and a − ∞ off to the left: Option B), however, looks more like We fold the entire real line on itself, sending both positive and negative numbers towards a single infinite point. This is the real projective line R P 1 , and it is just a circle. There are several reasons why I’m emphasizing these two distinct options. First of all, they are both meaningful and important. The first one is common in real analysis, engineering and various contexts where the distinction between positive infinity and negative infinity is necessary. The second option is crucial in geometry, among other places: it is the projective point of view, where we complete the real line into the projective line R P 1 and the real plane into the projecive plane R P 2 , and so on. The second reason is sort of a meta-reason: I always wish to emphasize that concepts like “infinity” aren’t divinely ordained. We define those things as we see fit, and sometimes we see fit different things in different contexts. And finally, I wish to dispel the notion that the distinction between double and single infinities is somehow associated with the distinction between real and complex numbers. It is true, as we’ll see, that the complex numbers can really only handle a single point at infinity; but it’s not like the real numbers must have two of them. The process of projectivization of the complex plane to a sphere with a single additional point can be applied just fine to the real line, and what you get is this R P 1 with its unique point at infinity. Option B. The real numbers are ordered, which gives us a good reason to care about things that are larger than a million and things that are smaller than a negative million. The complex numbers aren’t ordered: they can be ordered in various artificial ways, but none of those ways plays nice with the algebra of adding and multiplying complex numbers. The reason is that in any ordered field, squares must be positive, but in the complex numbers, − 1 is a square and it needs to be negative. So, C cannot be made into an ordered field. But we can still ignore order aspects and follow the process of forming the projective plane from the ordinary plane: we fold the plane on itself to form a sphere missing a point, and we call this point “the point at infinity”, or ∞ , for short. Just like option B before. What we get is the Riemann sphere: Or you may prefer this diagram (from here), which demonstrates the stereographic projection connecting the plane and the sphere: Finally, we can get back to your question. The real function f ( x ) = tan ( x ) x 2 ( x + 1 ) looks like this, around 0 : Clearly, as x approaches 0 from the right, it tends to + ∞ , and when it approaches 0 from the left it approaches − ∞ . So on the extended real line ( R with { − ∞ , + ∞ added in), this function has no limit as x → 0 ; it depends on how you choose to approach 0 . It does have a “right limit” of + ∞ and a “left limit” of − ∞ . In terms of the projective real line, however, this function has a perfectly good limit as x → 0 , and that’s ∞ . The one, unique projective point at infinity we’ve added. It’s not + ∞ nor − ∞ , or rather, it is both at the same time: just infinity. And the latter situation also applies in the complex plane: the complex-valued function f ( z ) = tan ( z ) z 2 ( z 2 + 1 ) tends to ∞ as z → 0 . In the complex plane, the meaning of “tending to infinity” is the same thing as “exceeding any prescribed value in absolute value”. And that’s just what happens here, in both the real and complex cases. So, finally, the difference you’re highlighting isn’t really a difference between real and complex. It’s a difference between drawing a distinction between highly positive and highly negative values (which only makes sense in the real case) vs not drawing that distinction, caring only about magnitudes. Hope this helps. (…)

Question: Is there an elementary proof that there are infinitely many prime numbers that are not part of a twin prime pair?
Answer: Fact: there are infinitely many primes in the arithmetic progression 37 , 67 , 97 , 127 , … and so on. Quite simply, start with 37 and “skip count” by 30 s. Question: Is SO(3) isomorphic to SU(2) by coincidence, or can something like the involved double cover generalize to higher dimensions?
Answer: First of all, SO ( 3 ) is not isomorphic to SU ( 2 ) . Rather, SU ( 2 ) is a double cover of SO 3 , meaning there’s a smooth homomorphism SU ( 2 ) → SO ( 3 ) with kernel ± I of order 2 . Is that a “coincidence”? Of course not; the word doesn’t mean anything in this context. You seem to be asking if this is a special case of a more general phenomenon, in the sense that “something like” such a double cover occurs at higher dimensions. Well, that depends on how far this “something like” is allowed to stretch things. For example, the next time the dimensions of SO and SU coincide is at SO ( 6 ) , which is 15 -dimensional, and so is SU ( 4 ) , but these groups are actually isomorphic. There’s a variety of double-cover situations between other real and complex Lie groups. For instance, SL ( 4 , R ) is a double cover of SO + ( 3 , 3 ; R ) , as observed here. But I don’t know that there’s such a general statement connecting special orthogonal and special unitary groups. (…)

Question: Flip a fair coin 100 times, it gives a seq of heads (H) and tails (T). For each HH in the sequence of flips, Alice gets a point; for each HT, Bob does, so e.g. for the sequence THHHT Alice gets 2 points and Bob gets 1 point.Who is more likely to win?
Answer: I have a whole talk about this 🙂 I won’t make you watch the whole thing: you can skip straight to the relevant part. This is at the National Museum of Mathematics in 2019, and if you do choose to watch the whole thing you’ll see David S. Rose introduce me in the most kind way (thank you, again, David.) A lot of people get this question wrong, including very prominent researchers publishing very prominent papers. You see, at any point in the game you describe, everything seems fair. If we just threw a T then nothing happens. If we threw an H then the next throw determines who’s getting a point: if it’s an H then Alice gets a point, if it’s a T then Bob does. What happens next depends: if we just had an HT then we are back at square one and need to wait for our next H to pop up; if we had HH then we are once again at the position of “we just had an H”, and again the situation is fair: the next flip yields a point for either Alice or Bob, with equal probability. At any moment in the game, the situation is fair. So the game must be fair. Right? Wrong. Instead of 100 flips of a coin, imagine we’re playing the game with fewer flips. Let’s see what happens. 2 flips: that’s easy, and the game is totally fair. Two coin flips may yield TT (no one wins anything), TH (same), HT (Bob wins) or HH (Alice wins), and those all have equal probability. Fair game. 3 flips: Let us count. In this game, flipping a coin three times and awarding HH points to Alice and HT points to Bob, Bob is more likely to win. He wins 3 / 8 = 37.5 % of the time, while Alice wins 1 / 4 = 25 % of the time. Big difference. You may notice something interesting: there is indeed a sense in which the game is fair, if we actually keep a long-term count of the score. When Bob wins, it’s always 0:1, but when Alice wins, it’s sometimes 1:0 and sometimes 2:0. Both players earn 1 / 2 a point in each round, on average. But Bob does so by winning 3 games out of 8, with a score of 1 each (and one draw, giving him another point), but Alice does so by winning just 2 games out of 8, with a score of 1 for one game and 2 for the other (and one draw for another point). The players achieve the same score, on average, but we’re not talking about scores. We’re talking about the chances of winning a particular game of 3 coin flips, and Bob is a lot more likely to win. Here’s a visual which may help: it shows the score gap (Bob’s score minus Alice’s) for all possible games of length 3 . The 3 winning games for Bob are in Orange, and the 2 winning games for Alice are in green; you can see that Alice has a deeper advantage in one game, but she wins fewer games. 4 flips: Some patient counting should tell you that Bob is still ahead, and in fact with the exact same winning probability: it’s still 37.5 % ( 6 of 16 ) for Bob, 25 % ( 4 of 16 ) for Alice. Once again, the average score is even: Alice wins fewer games, but with a higher average advantage. Here’s what it looks like: 10 flips: There are now 1024 possible outcomes of 10 flips. Bob wins 464 of them, Alice wins 371 . This is about 45.3 % vs 36.2 % . Once again, we see more orange bars, but they are shorter. The total score is the same. 100 flips: it should be possible to compute the precise proportions but there’s no need to; the key observation is the same. In a random sampling of 100 000 such games, Bob won 48 710 games against Alice’s 45 602 . This exact same mistake was made in a very influential paper by Gilovich, Tversky and Malone from 1985, “proving” that there’s no evidence of a hot hand in Basketball. It took more than 30 years for the mistake to be noticed: Miller and Sanjurjo showed in 2018 that Gilovich et al made a mistake very similar to the assumption that Alice and Bob have equal chances of winning. If everything is random, sinking two shots in a row (“HH”) is less likely then missing after a successful shot (“HT”), when you’re running your stats on short sequences (games) with a limited number of attempts (coin flips). Therefore, if you observe roughly 50% of HH’s, this is strong evidence of a hot hand – which you may, amusingly, abbreviate to “HH”. Thanks for asking the question! (…)

Answer: There isn’t such an example - a manifold of dimension m admits an atlas with at most m + 1 charts. This is simply because the topological dimension (covering dimension) of such a manifold is m . Is it possible that you’re thinking of atlases with connected charts only? This changes things dramatically. All definitions of charts and atlases I’m familiar with allow a chart to be homeomorphic to an open subset of R m , but such an open subset isn’t necessarily connected. When we think of charts we usually think of them as being homeomorphic to an open ball, but this isn’t a requirement, generally. If you are interested in atlases in which each chart is homeomorphic to an actual open ball, I think it should not be hard to find (non-compact) examples of manifolds which cannot be covered by finitely many charts – for example, I would expect this to be the case for a surface of infinite genus. Question: Can we turn every group into a vector space?
Answer: Far from it. The additive group of a vector space is commutative, which already rules out the vast majority of groups. But let’s say you meant to ask whether every abelian group is the additive group of some vector space. Still a hard no. Over fields of characteristic 0 , the additive group of a vector space is torsion-free and divisible (you never have n v = 0 for any element v and nonzero integer n , and the equation u = n v can be solved for any given u and nonzero n ). Over fields of characteristic p you have p v = 0 for every v , meaning the group has a prime exponent. Therefore, any abelian group which doesn’t have a prime exponent and isn’t both torsion-free and divisible cannot be the additive group of any vector space. Among many other things we have ruled out Z , Z r , Z / m Z for composite m , and frankly every finite abelian group except ( Z / p Z ) m . (…)

Question: Let p, q and r be prime numbers, and n > 0, such that all belong to Z and p^n + q^n = r^2. How can I demonstrate that n most be 1?
Answer: First, let’s see what happens when n is even. If the primes p , q are both odd then p n ≡ q n ≡ 1 ( mod 4 ) , so the sum p n + q n is 2 mod 4 and cannot be a perfect square. Therefore one of p , q , let’s say q , satisfies q = 2 , and for now let’s consider p odd. We have p n + 2 n = r 2 . We may write n = 2 m (since n is even) and so p 2 m = r 2 − ( 2 m ) 2 = ( r − 2 m ) ( r + 2 m ) If r − 2 m > 1 then it’s divisible by some prime, and the only possible prime is p , so p divides both r − 2 m and r + 2 m and therefore also their difference 2 m + 1 which is impossible. So we must have r = 2 m + 1 , and p 2 m = 2 m + 1 + 1 . This is easy to rule out as p > 2 and either m = 1 (doesn’t work) or 2 m > m + 1 and the LHS is larger than the RHS. Finally, we should check the case p = q = 2 . Then p n + q n = 2 n + 1 = r 2 and r can’t be prime. So n can’t be even. If n is odd then the polynomial X n + Y n is divisible by X + Y , so p n + q n is divisible by p + q . Assuming n > 1 , p + q is a proper divisor of p n + q n = r 2 , but r is prime so we must have p + q = r . Now we have p n + q n = ( p + q ) 2 . Forget primes for a moment and consider the equation in real variables x n + y n = ( x + y ) 2 with n ≥ 3 . For any fixed value of the sum x + y = 2 t , x n + y n is minimized when x = y = t , and as soon as t > 2 we have t n + t n > ( 2 t ) 2 and there can be no equality. So x n + y n = ( x + y ) 2 can only be solved if x + y ≤ 4 , and going back to our primes this means p = q = 2 and then r = 4 isn’t a prime. So n can’t be odd and ≥ 3 either, and the only remaining option is n = 1 . ■ The case n = 1 is more subtle. We can obviously have p = q = r = 2 , but if r > 2 then it must be odd which means that q = 2 . We’re now looking at p + 2 = r 2 , or in other words we’re looking for prime numbers r such that r 2 − 2 is also prime. There are many such primes (over 1,500 with r < 10 5 ), and it’s not known if there are infinitely many. Therefore the equation p n + q n = r 2 is actually very subtle when n = 1 . (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: What are two graphs for which there exists an embedding geom(G) → (Injunctive relation)
Answer: I think I know what you mean, but let me make sure. With all that out of the way, here’s what the question is probably trying to show you: the relations minor and topological minor are asymmetric. If a graph G is a minor, or topological minor, of a graph H , then G is the smaller graph and H is the larger one. If G and H aren’t isomorphic then H cannot be a minor of G . This means, for example, that the graph C 3 = K 3 , the cycle on 3 vertices, is a minor and a topological minor of every cycle graph C n , n ≥ 3 , but not the other way around: C 4 is not a topological minor and not even a minor of C 3 . The same goes for topological minors (in fact, for graphs of max degree ≤ 3 , minor and topological minor are the same thing). But the geometric realization of all of these graphs is the same: it’s just a circle. Vertices of degree 2 don’t change anything as far as the geometry is concerned. So there’s an actual homeomorphism, and in particular an embedding, of geom ( C 4 ) into geom ( C 3 ) , even though C 4 is not a topological minor of C 3 . (…)

Question: Let α and ω be 2 circles such that ω goes through the center of α. ω intersects α at A and B. Let P be any point on the circumference ω. The lines PA and PB intersects α again at E and F respectively. How to prove that AB = EF?
Answer: Start with a simpler situation, with just one circle. We have a circle with center O , a point P not on the circle, and two lines from P such that P O is their angle bisector. Then A E = F B . You can prove this by sheer symmetry: the whole diagram is symmetric around the line P O . Flip it around and the line segments A E and F B map onto each other. Now here’s the situation described in the question: The point P now lies on a circle which passes through O . But this precisely ensures that P O bisects the angle between P A and P B , because the angles ∠ B P O and ∠ A P O subtend congruent arcs. (Proof, again, by symmetry, this time around the line Q O ). By the previous observation, A E = F B and we are done. ■ (…)

Question: S is a subset of the divisors of 2024^2024 such that no number in S has it's own multiple in S. What is the largest possible value of |S|?
Answer: Obviously, we shouldn’t get hung up on this particular (and peculiar) number, the current year raised to the power of itself. In general we have a positive integer N and we are looking for the maximum number of divisors of N , none of which divides another. The set of (positive integer) divisors of a positive integer is a partially ordered set, with “divides” being the order relation. If a , b , c divide N then a | a ; if a | b and b | a then a = b ; and if a | b and b | c then a | c . What we don’t have here is the requirement that for every two divisors a , b either a | b or b | a . This is what makes it into a partially ordered set rather than a (linearly) ordered set. A partially ordered set – poset, in brief – has a concept of antichains: an antichain is a collection of elements no two of which are in relation to each other. In our case, those would be divisors that don’t divide one another. For example: { 6 , 10 , 14 , 15 , 21 , 35 } are all divisors of 210 , and none of them divides any other one of them. So that’s an antichain of length 6 in the divisor poset of 210 , and indeed it has maximum length: there are no 7 divisors of 210 that are like that. Here’s why. The number 210 has a simple prime factorization: 210 = 2 ⋅ 3 ⋅ 5 ⋅ 7 . A divisor of 210 is the product of some of those prime factors. An antichain of divisors is corresponds to choosing various subsets of { 2 , 3 , 5 , 7 } such that no subset is contained in another. This brings us to the general question: given a finite set X , how many subsets of X can you find so that none of them contains another? Here’s an easy approach: take all the subsets of some particular size k . Two subsets of size k cannot contain each other. If X has n elements there are ( n k ) such subsets, and this is maximal when k = ⌊ n / 2 ⌋ . So among the subsets of a finite set X there’s definitely an antichain of size ( n ⌊ n / 2 ⌋ ) . A basic result known as Sperner’s theorem says that this is, indeed, the largest antichain in the poset of subsets under inclusion. For example, in a set of size 4 such as { 2 , 3 , 5 , 7 } , the maximal antichain is obtained by picking all subsets of size 2 : { 2 , 3 } , { 2 , 5 } and so on. This is how I got the sequence 6 , 10 , 14 , 15 , 21 , 35 mentioned above, and Sperner’s theorem shows that this is best possible: you cannot get 7 divisors of 210 without having one of them divide another. But what we need here is a bit more elaborate than Sperner’s theorem. When the number N is squarefree, it’s a product of some distinct primes, and its divisors then correspond to subsets of this set of primes, and Sperner’s theorem tells us how large of an antichain we can get. But if N is not squarefree things are a little different. In fact you can think of the prime divisors of a general integer N as a multiset, which is like a set where elements can be repeated. For example, the multiset of prime factors of 72 is { 2 , 2 , 2 , 3 , 3 } . Divisors of 72 are subsets of this multiset, but there are fewer options to choose such a subset than if you had 5 distinct prime factors. Therefore the structure of the poset of subsets of a multiset is different from the case of subsets of a set. What we need is an analogue of Sperner for multisets, or in other words to the poset of divisors of a number. What we expect such a generalization to say is this: Suppose N = p e 1 1 p e 2 2 ⋯ p e m m is the prime decomposition of N , and call n = e 1 + e 2 + … + e m . Every divisor d of N has the form d = p a 1 1 p a 2 2 ⋯ p a m m where the exponents a 1 , a 2 , … , a m all satisfy 0 ≤ a i ≤ e i . If we take those divisors for which a 1 + a 2 + … + a m = k for some particular fixed sum k , we get an antichain, since two such divisors having the same total amount of primes in them cannot divide each other. Our desired Sperner generalization would say that the largest antichain of divisors of N is obtained in this way when k = ⌊ n / 2 ⌋ . This generalization is correct, and can be proved by generalizing some of the familiar proofs of Sperner’s Theorem. A proof is available in the paper On the set of divisors of a number by de Bruijn, Tengbergen and Kruyswijk. You can also find it in Ian Anderson’s Combinatorics of Finite Sets, one of the first math books I ever owned for completely random reasons. We’ve made progress: given an integer N = p e 1 1 p e 2 2 ⋯ p e m m with n = e 1 + … + e m and k = ⌊ n / 2 ⌋ , the size of the maximum antichain of divisors of N is the number of solutions of a 1 + a 2 + … + a m = k with 0 ≤ a i ≤ e i . This is a form of a restricted ordered partition: we are splitting k into pieces a i , each of which must be non-negative and also no more than some bound e i . Let’s denote the number of such partitions by P ( e 1 , e 2 , … , e m , k ) . It would be fun to go off on a tangent now and explore this function in general, but honestly there’s no need to. We just need a fairly simple instance to solve the problem at hand. You see, in our case N = 2024 2024 . The prime decomposition of 2024 is 2024 = 2 3 ⋅ 11 ⋅ 23 , so (if we denote t = 2024 ), N = t t = 2 3 t ⋅ 11 t ⋅ 23 t So n = 5 t and k = 5 t / 2 , an integer because t is even. We need to figure out P ( 3 t , t , t , 5 t / 2 ) which is the number of ways of writing 5 t / 2 as a sum a + b + c where 0 ≤ a ≤ 3 t , 0 ≤ b ≤ t and 0 ≤ c ≤ t . The point is, we can choose b and c completely arbitrarily within their allotted ranges; any such choice yields precisely one solution, since b + c < 5 t / 2 so a can step in to fill the gap, and it’s always sufficient because 3 t > 5 t / 2 . We want to construct functions u , v : Z → Z which are bijections (one-to-one and onto) and such that u ( n ) + v ( n ) = n for all n ∈ Z . Once we do that, any bijection f can be expressed as such a sum by composing it with u and v , as Schlitzer explained. The idea of Just Do It proofs is that we construct what we need step by step, always ensuring we satisfy whatever constraints we must satisfy. The trick is to show that any partial construction allows you to take the next step while maintaining the requirements. The result may not be easy to define explicitly, but no matter: we have shown that the required object exists. To construct something step by step on the integers, rather than the positive integers, it’s useful to arrange the integers in a sequence such as 0 , 1 , − 1 , 2 , − 2 , 3 , − 3 and so on. Whenever I say something like “the least integer such that…”, I’m referring to this ordering. For example, the least integer which isn’t in the set { 0 , − 1 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 } is − 2 . Question: Given f(t) = (cost, sin2t), why is f immersion but not embedding?
Answer: I know what you mean, but the question is not phrased correctly. To ask if something is an immersion or an embedding you have to specify what is being immersed or embedded into what. The same expression, f ( t ) = ( cos ( t ) , sin ( 2 t ) ) can denote a function f 1 : [ 0 , 1 ] → R 2 , or f 2 : [ 0 , 2 π ] → R 2 , or f 3 : R → R 2 , and many other options. This matters. It always matters. You should always clarify, when speaking about a function, what is the domain and what is the codomain. But it’s especially important here. All of the functions f 1 , f 2 , f 3 are immersions. Being an immersion is a local property: for every x 0 in the domain of the function you need some ϵ , however small, such that f is a homeomorphism from I = ( x 0 − ϵ , x 0 + ϵ ) to its image f ( I ) . This is indeed the case here, since f is smooth and has a non-vanishing derivative everywhere. Being an embedding is a global property: If f : X → Y then f must be a homeomorphism from all of X to the image f ( X ) . And this is true for f 1 but false for f 2 and f 3 . The function f 1 maps the interval [ 0 , 1 ] onto this: This curved path is homeomorphic to the interval [ 0 , 1 ] just fine. The function f 1 is such a homeomorphism: it’s continuous, one-to-one, onto, and has a continuous inverse. The function f 2 maps the interval [ 0 , 2 π ] into that: This thing, whatever you call it, is not homeomorphic to an interval. The function f 3 maps the entire real line onto the same thing. Neither f 2 nor f 3 are homeomorphisms onto their image: nothing is a homeomorphism from an interval, or the line, onto this bowtie. In general, the function f ( t ) = ( cos ( t ) , sin ( 2 t ) ) from the closed interval [ 0 , a ] to R 2 is an embedding for a < 3 π / 2 and not an embedding for a ≥ 3 π / 2 , for the very simple reason that it’s no longer one-to-one. Not one-to-one, not a homeomorphism. One more word of caution: If you take the same expression to define a function on the half-open interval [ 0 , 3 π / 2 ) , then the function is one-to-one but it’s still not a homeomorphism onto its image, because its inverse is not continuous. Question: Are there infinitely many rational points on the graph of x*sin(x)?
Answer: No. There’s only one. Let’s first talk about rational points on the graph of y = sin ( x ) , which is a more natural question. A rational point in the plane is a point ( x , y ) such as both x and y are rational numbers. A rational point on the graph of y = sin ( x ) is, therefore, a rational number x such that sin ( x ) is also rational. There is one obvious point like that, which is ( 0 , 0 ) . However, it’s the only one: when x is a rational number then sin ( x ) is irrational. In fact, if x is rational then sin ( x ) is transcendental, namely, not algebraic. Here’s why: suppose that sin ( x 0 ) is an algebraic number, for some x 0 ∈ R . Then cos ( x 0 ) = √ 1 − sin 2 ( x 0 ) is also algebraic, which means that e i x 0 = cos ( x 0 ) + i sin ( x 0 ) is an algebraic number (since i is algebraic, and the sum of algebraic numbers is algebraic). By Lindemann’s theorem (1882), e u is transcendental when u ≠ 0 is algebraic. Contrapositively, if e u is algebraic then u must be transcendental. So in our case, i x 0 is either 0 or else it is transcendental, making x 0 itself transcendental as well. We conclude that the graph of y = sin ( x ) doesn’t even contain any algebraic points outside of ( 0 , 0 ) , let alone rational points. Back to the original question: we just proved that if x is rational then sin ( x ) is irrational, and therefore x sin ( x ) is irrational as well. The same goes for x + sin ( x ) , x 2 sin ( x ) and so on. (…)

Question: Let [math] r,s,t [\math] be three distinct lines passing through a point in [math] \R ^3 [\math] . Let [math] U= \R^3 - (r \cup s \cup t)[\math]. How can you calculate [math] \pi_1(U) [\math]?
Answer: Let’s do this more generally: we have n distinct lines through the origin in R 3 , and we are looking for the fundamental group of their complement in R 3 . Space without the origin is deformation-retractable into the unit sphere. This is true in any dimension. In fact it’s not hard to write down an explicit formula for the deformation: H ( x , t ) = ( 1 − t ) x + t ( x / ∥ x ∥ ) This is just the straight-line path from x at time 0 to the unit-length rescaling of x , namely x / ∥ x ∥ , at time 1 . We plainly have H ( x , 0 ) = x , H ( x , 1 ) = x / ∥ x ∥ , and the whole thing is continuous (this wouldn’t be true if we didn’t omit the origin from R 3 . The whole of R 3 is not homotopy equivalent to a sphere). We’re literally deforming the whole space, except the origin, to a sphere. In two dimensions, it looks something like this: The exact same homotopy H works just fine on R 3 minus the union of any number of lines through the origin (provided that something is left to deform), because the path of any point under the homotopy is aligned with straight lines through the origin. This means that R 3 minus n lines is homotopy equivalent to the 2 -sphere S 2 minus 2 n points, which are the points at which the missing lines meet the unit sphere. Therefore π 1 ( R 3 ∖ n ⋃ i = 1 L i ) ≅ π 1 ( S 2 ∖ 2 n ⋃ j = 1 P j ) The fundamental group of the sphere minus N points is the same as that of the plane minus N − 1 points: these spaces are homeomorphic, by stereographic projection. And the fundamental group of the plane minus N − 1 points is F N − 1 , the free group on N − 1 generators, those generators being loops around each of the points. So π 1 of R 3 minus n intersecting lines is isomorphic to F 2 n − 1 , and in our case, the answer is F 5 , the free group on 5 generators. (…)

Furthermore, even if we had all of the c n 's somehow readily available, we would be able to write an expression of f ( z ) as an infinite sum or product… with the c n 's right there in the expression, so that’s not doing us any good. For example, if c n are rapidly-increasing numbers (as your numbers are), then f ( x ) = ∑ c − 1 n x n is an analytic function. Sure. And the Taylor series of that function is… exactly that: ∑ c − 1 n x n . So… what? If you can’t compute the c n 's, you still can’t compute them just because you packaged them in a power series and called it f . Perhaps by “find” you mean that we can write f ( z ) as some kind of elementary explicit expression, and of course, we can’t. If we could, the c n 's would be computable, and they aren’t. Taylor’s theorem doesn’t “transform” anything uncomputable to anything computable. It simply observes that taking derivatives of an analytic function and evaluating those derivatives at x = 0 yields the coefficients of the power series with some factorials thrown in. That’s all. It doesn’t make it easier to compute anything. Finally, the Busy Beaver function doesn’t “grow faster than anything”, because that doesn’t mean anything. The BB function grows faster than any computable function. There are many functions which grow faster than BB ( n ) , such as 2 BB ( n ) , or the BB function of a Turing machine with an oracle for the halting problem. (…)

Answer: I’m not sure I can guess what “ n = 2022 , 2024 ” means, but perhaps it’s asking us to solve the problem twice: once with n = 2022 and again with n = 2024 . First of all, why should there be a “largest composite number Bob will never be able to write”? It appears that Bob can only write numbers that are somewhat skippily separated, so is it not the case that larger and larger numbers would be unreachable, composite or not? It turns out that no, you can actually reach every sufficiently large composite number, but this wasn’t obvious to me. So I looked at a simple case where the starting number is n = 2 . What can you do with n = 2 ? Clearly the only d available to you is d = 2 , so you can move to 2 + 2 = 4 . You can still you d = 2 as the divisor, so you can proceed with 2 → 4 → 6 → 8 and so on: all even numbers are reachable. Great. What about the odd ones? We certainly can’t reach 3 , or 5 , or 7 . In fact, if p is any prime, there’s no way to reach p : if you arrive at some m > 0 divisible by some d > 1 and move to m + d = p then p is also divisible by d , but p is prime so d = p and m = 0 , contradiction. There’s no way to reach any prime you didn’t happen to start with. But the question is only about composite numbers, and we already secured all even numbers, so we only worry about odd composites. For example, 9 . Can we reach 9 ? Sure: we go 2 → 4 → 6 → 9 . The trick was to land on some multiple of 3 (we landed on 6 ) and from there we can add 3 's for as long as we want to reach any larger multiple of 3 . So even numbers and multiples of 3 are fine. What about multiples of 5 ? Same idea: 2 → 4 → 6 → 8 → 10 → 15 → 20 → 25 → … . We just need to hit some multiple of 5 and from there we are good. And the same would go for multiples of 7 , or 11 , or 13 : we get to their even multiples 14 , or 22 , or 26 and from there we can get to all of their other multiples. So in fact, starting with n = 2 , we can reach any composite number. Indeed, suppose that M is composite, and let p be its smallest prime divisor. Then M = m p with m ≥ 2 . Starting with n = 2 we can get to all even numbers, so in particular we can get to 2 p , and from there we can keep adding p 's until we get to m p = M . What if our starting number is some larger n > 2 ? Let’s assume that n is still even, as strongly suggested by the question. So we can still move forward from n by adding 2 's, and we can still reach all even numbers greater than (or equal to) n . In particular, for any odd prime p we can reach any even multiple of p which is at least n , and from there we can add p 's and reach any multiple of p , even or odd. So which composite numbers ≥ n may we not be able to reach? Even composites are fine. For an odd composite number M = m p with m odd, we can still reach it if ( m − 1 ) p ≥ n , because m − 1 is even. The problem, then, is with M = m p with m p odd, m p > n yet ( m − 1 ) p < n . Once again, it’s best to look at the smallest prime p dividing M . In that case, m ≥ p , and from ( m − 1 ) p < n we can conclude ( p − 1 ) p < n . This gives us a finite list of primes p to worry about: only those for which p ( p − 1 ) < n . For each such prime we need to find the smallest multiple m p such that m p > n , and then see if there’s a way to reach it (it’s not reachable with + 2 's but it may still be possible to reach it with some other small step if n happens to be divisible by that small step). If there’s no way to reach it we mark it unreachable, but there’s no need to look at any other multiple of p which is ≥ n : they are all reachable, since n and ( m + 1 ) p are both even. When n = 2022 , the prime 47 is already too large because 47 × 46 > 2022 . So we only need to check the primes through p = 43 . 2022 is divisible by 2 , 3 and no other small prime, so we can use 2 and 3 to reach our near targets but nothing else. I don’t see an elegant way of doing this, so case by case analysis it is: Therefore, the largest unreachable composite number when starting with n = 2022 is 2033 . Repeating the analysis with n = 2024 , we no longer have 3 as an available divisor: 2024 = 2 3 × 11 × 23 . So the answer for n = 2024 is the same: the largest unreachable composite is 2033 . If we start at 2026 , however, there’ll be a larger one: 2047 = 23 × 89 would be unreachable. (…)

Answer: Since 2 and 81 are relatively prime, powers of 2 mod 81 are cyclic: there’s an order of 2 mod 81 , which is the least positive integer m such that 2 m ≡ 1 ( mod 81 ) , and once you have this m you can find 2 N ( mod 81 ) by studying N mod m . How you find that order depends a little on some background knowledge you may or may not possess. If nothing else you can tediously start with 2 and keep multiplying by 2 , reducing mod 81 as you go, and keeping count: 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 ≡ 47 , 94 ≡ 13 , 26 and so on, until you hit 1 (guaranteed). Doable. Tedious. With a tad more prior art you may be aware that the order of anything mod 81 must divide φ ( 81 ) = φ ( 3 4 ) = 3 3 ( 3 − 1 ) = 54 . You should also notice that odd powers of 2 aren’t even congruent to 1 mod 3 , so they can’t possibly be congruent to 1 mod 81 . So we’re interested in even divisors of 54 , but 2 2 = 4 and 2 6 = 64 are clearly not 1 mod 81 . We’re left with ruling out 2 18 ≡ 1 ( mod 54 ) , and there are several ways to proceed: the easiest would be to simply not do that; the only impact is that we may not be simplifying our subsequent work as much as we could have. The congruence 2 54 ≡ 1 ( mod 81 ) holds in any case. If you do wish to confirm that the order of 2 mod 81 is 54 and nothing less, you may either compute 64 3 mod 81 or bring in a bit more of the theory. At any rate, to figure out 2 N mod 81 , it’s enough to know N mod 54 . Our problem is now reduced to finding 2 3 ⋅ 5 22 mod 54 . The good news is that we’ve made dramatic progress: instead of a tower-power of height 3 we have just simple exponents. The bad news is that 2 3 ⋅ 5 22 is not relatively prime to 54 , so we need to be a bit more careful. Finding something mod 54 means finding it mod 2 , and mod 27 , and then using the Chinese Remainder Theorem to piece those into a residue mod 54 . The mod 2 part is easy: our number 2 3 ⋅ 5 22 is clearly even, so it is 0 mod 2 . What is it mod 27 ? The 2 3 = 8 is easy again: it is 8 . The 5 22 thing requires, once again, that we find the order of 5 mod 27 (they are relatively prime). The order of anything mod 27 divides φ ( 27 ) = 18 , and odd powers can’t work for the same reason as before ( 5 ≡ 2 ( mod 3 ) ), so we need an even divisor of 18 and that’s either 2 (nope) or 6 (also nope; 5 2 ≡ − 2 and the cube of that is − 8 ). So it’s 18 itself. Finally, 22 mod 18 is 4 , so we can say that 5 22 ≡ 5 4 ( mod 27 ) . This isn’t hard: 5 2 = 25 ≡ − 2 , so 5 3 ≡ ( − 2 ) × 5 = − 10 , and ( − 10 ) × 5 = − 50 which is 4 (because − 54 ≡ 0 ). So we can work back now: mod 2 we have 0 , and mod 27 we have 8 × 4 = 32 ≡ 5 , and hooray, the number 32 is even so it works as is: it’s the unique residue mod 54 which is both 0 mod 2 and 5 mod 27 . Going further back, our 2 N mod 81 is now seen to be 2 32 mod 81 , which still looks like some work but it’s clearly a significant improvement over 2 8 ⋅ 5 22 . I think the fastest way at this point is just repeated squaring: 2 2 = 4 2 4 = 4 2 = 16 2 8 = 16 2 = 256 ≡ 13 ( mod 81 ) 2 16 ≡ 13 2 = 169 ≡ 7 ( mod 81 ) 2 32 ≡ 7 2 = 49 and that’s your answer. (…)

Question: What does p stand for in mathematics, for example p-adic, p-Laplace operator, Fourier's p-capacity?
Answer: (Very) different things. The letter p often stands for a prime number ( 2 , 3 , 5 , 7 and so on). This is the case with p -adic numbers, p -primary components of groups, fields of characteristic p , and more. In fact, throughout algebra, number theory and combinatorics, p is almost always taken to mean “prime number” without explicit indication. In analysis, on the other hand, p often refers to a real number ≥ 1 or ∞ . It’s now not a prime number – it’s not even an integer (and possibly not a real number at all!). This is the case with L p spaces, ℓ p spaces, p -norms, Sobolev W k , p spaces, as well as the p -Laplacian you mentioned in the question. I’m not familiar with “Fourier’s p -capacity” but I would guess it’s referring to the latter convention. As a rule, mathematical symbols rarely refer to one consistent thing throughout math. You’ll find π used in algebra to refer to a collection of primes, or as a projection operator in topology. q could be a prime, or a prime power, or none of these (as in the concept of q -analogs.) Even whole words don’t have a consistent meaning (I contributed “primitive” to this fun list). Non-alphanumeric symbols don’t fare much better: the symbol = is universally take to mean equality, but ! isn’t always factorial, X ∘ isn’t always degrees, and ∧ isn’t always the logical AND operator. We simply have too many concepts and too few typographical elements. (…)
