Question: Why do we have several geometries (Euclidean, Spherical, Non-Euclidean…) but only one arithmetic? Why everything can be described with same arithmetic but requires different geometries?
Answer: Both “Arithmetic” and “Geometry” are not formally defined terms. If you take a very broad view of what counts as “Geometry” and an extremely narrow view of what counts as “Arithmetic” then, sure, you could find many geometries and a single arithmetic, but this is merely a reflection of the choice of interpretation of these particular terms. To describe “everything” we need many, many more than “several” geometries, and many, many more than a single arithmetical structure. The ancient Euclidean geometry evolved into a small part of what is now called synthetic geometry, which itself is just a small part of geometry - differential geometry, algebraic geometry, Riemannian geometry, and many other types of geometry are being studied nowadays, each offering infinitely many spaces and structures to explore. Similarly, school arithmetic is now a tiny part of what can variably be described as Number Theory (and specifically Algebraic Number Theory), Abstract Algebra, Ring Theory, Field Theory and various other overlapping domains. Both Geometry and Arithmetic, in a broad sense, are huge parts of modern mathematics, and exist in infinitely many different shapes and forms. (…)

Name: Alon Amit
Question: How come the golden ratio is taught in high school algebra class but the plastic ratio isn't?
Answer: “Taught in high school algebra” is not a meaningful expression. Different countries, different counties, different school districts, different individual schools and different teachers may include or exclude any topic from a high school math curriculum, and there’s always more than one single curriculum: students get to choose the high school math program they take. The golden ratio may or may not be mentioned in any specific high school course sequence. If it is, it may be mentioned in passing, or it may be presented with some of its properties, or it may be over-represented with some of the imagined properties it doesn’t actually have (many, many people think the golden ratio means far more than it actually does.) There are cool things to do with it that could fill a nice 2-hour class for interested kids, but that’s as much as I would dedicate to it. The “plastic ratio” is the unique real solution of X 3 = X + 1 . What would you teach about it? Without some really interesting, compelling context, I’ve no idea what teachers and kids are expected to do with it. Solving cubic equations isn’t part of almost any high-school curriculum I’m aware of (as always, Proof School is likely an exception). If anything, that might be a nice thing to include in some curricula for some audiences. Solving X 3 = X + 1 in radicals can then be a tedious but not-entirely-useless exercise. A possible interesting context could be Pisot-Vijayaraghavan numbers and their nice almost-integer powers. There’s absolutely no reason to force this topic into any general math curriculum, but in specialized contexts for curious students that’s a wonderful thing to study. In that context, the plastic ratio has a nice feature: it’s the smallest positive Pisot number. Ok, but again, this isn’t reasonable fodder for generic high-school curricula by any stretch of the imagination, and… anything else you’d like to teach about it? (…)

To solve this question, then, we need to determine v 2 of a central binomial coefficient ( 2 k k ) . If this question is from some math competition or Number Theory textbook, the assumption is that you already know what that v 2 is. But let’s say you don’t. So you start by gathering some data: You don’t actually need to compute those binomial coefficients: you just want to know how many 2 's are in their prime decomposition. For example, ( 8 4 ) = 8 ⋅ 7 ⋅ 6 ⋅ 5 1 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 3 ⋅ 4 We count 4 occurrences of 2 in the numerator ( 3 for the 8 , 1 for the 6 ) and 3 in the denominator ( 1 from the 2 , 2 from the 4 ), which leaves just 1 overall. So v 2 ( ( 8 4 ) ) = 1 . You now look at this sequence 0 , 1 , 1 , 2 , 1 , 2 , 2 , 3 , 1 , 2 , and it either rings a bell or it doesn’t. If it doesn’t, you’ll have to hit upon the idea of writing k in binary (since, after all, we’re looking at powers of 2 ). Once you do that, observing that v 2 ( k = 111 ) = 3 , v 2 ( k = 1000 ) = 1 and v 2 ( k = 1001 ) = 2 should be enough to convince you that v 2 ( ( 2 k k ) ) = number of  1 's in the binary representation of  k . Once you have this conjecture, you want to prove it. This is easy to do if you’re familiar with Kummer’s theorem about p -valuations of binomial coefficients: in our case, it says that v 2 ( ( 2 k k ) ) is the number of carries when you add k to itself, which is just the number of 1 's in its binary representation. (If you’re not familiar with Kummer’s theorem, you’ll have to prove the boxed conjecture from scratch. The number-of-1’s function satisfies two simple recurrence relations connecting the value at k to the values at 2 k and 2 k + 1 ; show that the binomial valuation satisfies the same relations.) Answering the original question now boils down to counting the total number of 1 's in the binary representations of the numbers 0 , 1 , 2 , … , 2 11 . If you ignore the last number for a second and imagine the binary representations of 0 , 1 , 2 , … , 2 11 − 1 arranged in a table with 2 11 rows and 11 columns: you should be able to visualize, or directly notice, that there’s a symmetry here: exactly half of that table is 1 's, because the number of 1 's in k is 11 minus the number of 1 's in 2 11 − k . Overall, then, there are 11 × 2 10 1’s in this array, so 1 + that if we bring back the 2 11 term. The answer of the question is 11 × 2 10 + 1 , and in general it’s M × 2 M − 1 + 1 where the product runs from k = 0 to k = 2 M . (…)

Question: Is it possible to extend the factorial function further than the gamma function, so that it is also defined for the negative integers? How would this be done?
Answer: Any function can be extended to anywhere you want. Just set its value to be 2.3 anywhere it’s not currently defined. Or − 7 . Or 0 . This isn’t the question. The question is what features and properties do we wish the extended function to retain. Should it be continuous? Should it satisfy any equations that are inherited from the parent function before the extension? The gamma function doesn’t merely satisfy Γ ( n ) = ( n − 1 ) ! . That’s ridiculously easy to achieve. What it achieves is being continuous and in fact analytic everywhere it’s defined, and furthermore, it satisfies Γ ( z + 1 ) = z Γ ( z ) everywhere, which mimics the familiar rule ( n + 1 ) ! = ( n + 1 ) n ! . For a moment let’s use the more familiar exclamation mark notation rather than Γ to avoid the nuisance shift-by- 1 . We know that 1 ! = 1 = 1 × 0 ! , which is one of the many reasons we choose to set 0 ! = 1 . What then? We need 0 ! = 1 = 0 × ( − 1 ) ! . See the problem? No real or complex value we could pick for ( − 1 ) ! would satisfy that. You could choose to make ( − 1 ) ! = 0 , or anything else. Your prerogative. But you would lose continuity and the property that ( x + 1 ) ! = ( x + 1 ) ⋅ x ! . So there’s really no point in doing that. We wouldn’t get anything useful. The function Γ is amazingly useful. The extension of s ! to Γ ( s − 1 ) is unique given a few natural requirements. Even if you focus on real numbers only, and even if you don’t require continuity, Γ is the only function satisfying Γ ( 1 ) = 1 , Γ ( x + 1 ) = x Γ ( x ) and being log-convex. So we choose it over all other alternatives, and keep those simple poles at the negative integers and at 0 . There may still be some cycles, but the general trend is up and it would be easier to show that most or all numbers just fly off to infinity. The nice thing about the 3 x + 1 map is that it is more or less balanced: you move up by a factor of 3 and then down by a factor of 2 , but sometimes another factor of 2 , and sometimes another, and so on. The overall pressure is actually down, which makes it reasonable to expect that all starting points would eventually lead to 1 . With your proposed maps, it’s the opposite. I’m not claiming that they are fully resolved, but they should be easier, and their conclusion very different. There’s apparently a 1999 paper by Metzger that claims to settle the 5 x + 1 case, but I’m not sure if it’s complete or correct (it’s published in a less well-known journal, and Lagarias’ review of it is somewhat non-commital). Problem solving is an important part of math research, but it’s not quite the same kind as Olympiad problem solving, and earning a Ph.D. in math takes skills and dedication of a different character. Some mathematicians enjoy Olympiad-style problem solving and can handle many Olympiad problems faster than you or me, but many don’t, and even the best of them may not be able to earn top scores at a recent IMO. The kids who participate at the IMO are deeply immersed in this style of problems, they are well trained, and they have just the right type of smarts for this challenge: creative structuring of strategies, blazing fast assessment of different ideas and directions to pursue, tenacity, imagination and a keen sense of abstract analogies. Answer: Nice question. As a rule, roots of integers don’t tend to allow such coincidences to happen, and it’s actually possible to prove that, with suitable caveats: see this Quora question, or Iurie Boreico’s article mentioned in my answer (especially p. 90, “Higher powers”). So when you see such a question you should think there are no solutions, but then you should also think wait, what suitable caveats? You see, 3 √ 5 + 3 √ 5 = 2 3 √ 5 3 , obviously, and now we can slide the 2 inside the radical and find 3 √ 5 + 3 √ 5 = 3 √ 40 3 . So here we have a sum of two cube roots of integers being another cube root of an integer, but it’s hardly a coincidence. It’s not a genuinely surprising relationship between cube roots of distinct integers. So, does something like that happen in the present question? The thing about 40 is that it’s divisible by 2 3 , which makes 3 √ 40 3 be 3 √ 5 3 in disguise. We should immediately wonder what 2025 happens to be divisible by. You are, of course, aware that next year is a perfect square year: 2025 = 45 2 , and lo, 45 is itself divisible further, so 2025 = 3 4 ⋅ 5 2 , and then 3 √ 2025 = 3 3 √ 75 3 . Huh. Rather than twice a cube root we have thrice a cube root, which leads us to write 3 √ 75 + 2 3 √ 75 = 3 3 √ 75 = 3 √ 2025 3 or 3 √ 75 + 3 √ 600 = 3 √ 2025 3 That’s definitely a solution to the given equation, with a = 75 and b = 600 (and we can clearly also swap them around). The thing is, aside from this sneaky maneuver around the caveats, there are no further surprises. The equation 3 √ a + 3 √ b = 3 3 √ 75 3 is only solvable when a and b are themselves multiples of 75 , which is a particular case of the general claim we proved in that previous answer: Claim: Suppose that q 1 , q 2 , … , q n are nonzero rational numbers, m 1 , m 2 , … , m n are integers ≥ 2 , and r i = m i √ q i . Suppose further that r i / r j is irrational for all i ≠ j . Then the numbers r i are linearly independent over Q , meaning: if c 1 r 1 + c 2 r 2 + … + c n r n = 0 with c i ∈ Q , then c i = 0 for all i . Here, we can take q 1 = a (an integer), q 2 = b (another integer), q 3 = 75 (also an integer), m 1 = m 2 = m 3 = 3 ≥ 2 , and r i = m i √ q i . We get told that r 1 , r 2 , r 3 are linearly independent over Q (meaning, there’s no way to combine them with rational coefficients to get 0 , unless all the coefficients are themselves 0 ), with the caveat that r i / r j should be irrational. In our present context, the claim tells us that 3 √ a + 3 √ b = 3 √ 2025 3 cannot possibly happen unless one of a / b , 2025 / a or 2025 / b is the cube of a rational number. If a / b is such a cube, dividing the equation by 3 √ b 3 reveals that 2025 / b is also such a cube, so we can focus just on 2025 / a (or 2025 / b , doesn’t matter) being a rational cube. If 2025 / a is a rational cube, remembering that a must be an integer, it must be divisible by 5 2 , exactly, to cancel the 5 2 in 2025 . It would have been possible for a to be divisible by 5 2 + 3 m for some m > 0 , but since b is positive a must be ≤ 2025 , so 5 5 and up are out of the question. Similarly, a must be divisible by 3 or by 3 4 ( 3 7 is too much). It’s also possible for a to be divisible by p 3 for other primes p , but since a is already known to be at least 75 , even 7 3 is too much. So a must be 2 a 3 b 5 2 with a = 0 or 3 and b is 1 or 4 . All told, a must be 75 , 600 or 2025 ( 16200 is too much). Since the question requires b > 0 , a = 2025 is also too large so the only solution is 3 √ 75 + 3 √ 600 = 3 √ 2025 3 . All this hinges on the Claim we’ve cited. If the context of the question is some math contest or problem set, it may or may not be feasible for you to cite this result. If not, there may be an easier ad-hoc argument for this particular question that shows that ( 75 , 600 ) is the only solution – I don’t know, I didn’t really look. At any rate, merely finding ( 75 , 600 ) isn’t enough. A complete answer to this question must also argue why this is the only positive solution. (…)

Now we are down to m 2 + m + 1 = 5 n 2 + 3 or m 2 + m = 5 n 2 + 2 . To complete the square we can multiply by 4 and add 1 , obtaining ( 2 m + 1 ) 2 = 20 n 2 + 9 . If n isn’t divisible by 3 then 20 n 2 + 9 ≡ 2 ( mod 3 ) , which is incompatible with the LHS being a square. So n , and therefore also 2 m + 1 , must be divisible by 3 . We write n = 3 y and 2 m + 1 = 3 x , and now 9 x 2 = 180 y 2 + 9 or x 2 = 20 y 2 + 1 . This is Pell’s equation x 2 − N y 2 = 1 with N = 20 . Any integer solution of this must have odd x , which is just what we need to make 2 m + 1 = 3 x work, so the solutions of m 2 + m = 5 n 2 + 2 correspond exactly to the solutions of this Pell equation, where we simply need to set m = ( 3 x − 1 ) / 2 and n = 3 y . For example, the solution x = 9 , y = 2 leads to m = 13 , n = 6 which indeed solves m 2 + m + 1 = 5 n 2 + 3 . The theory of Pell’s equation is already explained in many places on Quora, so I won’t repeat it here: the solution ( 9 , 2 ) is, in fact, a fundamental solution, and all other solutions can be found by comparing x + y √ 20 = ( 9 + 2 √ 20 ) n for n = 1 , 2 , 3 … . ( 9 + 2 √ 20 ) 1 = 9 + 2 √ 20 ⟹ ( x , y ) = ( 9 , 2 ) ( 9 + 2 √ 20 ) 2 = 161 + 36 √ 20 ⟹ ( x , y ) = ( 161 , 36 ) ( 9 + 2 √ 20 ) 3 = 2889 + 646 √ 20 ⟹ ( x , y ) = ( 2889 , 646 ) and so on. Each of these solutions yields a solution ( m , n ) = ( ( 3 x − 1 ) / 2 , 3 y ) of m 2 + m + 1 = 5 n 2 + 3 , where we can clearly also attach a minus sign to n . Those are all solutions. (…)

Answer: This √ | G | thing is a clue. If H has more than √ | G | elements, and K has more than √ | G | elements, than we have more than | G | pairs of elements ( h , k ) with h ∈ H and k ∈ K . So perhaps what we’re really being asked here is this: if there are more than | G | pairs ( h , k ) , then | H ∩ K | > 1 . (This is actually a stronger statement). Taking the contrapositive, this is equivalent to: if | H ∩ K | = 1 then there are no more than | G | pairs ( h , k ) with h ∈ H and k ∈ K . If two subgroups intersect trivially then they can’t both be too large: the product of their sizes cannot exceed | G | , which is the same as saying that there no more than | G | pairs of elements ( h , k ) . Why would that be true? Well, a very natural and simple reason would be if the products h k of those pairs are all different. Right? The products are elements of the big group G , and if they’re different, well, there can’t be more than | G | of them. Our final reframing of the question, then, is this: if H , K ≤ G are two subgroups and H ∩ K = { 1 } then the products h k with h ∈ H and k ∈ K are all distinct. This immediately forces | H | ⋅ | K | ≤ | G | , and in particular it prevents | H | and | K | from both exceeding √ | G | . Great. So when do we get h k = h ′ k ′ ? You should always have the instinct of rearranging equalities to get things from the same group on the same side. Multiplying by k − 1 on the right and h ′ − 1 on the left, we find h ′ − 1 h = k ′ k − 1 . Now the element on the left is in H , and on the right it’s in K , but they are equal, and the only element in both H and K is 1 , so h ′ − 1 h = 1 and k ′ k − 1 = 1 , which means that h = h ′ and k = k ′ . Put differently, if the pair ( h , k ) and the pair ( h ′ , k ′ ) are not the same pair, then h k and h ′ k ′ are not the same product. And that’s what we wanted to prove. ■ (…)

Question: The 2022 U of Houston Number Sense Exam had 104 questions for 30 minutes, all meant to be done in your head. Is there a simple (30-second) way to solve #84 that I cannot see: "What is the shortest distance betweeen (0,-2) and 5x+12y=11"?
Answer: This is a doable question, I would argue, if and only if the solver happens to have learned a nice formula for the distance between a point ( x 0 , y 0 ) and a line given by a x + b y + c = 0 . The formula is simply to substitute the point in the equation of the line, obtaining a x 0 + b y 0 + c . Clearly, if the point is on the line, this yields 0 which is exactly what we want. However, if the point is off the line, this doesn’t quite yield the correct distance: you need to divide it by √ a 2 + b 2 (and take the absolute value). I was certainly taught this formula in high school, and I think Mr. Lieber showed us why it is true, but I don’t know that kids in the US nowadays are likely to be familiar with it. Someone seeing this for the first time in a 30-seconds-per-question context would need to have really quick mental abilities in order to figure this out in the allotted time. (Who is the Number Sense exam for…?) If you do know the formula, and especially if you’ve used it before, you’d immediately recognize the coefficients a = 5 and b = 12 as being friendly in a Pythagorean triple kind of way, so the square root of their sum of squares is 13 . The substitution yields − 35 , so the distance is 35 / 13 and we can move on to the next question. Are you sure the line wasn’t 5 x + 12 y + 11 = 0 ? This would make the answer be just 1 . I still don’t see a quick alternative way to see that. EDIT: The full exam is here, if you’re curious. The equation is, actually, 5 x + 12 y − 11 = 0 , so the distance indeed 35 / 13 and not 1 . Personally I like mental arithmetic, but this is downright grueling. I don’t think I’d have enjoyed it. Some kids clearly do, so, ok, that’s cool. (…)

Question: Is it indeed true that Princeton have a better math department than Harvard does? If so, then why does Harvard have far more Putnam Competition titles?
Answer: There’s no objective sense in which one math department is “better” than another; research, teaching, field focus and culture are all multi-dimensional and impossible to quantify in a meaningfully objective sense. (There’s no need to point out that the math department at prominent university X is likely “better” in most dimensions than that of a tiny college in some remote region of the world. I understand that. But putting the departments of strong research universities on a linear scale is truly meaningless, despite what the editors of US News would have you believe.) And of all the ways to gauge the quality or strength or suitability of a math department to your needs, counting Putnam titles is particularly pointless. Some universities happen to have faculty members who put a lot of effort into the Putnam, and a strong tradition of taking it very seriously; some universities don’t. MIT is almost ridiculously successful at it, but that doesn’t mean that its math department is 20x better than all other math departments combined. It just means that MIT puts significant emphasis on competition math, and that probably affects its applicant pool, acceptance criteria, efforts in preparing the team and maybe a few other factors. It doesn’t mean that its faculty has “better” researchers, or teachers, or human beings. (None of this is meant to criticize Yufei or the MIT Putnam contestants. They’re brilliant and awesome. Question: Are there large cardinals in abstract algebra?

Question: I have a 56×56 matrix with only around 200 nonzero elements. How do I write code that efficiently computes its determinant?
Answer: What are those nonzero elements? 0’s and 1’s, positive integers, integers, rational numbers, approximate reals, something else? Any known bounds? Do you need the precise determinant, or an approximation, or an estimate, or just to determine if it’s 0? Is the matrix symmetric? Hermitian? The answers to those questions matter a lot. For instance, a family of those algorithms (Lanczos and its improvements) find the eigenvalues In order of absolute value of their logarithm, letting you decide when to stop once a desired accuracy is achieved. (It is a lot more common to need the find top eigenvalues than it is to need the actual determinant. Is that the case for you?) Another important question is why you want to write code. Is this a course assignment, meaning you do need to produce your own code, or is it a genuine computational challenge, in which case you really shouldn’t because there are tons of highly optimized libraries out there? The one time in my life when I needed to wrestle with Fortran was when I tried to deploy one of those Lanczos variants from the LAPACK library in order to experiment with certain large graphs. Looking at the code, it was obvious to me that this isn’t something I would have been able to create from scratch. LAPACK, ARPACK and many variants are still in heavy use today. So either look around at those libraries, or say more about what you actually need and we may be able to help. (…)

Answer: The function 4 x + 5 x + 6 x is monotonically increasing throughout its domain (which is all of R ). More generally, this is true for the function f ( x ) = a x 1 + a x 2 + … + a x k whenever a 1 , a 2 , … , a k are any real numbers greater than 1 . If someone challenges you to solve f ( x ) = M for some specific list of a i (such as 4 , 5 , 6 ) and some specific positive value M (such as 405 ), you know immediately that there is exactly one solution for x . From now on, the important thing is context. If this is pitched to you as an exercise, a problem to be solved by hand, it is likely that a i and M are positive integers, and furthermore, it is likely that the solution x is also an integer. You can find it by bisection: start with x = 0 with f ( 0 ) = k which is very likely < M , find some N large enough such that f ( N ) > M , and now your search space is the integers between 0 and N . Check ⌊ N / 2 ⌋ and then move up or down depending on whether you overshot or undershot. Keep going. This isn’t merely “trial and error”. You know that there is a unique solution, you expect it to be an integer, and you’re conducting an efficient binary search. It’s an explicit algorithm which isn’t essentially better or worse than solving equations in more common ways. If you encounter such a question at random or in some other not gently-designed context, there’s no reason to assume that the solution is an integer. It could be rational but this is, again, highly unlikely unless deliberately designed to be so. Therefore, you seek a real number that is not expected to have a nicely explicit expression; you can present it as the limit of some iterative process such as Newton’s method. There’s no reason to expect anything nicer than this. (…)

Question:
Could we come up with new mathematical language that would make it possible for equations like
cos
x
=
x
to have exact solutions (instead of only numerical approximations)?
Answer: This seems to be something that many people don’t know about mathematics: coming up with new mathematical language is doing mathematics. Math has a built-in feature called “come up with new language”. It’s done all the time. Really. Easiest thing in the world, math-wise. The equation cos ( x ) = x already has exact an exact solution. It doesn’t have “only numerical approximations”, it has an exact solution, which is a real number. Once upon a time we didn’t have real numbers. We only had rational numbers. Back then you would be justified in saying, damn, why can’t we pinpoint the solution of cos ( x ) = x ? (Let’s pretend you already had cosine, back then). We can compare cos ( 3 / 4 ) and 3 / 4 , and it’s close but not the same. We can try x = 14 / 19 and it’s even closer. And x = 17 / 23 is really close. We keep going. Always getting closer. Never quite making the equality work. So, we invent a new language called real numbers, and now we have a unique, nice, precise solution to the equation. And not just that equation. We have √ 23 which is the precise positive solution of x 2 = 23 . And we have e which is the precise solution of ln ( x ) = 1 (yes, we can define the function ln without any reference to the particular number e .) And so on. This is very similar to the way real numbers were actually first observed, when early Greek thinkers wanted everything to be rational and noticed that some things, like the diagonal of a square, refuse. The formal definition of reals came much later, but the motivation was the same. I can see you're still dissatisfied. You want cos ( x ) = x to have an explicit, comprehensible, “closed-form” solution. Right? You want that. So let’s invent a new language. Say, let’s define H ( t ) to be the smallest positive solution of cos ( x ) = t x . And now the equation cos ( x ) = x has a beautiful explicit solution: it is x = H ( 1 ) . Still dissatisfied? Feel like I’m cheating? I’m not, I did exactly what you asked me to do. Do you feel that the function H is obscure? Sure, you’re not used to it. Neither am I. But do you think √ x is better? Why? Because your calculator has a √ ⋅ button? Casio can make a calculator with an H button. It works. Punch a number, press that button, get an answer. There’s nothing fundamentally more “explicit” about arccos or ln or any such function. They can be computed for any input with any desired precision. They define precise outputs for precise inputs (except for some inputs when there’s no result, like when ln insists on positive inputs). Same for H . We don’t need to “invent a new mathematical language”. We just need to do math. (…)

Question: Is it mathematically kosher to prove that the sum of the reciprocals of the prime numbers diverges by invoking the Prime Number Theorem, whereby the nth prime ~ n*log(n), and then doing a simple integration of d (log(u)) /log(u) from 1 to infinity?
Answer: Kinda yes, but actually no. The smaller issue is that the PNT doesn’t tell you that the n th prime is n log ( n ) , it just says that it is roughly that, in a sense that can be made precise. So you can’t just glibly replace p n by n log ( n ) in a computation. This can be handled by using appropriate upper bounds (e.g. Dusart’s bound), so it’s not a huge issue, and in many contexts you can totally get away with it even in its imprecise form. The bigger problem, however, is that this is essentially a circular argument. You’re using an advanced result, the PNT, to “prove” something that is itself a tiny step in the proof of the PNT. Or, at least, potentially so. I mean, it’s possible to write down a complete proof of the PNT without ever uttering the words “the series of prime reciprocals diverges”, but I don’t think it’s possible to write down such a proof without proving at some (early) point something stronger or essentially equivalent. There are, by now, many proofs of the PNT, and I’m sure it’s technically possible to start from first principles and write down an intricate proof of the divergence of ∑ 1 / p ∑ by first proving the full PNT in some way, then showing something like Dusart’s inequality, and eventually concluding the divergence of prime reciprocals. But this makes little logical sense. Many PNT proofs start by analyzing the behavior of ζ ( s ) near the pole s = 1 . The prime reciprocals sum can be understood as the value at s = 1 of the prime zeta function, which in this region is easily seen to be essentially the log of the usual Riemann zeta function. That’s all you need, and it would be bizarre to proceed all the way to the PNT just to go back and prove something you could have proven in line 5. At any rate, formally, if you wish to invoke Theorem T in order to prove fact F, you must make sure that you have a proof of theorem T which doesn’t in any way rely on fact F at any point. Otherwise, you’ve achieved nothing. This can probably be done here, but it’s hard to make sure, and it certainly doesn’t make sense. If anything, I would use Chebyshev’s much simpler and earlier results on the prime counting function to prove something like that. It’s still a much bigger hammer than necessary, but at least it’s not a nuclear weapon. (…)

Question: Could/how I become a volunteer researcher assistant if I’m still a bachelor’s student? I read a lot about improved estimates for the zeta function and prime number theorem.
Answer: That really depends on your school. If there’s a professor in your university who’s interested in providing early research experience for undergrads, she or he may be able to offer a project for you to tackle. Some schools have official REU programs (Research Experience for Undergraduates), so it’s good to check if your school has that. If you’re thinking of becoming an assistant to a researcher elsewhere, I would expect this to be nigh impossible. I would really encourage you to focus on whatever your school has to offer. Simply start by talking to your number theory professors. The zeta function and the prime number theorem aren’t exactly light topics, but an experienced researcher may be able to have an idea for something an undergrad can explore. (…)

Question: The song 'Golden Brown' by The Stranglers is a favourite. However, the time signature is … complex. I read that some parts are 13/8(!), but there are clearly changes within the song. What's the theory behind this, and how is such a song created?
Answer: The song 'Golden Brown' by The Stranglers is a favourite. Totally. Always loved that hook. However, the time signature is … complex. Why “however”? Complex time signatures are great. Different people react differently, but some find them intriguing and refreshing. I do. I read that some parts are 13/8(!) You’ve… read? There’s no need to read. You can easily count along the instrumental hook: um-pa-pa-um-pa-pa-um-pa-pa-um-pa-um-pa. That’s 13, naturally divided into 3+3+3+2+2. It’s often transcribed as 6/8 followed by 7/8. I find it more natural to think of it as 9/8 followed by 4/8. Doesn’t matter. This repeats four times, and then settles into a relaxed 6/8 for the verses, returning to that 13/8 each chorus (I think the hook serves kind of as a chorus). What's the theory behind this? I may be showing my ignorance here but I don’t believe there’s any actual theory behind odd time signatures which shift in and out. Much (not all) of music has a clear rhythm aligned with a time signature, and those time signatures are sometimes simple, sometimes more complex, and sometimes not constant throughout a composition. Pop songs overwhelmingly stick to 4/4 and 3/4 and such, but occasionally they stray off that beaten path, which is nice. Honestly, Golden Brown is a pretty mild instance. There are many songs out there with way more complex signatures. Other forms of music, like the traditional music of various distinct regions and ethnic groups in Africa, employ much more complex time signatures a lot more frequently. and how is such a song created? I wouldn’t expect the creative process behind “such” a song to be materially different than any other kind of song. Someone grabs a guitar or a piano or, well, a harpsichord, and starts improvising or doodling around, and sometimes – deliberately or not – they create an odd-timed verse or chorus or hook or an entire song. Before the internet, I fancied myself a collector of odd time signatures. They can be found in classical music (famously, Bartok), in Jazz (famously, Take Five), in Pop/Rock, and probably in every other genre except Polka. Nowadays it’s easy to find lists and playlists and YouTubes and TikToks and whatnot showcasing them. Wikipedia has a kind of list which is, no doubt, very, very incomplete. Some random personal favorites are Rolled in a Newspaper by Teapacks (based on a Moroccan folk song), Snarky Puppy’s Lingus, Japanese Legend by Ariel Zilber, Led Zeppelin’s Black Dog and Genesis’ Firth of Fifth, but there are thousands out there. I think you can find dozens by Sting alone (here’s one). Even youthful musicals have songs you can challenge yourself to count along with. I’m a fool for those. (…)
